Third, pass ObserveInstrument to NestFactory.create() so the SDK attaches to the application before it starts handling traffic warning Fastify With FastifyAdapter (or any explicit adapter), the adapter takes the second argument, so the application options and therefore instrument move to the third typescript const app = await NestFactory.create ( AppModule, new FastifyAdapter(), { instrument ObserveInstrument }, ); Passing the options object as the second argument alongside an adapter silently drops them, and the SDK never attaches. That completes the integration. Once the application receives traffic, requests, errors, and traces appear in your project's dashboard within moments, with no exporter to configure and no schema to design. The same instrument option is accepted by NestFactory.createMicroservice() and NestFactory.createApplicationContext() , so workers and standalone applications are instrumented the same way. info Hint createObserveModule() itself takes an options object that controls how trace ids are generated, how error source context is captured, and which providers are instrumented see Trace correlation and Error source context below. Everything else is configured through ObserveModule.forRoot() . Configuring the module Beyond the credentials in the quick start, these options decide how the SDK identifies your application, where it sends what it records, and how much it tells you about itself. Authenticating and identifying the application Option Type Default Description appKey string required Written into .env as OBSERVE APP KEY by npx @nestjs/observe link , or generated from your project's API Keys page see First project. Keep it out of source control. appSecret string required Issued alongside appKey , the same way, and written as OBSERVE APP SECRET . Keep it out of source control. serviceId string required Identifies this application in your dashboard. If you run multiple instances of the same service, use a value unique per instance (hostname, container id) to tell them apart in the Profiler. serviceVersion string \ false inferred Identifies the deployment a semantic version, a commit hash, or any other identifier, at most 50 characters. When it isn't set, the SDK infers it at startup (see below); false reports none. Every request and job records the release that served it, which is what powers the Releases view each version compared against the one before it, and a verdict on what it changed. You usually don't need to set serviceVersion . When it isn't set, the SDK infers the release when the application starts, from the first of these that has one 1. OBSERVE SERVICE VERSION in the environment, for a deploy that wants to be explicit without touching code. 2. The commit your platform or CI exposes at runtime Vercel, Render, Railway, Heroku (with dyno metadata), Coolify, and Dokku, or GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Bitbucket Pipelines, CircleCI, Buildkite, Azure Pipelines, and AWS CodeBuild for an application a CI job boots. GIT COMMIT SHA , GIT COMMIT , GIT SHA , COMMIT SHA , and SOURCE VERSION are read too. 3. The commit checked out where the process runs , read from the repository's .git . 4. The revision a container platform names each deploy by Cloud Run's K REVISION , Azure Container Apps' CONTAINER APP REVISION . A container image built by your own pipeline usually carries none of these, since the build excludes .git and CI variables don't survive into the image. Hand it the commit at build time with ARG GIT SHA and ENV OBSERVE SERVICE VERSION=$GIT SHA in the Dockerfile. A serviceVersion you pass yourself wins over all of the above. An inferred commit is reported in full, as git rev parse HEAD prints it, and the dashboard shortens it for display; that full form is also what to pass as fixedInVersion when resolving an issue. Linking from the terminal npx @nestjs/observe link puts a key pair on a developer's machine without copying a secret out of the browser, and sets the SDK up in an application that doesn't use it yet. Run it in the project's directory (the one with package.json ), or point it there with cwd 1. It prints an eight letter code, such as BCDF GHJK , and opens observe.nestjs.com/link in your browser. With no browser , in CI, or without a terminal, it only prints the address. The code expires after 15 minutes. If the application doesn't use the SDK yet, the command also says, below the code, that it will install and wire it once you approve. 2. Type the code on that page. If you don't have an account yet, you sign up first; if you're signed out, you sign in. Either way, you come back to the code afterwards. 3. Check the request the page shows the hostname of the machine and the package name the command sent. Then choose where the key goes. The page proposes your newest project, and in it the application named after your package, or a new application if there isn't one yet. You can change both, including to a new project. 4. Approve. The dashboard issues a new API key for that application, and the command writes it into the project. In every project, the command changes up to three files .env receives OBSERVE APP KEY and OBSERVE APP SECRET , single quoted, replacing an earlier pair and leaving every other line as it was. A new .env is created readable only by you. The quotes are deliberate a key or secret can contain $ and & , which dotenv expand (or ConfigModule with expandVariables ) would rewrite, and at which a shell sourcing the file would stop. .gitignore gets a .env entry, unless the file is already ignored (as it is in a project generated by nest new ). package.json every script whose command begins with nest start gets env file .env start , start dev , and start debug in a project generated by nest new , and a monorepo's per application scripts as well. Scripts that already pass an env file are left alone, and so is start prod ( node dist/main ). A start or start dev script that starts the application some other way is left alone too, but the command names it, so you can load .env there yourself (for example, with node env file=.env ). In an application that doesn't use the SDK yet (no source file imports @nestjs/observe ), the command also sets the SDK up, the way nest new does The SDK is installed at the command's own version ( @nestjs/observe@^0.3.16 from 0.3.16). The command uses the package manager that the project's lockfile belongs to (pnpm, Yarn, Bun, or npm), looking up to the repository's root, so that a package in a workspace finds the root's lockfile. Without a lockfile, it uses the one named by the packageManager field in package.json , and npm otherwise. An @nestjs/observe that is already installed but older than the command is upgraded the same way. In that case, run npx @nestjs/observe@latest link , because plain npx runs the version installed in the project. The root module , the one main.ts passes to NestFactory.create() (found by following its import), gets the createObserveModule() call, and ObserveModule.forRoot() as the first entry of its imports . The options read the key pair from OBSERVE APP KEY and OBSERVE APP SECRET , and set serviceId to the name of the application you approved, lower cased, with spaces turned into dashes and any other punctuation dropped ( Cats API becomes cats api ). main.ts passes instrument ObserveInstrument to NestFactory.create() , inside its options object, or as a new options argument if there is none. The edits follow each file's quotes, semicolons, and indentation, and either both files change or neither does. The command lists them, so you can review them with git diff . In some projects, the command leaves the wiring to you and prints why; the Quick start shows the edits to make. It does so in a workspace with several applications (the key belongs to one of them), in a JavaScript project, and wherever it can't edit the code safely, for example when main.ts imports the root module through a path alias rather than a relative path, when imports isn't a plain array, or when an instrument option is already passed. If the installation fails, the command prints the install command for you to run yourself, and leaves the wiring to you as well. Before it asks for a code, the command turns away a project that it would have to install the SDK in but that has no @nestjs/core , or runs a NestJS version older than 11. Nothing is written until the key arrives, so a denied, expired, or interrupted link leaves the project unchanged. warning Warning Approve only a code you started yourself, and only when it matches your terminal. The code is typed rather than carried in a URL so that nobody can send you a link that approves a key for them. The key appears on the project's API Keys page like any other, named CLI followed by the time it was issued, and expires after a year; run the command again for a new one. .env stays on the machine that ran the command, so each teammate (or each additional machine) runs npx @nestjs/observe link as well and gets a key of its own for the same application. Reading the key pair from the environment When appKey or appSecret is unset or empty, or still holds the placeholder that nest new generates ( 'YOUR APP KEY' and 'YOUR APP SECRET' ), ObserveModule reads OBSERVE APP KEY or OBSERVE APP SECRET from the environment instead. This is what lets a project generated with Observe report once it's linked, without any change to AppModule . A value you pass yourself always wins, and the same fallback applies to the options that forRootAsync() resolves. The variables are read when the options are resolved (for forRoot() , when the AppModule file is imported), so they must already be in process.env at that point. The env file flag loads them before any module runs. In production, set OBSERVE APP KEY and OBSERVE APP SECRET in the environment (your platform's secrets or environment settings) rather than shipping .env . A project generated by nest new runs node dist/main for start prod , which doesn't load .env anyway, and nest start skips an env file that doesn't exist, so a fresh clone or a CI run without .env still starts. Give production a key of its own from the project's API Keys page, so revoking a development key never stops it from reporting. info Hint The link command and the environment fallback require @nestjs/observe 0.3.15 or later. Installing and wiring the SDK into an application that doesn't use it yet requires 0.3.16 or later. Turning the SDK off outside production To keep an environment from reporting local development, a CI run keep ObserveModule imported and switch it off with enabled , rather than passing fake credentials, which are sent and refused enabled false records and sends nothing no traces, runtime metrics, or logs, and no request to any collector and needs no credentials. The module stays in place, so TracerService can still be injected and calling it is harmless. Leaving the credentials unset also sends nothing, but logs a warning at every start, since in production that usually means the environment variables never reached the process. enabled requires @nestjs/observe 0.3.13 or later. Asynchronous configuration When the credentials come from a configuration provider rather than directly from process.env , use forRootAsync() . It accepts the same useFactory / inject , useClass , and useExisting shapes as every other Nest dynamic module (a class implements ObserveOptionsFactory with a createObserveOptions() method), plus extraProviders and global Collector endpoint endpoint (default 'https //observe api.nestjs.com' ) is the base URL of the collector. Telemetry and profiles share it, so the two can never point at different places. To override it without touching the config, set the OBSERVE ENDPOINT environment variable. NestJS Observe is a hosted service and observe api.nestjs.com is the only collector it runs; change the endpoint when your traffic has to leave through a forwarding proxy, or to point a test environment at a stub that accepts the batches. Debugging the SDK itself debug (default false ) logs additional diagnostic information from the SDK to the console. Use it while getting instrumentation working, and turn it off in production. Shutdown When the application closes app.close() , or a SIGTERM once app.enableShutdownHooks() has been called the SDK sends what it still holds before it stops the requests and jobs that finished since the last batch, their errors, the log lines buffered before shutdown began, and a last runtime sample. It waits at most shutdownFlushTimeout (default 2000 ms) for the collector, then lets the application exit; 0 skips the final send. Two things decide what makes it in Signals. Nest runs shutdown hooks on SIGTERM only if the application called app.enableShutdownHooks() at bootstrap. Without it, a deploy or a scale in ends the process at once, and the last few seconds of telemetry are lost. Module order. Global modules shut down in reverse order of import. A job still running at shutdown is reported only if ObserveModule comes before BullModule , and before any module that registers a queue, in your root module's imports . In test suites that boot the application with real credentials, set shutdownFlushTimeout 0 , so every app.close() doesn't send that test's requests to your project or wait on a collector the test environment can't reach. The final send requires @nestjs/observe 0.3.10 or later. Automatic instrumentation Everything in this section is recorded without any code of your own; installing the SDK is enough. The options only narrow it or switch it off. Database queries and outbound HTTP Since @nestjs/observe 0.3.0, database queries and outbound requests appear as spans with no configuration, nested under the method that made them. A slow repository call shows which statement it was waiting on. Databases are instrumented at the driver rather than the ORM pg , mysql2 , mssql , and mongodb are detected if your application already depends on them, which covers TypeORM, MikroORM, Drizzle, Mongoose, Knex, Sequelize, and Prisma's driver adapters without naming any of them. SQL Server is the exception mssql is what TypeORM and Prisma's SQL Server adapter run on, but Knex, Sequelize, and MikroORM talk to SQL Server through tedious directly, which isn't covered yet (nor is mssql/msnodesqlv8 ). ORMs that ship their own nested copy of a driver (MikroORM and Mongoose do, whenever versions disagree) are handled too. The driver's own housekeeping (connection handshakes, authentication, pings) is not recorded. A query span is labeled with its verb and table ( SELECT users ) and carries the statement with every literal removed strings, numbers, IN (...) lists, and comments are replaced before the span leaves the process, and bound parameters are never read at all. Repeated queries under one parent fold into a single node with a count, so an N+1 reads as SELECT order items ×47 rather than 47 rows. Other clients, Redis and Kafka among them, aren't instrumented at the library. A Nest application almost always registers them as providers, though an ioredis client from a factory, a ClientKafka from ClientsModule and the SDK records every provider's method calls each call on the client is a span under the method that made it, and one that returns a promise, as ioredis commands do, is timed until it settles. A client created and called outside dependency injection isn't recorded. Outbound HTTP is read from Node's own diagnostics channels, so fetch , undici , and everything built on node http (axios, got, most SDKs) are covered with nothing patched. The span is labeled GET api.example.com and carries the URL with sensitive query parameters masked. The SDK also sends the current trace id as x request id , which makes HTTP to HTTP tracing automatic. With the openTelemetry option on, it sends a W3C traceparent as well http.traceContext false keeps that header off, and propagateTraceId decides where both headers go. Set outgoing false to switch all of it off, or database false / http false individually. info Hint These spans are not billed . They are detail about a method span you already sent, so they don't count toward your Observability Events or your rate cap. A request that runs ten queries costs the same as before. Model calls Since @nestjs/observe 0.3.20, a fetch to a model provider also records what the call used on its outbound span the model, the input, output, and cached input tokens the provider's response states, and, for a stream, the time to its first event. OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini and Vertex AI, Amazon Bedrock, Mistral, Groq, OpenRouter, Together AI, DeepSeek, xAI, Cohere, and Perplexity are recognized by host, so the official SDKs, the Vercel AI SDK, and LangChain are all covered without being named. Read as the response passes through. The SDK reads the response at the pace your code does, streams included, and hands it on unchanged. A stream your code cancels is cancelled at the provider too. Prompts and completions are never sent. Only the model and the token counts leave the process. fetch only. A call made through node http axios, or the AWS SDK's default client for Bedrock keeps its ordinary outbound span without the model or tokens. A gateway in front of the providers (LiteLLM, Portkey, your own proxy) or a self hosted model with an OpenAI compatible API is added by host, and its calls are tagged with the provider custom . outgoing {{ '{' }} llm false {{ '}' }} stops reading model calls while keeping their plain spans A production rule can bound how many model calls a request makes. WebSocket gateways Messages handled by @SubscribeMessage() are reported as requests with the ws protocol and an operation id of GatewayClass pattern , on any platform adapter. The ws option block takes the same ignore , tags , setAttributes , and getUserId hooks as the other transports; each receives {{ '{' }} gateway, pattern, client, data {{ '}' }} . Connections and disconnections are not operations and are not reported. Queues @nestjs/bullmq and the original @nestjs/bull are both instrumented every processor run is reported as a job, with its queue wait, attempt number, and outcome. A job added from inside a traced operation inherits that operation's trace id see Distributed tracing. Runtime metrics and profiling runtimeMetrics (default true ) samples memory, CPU, garbage collection, and event loop latency on an interval ( runtimeMetricsInterval , default 60000 ms) and feeds the Profiler . The same samples double as the application's heartbeat a Telemetry silence alert fires when they stop arriving, which gives you lightweight uptime monitoring without an external probe. Errors and failed requests An error that escapes a controller, resolver, or job is captured automatically. These options decide what comes with it the source code around the failing frame, and the headers and body of the request that failed. Error source context Errors that propagate out of a controller, resolver, job, or span are captured automatically. When sourceContext is enabled (the default), the SDK also reads the source lines around each in app stack frame of a captured error and attaches them. This lets the dashboard show the failing code alongside the stack trace, even for a production failure on a build you don't have checked out. This is an option of createObserveModule() , not forRoot() . Set sourceContext false to disable it, or pass an object to tune the defaults Option Type Default Description linesOfContext number 5 Lines read on either side of the frame's line. maxFrames number 5 How many in app frames, counted from the top of the stack, get source attached. Bounds the payload on deep stacks. sourceMaps boolean false Resolves compiled frames back through source maps before reading source. Only needed if the process runs compiled output without Node's own source map support ( enable source maps or process.setSourceMapsEnabled(true) ); with that on, frames already carry original positions and this is redundant. Costs a map parse per compiled file on first touch, cached after. warning Warning Enabling this ships fragments of your application's source code (usually a few lines around the error) to your dashboard, where they are stored alongside the error. Frames inside node modules and Node internals are never read, only application source. Turn it off if shipping any source is not acceptable for your codebase. Capturing failed and slow requests When an HTTP request fails , the SDK records a small, fixed allow list of its headers alongside it user agent , content type , content length , accept , host , origin and referer . None of these authenticate or identify the caller. If you set slowerThanMs , requests that ran at least that long are captured the same way, failed or not. An ordinary request records nothing. Request bodies are off by default; turn them on explicitly if you want them Everything captured passes through redaction before it leaves the process sensitive keys ( password , token , authorization , ...) are masked by name inside the body, and naming a sensitive header records [REDACTED] instead of its value. capture false records nothing. The capture is shown on the request's detail page as a Request card. Logs and trace correlation Every execution gets a trace id. These options decide how your log lines relate to it forwarded to the dashboard, or only stamped with the id so your own log stack can link to the trace. Logs forwardLogs (default false ) sends your application's log lines (anything written through Nest's Logger ) to the dashboard, correlated to the trace that was active when each line was written. On an execution page, every line is placed on the trace's clock next to the span that was in flight when it was written. Log forwarding is available on Pro and above. Forwarding logs moves them onto infrastructure you don't control, so redaction is on by default. The same redaction also scrubs the message and stack of every captured error and any captured request data, whether or not forwardLogs is on redaction field Type Default Description enabled boolean true Whether anything is scrubbed at all. useDefaultPatterns boolean true Applies the built in patterns bearer tokens, JWTs, AWS key ids, PEM private keys, key=value secrets, and Luhn valid card numbers. Disable only if you're replacing them wholesale with your own patterns ; there's no supported case for forwarding logs unredacted. patterns RegExp[] Extra patterns to mask, for secrets shaped in a way only your codebase knows (internal token prefixes, customer identifiers). Always applied as if global, so a match is never limited to the first occurrence in a line. keys string[] Extra keys whose values are masked outright (in log attributes, captured headers and bodies, and URL query strings), on top of the built in list. Compared case insensitively and ignoring / , so apiKey , api key , and API KEY are one entry. replacement string '[REDACTED]' Text substituted for anything matched. info Hint Even with forwardLogs off, the SDK augments ConsoleLogger so every line written inside a traced execution carries its trace id ( attachTraceIdToLogs , see Trace correlation). That lets you correlate your own log aggregator with traces in the dashboard without shipping the log content anywhere. Trace correlation These are also options of createObserveModule() . They shape how requests get a trace id and how that id shows up in your own logs Option Type Default Description traceIdKey string 'traceId' The key used to store the trace id in the request context, for later retrieval through TracerService . traceIdGenerator (req unknown) = string Adopts a well formed x request id (HTTP header, or microservice packet metadata) if present, else a UUID v7 Generates the trace id per request. Called with the request object for HTTP; for other protocols it receives the transport context. attachTraceIdToLogs boolean true Augments ConsoleLogger to include the trace id in log messages, so logs can be correlated with traces even without forwardLogs . In the default text format the id ends the line, after the message ( Trace ID ); with JSON logging it is a traceId field. Lines written outside a traced execution are unchanged. Because the default generator adopts an incoming x request id , a chain of HTTP services already shares one trace with no extra configuration. Services instrumented with OpenTelemetry pass the trace on in traceparent instead, which the openTelemetry option of forRoot() reads and sends see Running beside OpenTelemetry. The same applies to the microservice transports TCP and Redis on @nestjs/microservices 12.0.4 or later, and NATS, Kafka, RabbitMQ, MQTT 5, and gRPC on 12.3.3 or later. Propagating across earlier versions and GraphQL takes a few lines see Distributed tracing. Shaping what is recorded These options enrich what the SDK records (who a request was for, what it concerned) and keep out what you don't need. Associating users with telemetry getUserId reads the incoming request and returns whatever identifier your system uses for a person a user id, an account id, or a tenant scoped id. Set it once and the Users view populates automatically The same option exists on rpc (receiving the transport id and the BaseRpcContext ), grpc (receiving the call object), graphql (receiving the GraphQL context, for operations with no enclosing HTTP request), and ws (receiving the gateway message), each reading the transport's own context instead of an HTTP request. Reporting a user identifier is optional traffic without one still shows up everywhere except the per user views. The dashboard treats the identifier as an opaque string and never tries to resolve it into a name or an email, so prefer an opaque internal id over anything personally identifying. Tags and custom attributes http , rpc , grpc , graphql , and jobs each accept the same two options for attaching your own data to every request they cover Option Applies Description tags The same static Record to every request Sent to Observe. For constants that don't vary per call, e.g., project , env , region . setAttributes A function of the request/call/job, returning key value pairs Kept in your application. For per call context your code reads later, e.g., a tenant id, a feature flag. tags appear as tags on the resulting request or job, and are searchable and visible on its detail page. setAttributes values are not sent to Observe and don't appear in the dashboard. As each call starts, they're written to its request scoped attributes, the same as calling setAttribute() for each key yourself, so any code handling that call can read them with getAttribute() . The function receives whatever the transport has the request for http , the transport id and BaseRpcContext for rpc , the call object for grpc , the resolve info and GraphQL context for graphql , and {{ '{' }} queueName, name, id {{ '}' }} for jobs . To see a per call value in the dashboard, add it as a tag on a span with TracerService (see Manual instrumentation) info Hint A GraphQL server is usually an HTTP endpoint, so its requests are already subject to the http options http.ignore drops a request before the GraphQL layer sees it, and http.getUserId supplies the user for queries over HTTP. The graphql block tunes what happens inside a request that was let through, per operation rather than per resolver, and graphql.getUserId is only consulted for operations that aren't already inside an HTTP trace, such as subscriptions over a WebSocket. Ignoring noisy operations Every inbound transport block ( http , rpc , grpc , graphql , and ws ) has an ignore option that skips instrumentation en
observability/manual-instrumentation: Manual instrumentation Most of the SDK is automatic instrumentation you configure it once and it decides what to record. TracerService is the manual half. Inject it anywhere in your application to add spans inside an already traced request, attach context to that request, capture errors you handled yourself, and report your own metrics. ObserveModule.forRoot() registers a global module that exports TracerService , so you can inject it in any module without importing ObserveModule again. ( forRootAsync() is global too, unless you pass global false .) Every method reads the trace from the ambient async context, so calling one outside of a request, job, or other instrumented operation throws there is no trace to attach to. This is deliberate, because a silently dropped span is harder to notice than an error. The exceptions are currentTraceId() , which returns null instead, and custom metrics, which aren't tied to a trace. Creating spans createSpan(name, callback) runs the callback inside a new span nested under the currently active one, and returns a promise of the callback's return value. The span's duration is the callback's duration, so await anything you want measured Spans nest by call stack a createSpan() inside another createSpan() callback becomes its child, which produces the waterfall on the trace detail page. The callback may be synchronous or asynchronous. Auto instrumented spans (controller methods, providers, database calls) and your custom spans share the same tree, so a hand named span appears exactly where it ran relative to everything else. The span argument is a TraceSpanDelegate . Its addTags(tags) method (or setTag(key, value) for a single entry) attaches key value pairs to that span alone. Like the tags option described in SDK → Tags and custom attributes, they're searchable and shown on the span in the trace view. The difference is scope that option covers every request, while these tags cover one span. activeSpan() resolves to the TraceSpanDelegate of the currently active span without creating a new one. Use it to tag the enclosing span from code that didn't create it It rejects if no span is active for the current trace. info Hint The Spans analytics view aggregates by span name, across every route that calls them. Pick names that describe the work ( orders.recalculate , cache.lookup ) rather than the caller, so the dashboard can tell you whether something is slow everywhere or only from one endpoint. Capturing handled errors Errors that propagate out of a controller, job, or span are recorded automatically. captureError() is for the ones that don't anything you caught and handled but still want visible in the dashboard The error is attached to the current trace, with the optional tags recorded alongside it, and gets the same source context treatment as any other captured error if sourceContext is enabled. Request scoped attributes setAttribute(key, value) and getAttribute(key) write and read the trace's own context store. Its values live for the duration of the request and are readable from anywhere downstream, without threading them through every function signature getAttribute() returns undefined for a key that was never set. Both throw when called outside a traced context. The trace id lives in the same store, so getAttribute(traceIdKey) retrieves the current trace id, e.g., to correlate with an external system or to propagate it to another service. currentTraceId() is a shorthand for that lookup with one deliberate difference it returns null outside a traced context instead of throwing, because forwarding a trace id downstream can legitimately happen when there is no trace yet. To type the store, pass its shape as TracerService 's first type argument. Keys and values are then checked against it, including nested paths info Hint ObserveModule also exports the AsyncLocalStorage instance that holds the trace context. setAttribute() / getAttribute() are the supported way to reach it; inject the store directly only if you need something they don't expose. If you already use the pattern described in the Async local storage recipe, this store can replace your hand rolled one. Custom metrics Three metric types are available, each created by name (or retrieved, if the name already exists). They report into the Custom section of the dashboard, and you can alert on them like any built in metric. Unlike the methods above, metrics aren't tied to a trace, so you can report them from anywhere, including startup and shutdown code, onModuleInit() hooks, and cron jobs. Method For Reporting method counter Values that only go up requests served, orders placed, retries attempted increment() gauge Values that go up and down queue depth, active connections, cache ratio increment() , decrement() , setValue(value) summary Distributions you want quantiles over latency, payload size observe(value) Calling counter('orders.placed') twice returns the same instance, so you don't need to hold a reference in a field, though doing so is cheaper on a hot path. Passing attributes on a later call updates the existing metric's description and labels in place. Attribute Applies to Description description counter, gauge, summary Shown alongside the metric in the dashboard. Worth setting a bare metric name rarely explains itself to a future reader. labels counter, gauge, summary Dimensions the metric is broken down by, so the chart can be split rather than showing one aggregate line. initialValue counter, gauge Starting value. Only applied while the metric is still at 0 , so a restart time declaration doesn't clobber a value already counted. kind gauge 'ratio' (default) for values that stand alone per report, or 'additive' for values that sum across reporting instances. sampleSize summary How many observations per label are retained to compute quantiles from, which bounds the summary's memory under load. A metric that has been declared but never reported reads as "unknown" rather than 0 in the dashboard. This is a real state, not missing data "we have never heard from this metric" and "this metric is currently zero" are different facts, and showing the second in place of the first would hide a broken deploy. API summary Method Needs a trace Description createSpan(name, callback) ✓ Run callback inside a new child span; returns its result activeSpan() ✓ Resolves to the TraceSpanDelegate of the span in flight captureError(error, tags?) ✓ Record a handled error on the current trace setAttribute(key, value) ✓ Write to the request scoped context store getAttribute(key) ✓ Read from the request scoped context store currentTraceId() ✗ The active trace id, or null outside a trace counter(name, attributes?) ✗ Get or create a monotonically increasing metric gauge(name, attributes?) ✗ Get or create a metric that can go up and down summary(name, attributes?) ✗ Get or create a distribution metric with quantiles Where to go next Distributed tracing use currentTraceId() to keep one trace across service boundaries. Dashboard where spans, captured errors, and custom metrics show up.
observability/distributed-tracing: Distributed tracing A trace is everything your applications recorded under a single trace id the request or job that started it, and every span underneath. Within a single service this is automatic. The SDK generates a trace id when work starts, and every span underneath, including ones you add manually with TracerService , inherits it. Across services, it depends on the channel. HTTP calls and queue jobs carry the trace id on their own, and so do the built in microservice transports on a recent enough @nestjs/microservices (12.0.4 for TCP and Redis, 12.3.3 for NATS, Kafka, RabbitMQ, MQTT 5, and gRPC). On earlier versions, the trace id needs forwarding. A single user action that touches more than one service (an API call that fans out to a gRPC service, or a message sent to another application over a microservice transport) shows up as one trace in your dashboard only if every service involved uses the same trace id. Otherwise, each service mints its own via traceIdGenerator , and the action shows up as several disconnected traces, one per service. Where forwarding is needed, it is application code, not a dashboard setting, and the pattern is always the same the caller puts its current trace id on whatever channel the protocol has, and the callee's traceIdGenerator reads it back out. This page shows how for each transport. Reading the current trace id To forward a trace id downstream, a service first reads the one it's currently running under. TracerService.currentTraceId() returns it It reads from the same context store as getAttribute() / setAttribute() , but unlike those it doesn't throw outside a traced context. It returns null instead, so code that forwards a trace id from startup hooks or other untraced paths doesn't need a try / catch . If your code can run outside a trace, check for null before setting a header. HTTP to HTTP HTTP propagation is automatic in both directions. On the way in, the default traceIdGenerator adopts a well formed x request id header and otherwise mints a time ordered UUID (v7). On the way out, the SDK adds the current trace id as x request id to outbound requests that don't already carry one, so a call from one instrumented service to another lands in the same trace with no application code. Outbound propagation covers fetch and undici , including the HTTP client, on every supported Node version, and clients built on node http (axios, got, @nestjs/axios ) on Node 22.12 and later, the first release that lets a header be added after the request object is created. To limit which hosts receive the header, or switch it off, see outgoing.http.propagateTraceId . On an older Node version with an axios based client, register a request interceptor once to forward the id yourself info Hint Many reverse proxies and load balancers (nginx, Envoy, AWS ALB) can set x request id on every inbound request. When they do, the trace id in your dashboard matches the request id in your proxy's access logs. With the openTelemetry option on, a W3C traceparent takes precedence over an x request id that names a different trace. OpenTelemetry and W3C Trace Context Services instrumented with OpenTelemetry pass the trace on in the W3C traceparent header rather than in x request id . With the openTelemetry option on, the SDK reads traceparent on the way in, and the trace id it names becomes the request's trace id. On the way out, it sends traceparent beside x request id . A Nest service then joins the traces the services around it share, whatever language they're written in. See Running beside OpenTelemetry. gRPC gRPC has no headers, only metadata. On @nestjs/microservices 12.3.3 or later, the trace id travels in it on its own the SDK adds the current trace id as x request id metadata to every call made through a ClientGrpc registered as a provider (e.g., with ClientsModule ), and the default traceIdGenerator of the gRPC service adopts it, so no application code is needed. Metadata you pass to a call yourself wins an x request id in it is the one the service adopts. With the openTelemetry option on, the metadata carries a W3C traceparent too, so a gRPC server instrumented with OpenTelemetry, in any language, continues the trace. On earlier versions, the caller attaches the trace id as metadata, and the gRPC service overrides traceIdGenerator to read it back out, since the default generator doesn't read gRPC metadata there See the gRPC chapter for how metadata is read and written on both sides of a call. TCP, Redis, NATS, and other microservice transports Every built in microservice transport carries the trace id on its own, once both services run a recent enough @nestjs/microservices , with @nestjs/observe 0.3.0 or later Transport From @nestjs/microservices The trace id travels TCP, Redis 12.0.4 inside the packet NATS 12.3.3 as a message header Kafka 12.3.3 as a record header RabbitMQ 12.3.3 in the message's headers property MQTT 12.3.3, over MQTT 5 ( protocolVersion 5 ) as a user property gRPC 12.3.3 as call metadata (see gRPC) The SDK attaches the current trace id, as x request id , to every packet sent through a ClientProxy registered as a provider (e.g., with ClientsModule ), and the default traceIdGenerator on the receiving side adopts it, so no application code is needed. On the transports that carry it as a header, a header of the same name that your code sets itself, on a record builder or in the client's headers or userProperties option, wins over the SDK's. Because the id is a plain x request id header there, a service that isn't written with Nest can read it, or send one to a Nest service. With the openTelemetry option on, a W3C traceparent travels beside it the same way, so such a service instrumented with OpenTelemetry, in any language, continues the trace. On an earlier @nestjs/microservices , and over MQTT 3.1.1, which has no user properties, the trace id doesn't travel on its own, and each service starts its own trace. If you can't upgrade, forward the id in a header the transport does carry ( NatsRecordBuilder setHeaders() , RmqRecordBuilder setOptions({{ '{' }} headers {{ '}' }}) , a Kafka message's headers ), and override traceIdGenerator to read it back from the context the transport hands it The generator receives the transport's context object, so the same code works for request response ( send() ) and event based ( emit() ) messages. A custom transport carries the id like the built in ones when its client sends a packet's metadata along with it, and its context returns that from a getMetadata() method the default generator adopts an x request id from there. warning Warning The same traceIdGenerator is called with HTTP requests and RPC contexts alike. In a hybrid application that serves both HTTP and a microservice transport, write the generator defensively check for headers first, then fall back to the transport's context. GraphQL No extra configuration is needed when the GraphQL server sits behind the same service's HTTP layer. It joins whatever trace the HTTP agent already opened for that request, which may itself have been propagated via x request id as described above. Only operations with no enclosing HTTP trace, such as a subscription over a raw WebSocket, need separate handling, and there's currently no built in propagation hook for that case. Queue jobs (BullMQ and Bull) Queue propagation is automatic. When a job is added from inside a traced operation (a request handler, an RPC handler, another job), the SDK stamps the current trace id onto the job's options, and the processor that picks the job up runs under that id instead of minting its own. The request and every job it enqueued render as one trace, with no application code involved This works the same way for @nestjs/bullmq and @nestjs/bull , for add() and addBulk() , and whether the worker runs in the same process as the producer or in a separate service the id travels through Redis with the job. A retried job keeps the id it was enqueued with, so every attempt lands in the same trace. Two cases deliberately start a trace of their own Repeatable jobs and @nestjs/schedule handlers. A schedule outlives the operation that registered it, so each firing is its own trace rather than part of an ever growing trace attached to whichever request set the schedule up. Jobs added outside any traced operation , e.g., from a bootstrap hook or a plain script. There is no trace to inherit. info Hint The trace id is stored under the observeTraceId job option. To attach a job to a trace the SDK did not see (e.g., one enqueued by a non Nest producer), set that option yourself when adding the job. With the openTelemetry option on, from @nestjs/observe 0.3.23, a job also carries the W3C trace context it was added in, under the observeTraceparent job option, and the processor runs in it. An OpenTelemetry SDK in the process that runs the job then continues the request's trace the job's spans in your OpenTelemetry backend, and the services the job calls, are in the same trace as the request, as the job is in Observe. With BullMQ's own OpenTelemetry add on, bullmq otel , on the queue and the worker, the processor runs in the consumer span the add on opens, a span of the same trace, and from @nestjs/observe 0.3.24 the job's spans nest under it. warning Warning Trace inheritance for jobs requires @nestjs/observe 0.3.0 or later on both the service that adds the job and the service that processes it. With an older producer, jobs carry no id and each run opens its own trace, as before. What a trace looks like in the dashboard Once services agree on a trace id, the trace detail page renders every execution that ran under it, across services, requests, and jobs, as one waterfall nesting depth as indentation, duration as bar length, and horizontal position as when the span ran. When reading it, keep the following in mind Self time is the number that matters. A span's duration minus the time its children account for is the time the span spent in its own code. Ranking by total duration always puts the controller at the top (it contains everything); ranking by self time surfaces the repository call that actually burned the time. Every execution page carries a spans table sorted this way. Overlapping children are flagged. When a span's children sum to more than the span's own duration, they ran concurrently ( Promise.all , a parallel fan out) and the row says so. Failing spans are marked , and the execution page leads with an error card for the first span that threw class, message, the trimmed stack trace with the throwing frame marked, and the source lines around it when sourceContext is on. Logs sit on the trace's clock. With forwardLogs enabled, each line is placed at its offset from the start of the trace and labeled with the span that was in flight when it was written; hovering a line marks that instant on the waterfall. From any failed or unusually slow execution, the Copy agent prompt button packages the whole page (context, error, stack trace with source, top spans by self time, and logs) as a self contained markdown prompt for a coding agent. See Dashboard.
observability/error-monitoring: Error monitoring Error monitoring is included in every NestJS Observe plan, Free included, and needs nothing beyond the SDK. Once your application is instrumented, every error that escapes a controller, resolver, or queue consumer is captured with the request it broke, the code that threw it, and the trace it ran in. This page covers what gets captured, how occurrences are grouped into defects, how you get told about a new one, and how an error turns into a verified fix. info Hint To see it before installing anything, open the live demo. It shows a busy service's errors, grouped defects, and stack traces with source, with no signup. What is captured Errors that propagate out of a controller, resolver, job, or span are recorded automatically, across HTTP, GraphQL, gRPC, and @nestjs/microservices transports, and for queue consumers and cron runs. There is no error handler to register and nothing to call from your exception filters. A filter still decides what the client sees, and the SDK observes the failure on its way there, so the two work side by side. An error is not stored as a detached log line. An individual error is the failed request, so its detail page is the request's own page with the failure leading error class, message, stack trace, and source code first, then the request's context, then the trace waterfall and the logs written during that request. When an HTTP request fails, the SDK also records a small allow list of its headers, and optionally its body (see Capturing failed and slow requests). A job run that throws is recorded as a failed run, with its failure reason and attempt number, in the Jobs view. Not every error is a bug. An exception your code throws on purpose, such as a NotFoundException or a failed validation, still shows up in the Errors view, since it is still a failed request, but it doesn't count as a new defect for alerting. Only unhandled failures do an error whose request answered with a 5xx, or one that failed on an entry point with no HTTP status at all, such as an RPC handler or a gateway message. Source context A stack trace from production usually points at compiled output you don't have checked out. With sourceContext enabled (the default), the SDK reads the source lines around each in app frame of a captured error and sends them with it, so the dashboard shows the failing code next to the stack trace To see your TypeScript rather than the compiled JavaScript, run Node with source map support ( enable source maps , or process.setSourceMapsEnabled(true) ), or set sourceContext.sourceMaps true to have the SDK resolve compiled frames itself. Frames inside node modules and Node internals are never read. See Error source context for every option. warning Warning Source context ships a few lines of your application's source code to your dashboard, stored alongside the error. Set sourceContext false if shipping any source is not acceptable for your codebase. Handled errors An error you catch and recover from never propagates, so it is never captured automatically. When you still want it visible, report it with captureError() on TracerService The error is attached to the current trace with the optional tags recorded alongside it, and gets the same source context as any other captured error. See Capturing handled errors. Grouping errors into defects A spike of 3,140 TypeError s is one bug, not 3,140. The Group into defects switch on the Errors page collapses occurrences with the same exception class and the same normalized stack shape into one error group , fingerprinted server side, regardless of how the message was worded, which line numbers moved, or which deploy produced it. A group carries what triage needs, rather than the details of a single occurrence Field What it tells you Class and sample message What the defect is, taken from its first occurrence Status Open, Resolved, or Ignored First and last seen Whether it's new, ongoing, or has gone away Introduced in The release the first occurrence ran on, when it reported one Occurrences How often it fired in the selected window, not all time Issue The issue it was promoted to, if any Introduced in comes from the serviceVersion your application reports (a semantic version or a commit hash, passed to forRoot() ). Without it, a group can't tell which deploy it arrived with. The two closed states are deliberately asymmetric. Resolved is a claim about the code, so a resolved group reopens as soon as the error recurs; a fix that didn't hold surfaces instead of staying quietly green. Ignored is a decision about noise, and stays ignored. Getting notified Every plan, Free included, gets a built in new error email with no rule to set up one email per project listing the errors it has never seen before, at most six a day. Each member can switch it off for themselves under Settings → New error emails . Free also watches each application that runs around the clock for an unusual error rate, with at most one alert email per account every 30 days. On paid plans, alert rules go further, starting with an unusual error rate rule that every application gets on its own A new error groups rule fires when a defect appears for the first time, for one application or the whole project. It notifies through email, Slack, a webhook, or an in app notification, or by opening an issue. An error rate rule watches the share of requests that failed with a server error (5xx) for an application, or for one route and method, against a fixed threshold or against its own recent baseline with anomaly detection. A job failure rate rule does the same for queue consumers and cron runs. On the higher tiers, an availability SLO (the share of requests that finished without an unhandled error) turns the same errors into an error budget with burn rate alerts. From an error to a fix Because each error already carries its stack trace, source lines, trace, and logs, Copy agent prompt on its page packages all of it into a self contained prompt for a coding agent such as Claude Code, Cursor, or any other tool that has your repository open. An agent connected to the MCP server can go further on its own list error groups with their introducing release, pull recent occurrences with their trace ids, tell whether an error is growing or decaying, and see which users it affected. To track the work, promote an error group into an issue in one click; promoting a group that already has an open issue links to it instead of opening a second one. Before you resolve it, Did a release fix this? on the issue answers from production it judges a release on its own requests, on the routes the error failed on, against how often the error failed there before. An agent asks the same question with verify fix over the MCP server. When you mark the issue resolved (optionally naming the release the fix shipped in), the dashboard watches the affected operation against its pre incident baseline, and either closes the issue once the fix has held or reopens it with the reading that broke it. After a deploy, the Releases view compares each serviceVersion against the one before it, error rate included, so a regression shows up as a difference between two versions rather than as a bump somewhere in a week long chart. Each release's verdict also lists the error groups first seen in it.
observability/dashboard: Dashboard Once an application is instrumented and sending data, its project dashboard fills in automatically, with no queries to write and no dashboards to build. This chapter covers what each view shows, how the views relate to each other, and how the features built on top of the telemetry (release verdicts, status pages, alerts, SLOs, issues, and the agent handoff) fit together. For the full reference, see the NestJS Observe documentation. info Hint Every view described below can be clicked through in the live demo, which runs the dashboard over a generated dataset from a busy service realistic request volumes, traces with waterfalls, errors, jobs, and alerts. It needs no account and runs entirely in your browser. How the views nest Almost every telemetry view belongs to one of three levels, and you move between them by clicking through 1. Analytics the list view. Every route, job, span, or metric your applications reported in the selected window, aggregated throughput, latency, failure rate. This is where you notice something. 2. Operation one route ( GET /orders/ id ), one job name, one span name. The same numbers over time, plus the list of individual executions behind them. This is where you confirm the shape of a problem constant or spiky, everywhere or one release. 3. Execution a single request, a single job run, a single span invocation. Its exact duration, status, user, tags, the error it raised, the waterfall of everything it did, and the logs it wrote. This is where you diagnose. Aggregates tell you that something is wrong and how much it matters; a single execution tells you why . Every view shares one control bar (a time range and an optional application filter), and everything on the page follows it. Telemetry views View What it shows Requests Every HTTP, GraphQL, gRPC, microservice and WebSocket gateway request, broken down by operation. A request detail page compares the call against the route's own baseline ("slower than 95% of calls") and, when the process was struggling, states by how much host pressure slowed this operation. Services Time spent per NestJS class and method , split into own time (with everything awaited subtracted out) and total time. Only instrumented classes appear, so a short list means low coverage, not low traffic. Errors Every unhandled error, grouped by operation, with the failure leading the page class, message, stack trace, and source code. The Group into defects switch collapses occurrences with the same class and stack shape into one fingerprinted group with first/last seen and the release that introduced it. See Error monitoring. Jobs Background work queue consumers, cron runs with queue wait time, attempt number, and failure reason alongside duration and failure rate. Spans Analytics over the custom spans your code creates with TracerService.createSpan() , across every route that calls them "how slow is OrdersService.recalculate everywhere", rather than "how slow is this one endpoint". The spans the SDK records on its own are read in each execution's waterfall instead. Traces The waterfall for a trace id, across every service that shares it see Distributed tracing. Users Per user activity when getUserId is configured failure rate per user, calls grouped into the actions they performed, a replay of each action, and the paths between them. A Group by customer switch rolls identities up by email domain. Custom Counters, gauges, and summaries reported through TracerService , grouped by metric name and labels. Releases Each serviceVersion compared against the one before it error rate, latency, and throughput side by side with a verdict on whether the deploy made things worse or changed what the code does. See Releases and their verdicts. Logs Everything your services logged (with forwardLogs on), correlated to the traces they ran in. On an execution page, each line is placed on the trace's clock next to the span that was in flight. Profiler CPU, memory, event loop delay and utilization, and garbage collection per application, with per instance comparison when an application runs on more than one node. Click a spike on the Memory or Event loop delay chart to see which operations ran at that moment, ranked by deviation from their baseline. Rules Production rules what a request or job may do, checked against every kept trace, with the traces that broke each rule and the release they came from. Paid plans. Queries, outbound calls, and captured requests In a trace's waterfall, a database query or an outbound HTTP request is a row of its own under the method that made it an icon, the operation ( SELECT orders , POST api.stripe.com ), and the statement or URL beside it, visible without hovering. The row's caret opens the full statement laid out by clause, with its placeholders highlighted and a copy button. Values never appear, because the agent removes them before anything is sent. The spans table beneath lists only your application's methods; the agent's query spans are left out and their time counts as the calling method's own, so the table still answers "which of my methods took the time". The Services page follows the same rule drivers ( pg , mysql2 , mongodb , http ) are not listed as classes, and a query's wait counts as the own time of the method that ran it. When the agent kept a request's own inputs (because it failed, or ran past the slowerThanMs threshold you configured), the request's Details card has two extra folded rows, Request headers and Request body . A request with nothing captured has no such rows. The service map A project's Activity → Map page shows how its applications, queues, and databases talk to each other. Applications and queues run left to right in call order, and the databases and external services each one depends on hang beneath it. A line's thickness and the speed of the traffic along it show volume. Soft red marks an error rate above 1%, full red above 5%, and teal means healthy. Hover over any node to isolate what it touches, and click it for its numbers for a database, the statements the time went to; for an application, what it calls and what calls it, with a link to its requests. The map needs no configuration and collects nothing new. Databases and external hosts come from the agent's query and outbound HTTP spans, queues from the jobs an application works, and the dashed lines between applications from executions that share a trace id. Each application gets one database node per driver, so two services on Postgres usually show as two databases, since nothing on the wire says they share one. An external host, by contrast, is a single node shared by every caller, up to the eight busiest per application. An application with no lines at all is almost always running an SDK older than 0.3.0 , which does not report queries or outbound calls. info Hint Links between applications are inferred from the most recent requests rather than counted over the whole window. Read a dashed line as "this calls that", not as an exact total. Releases and their verdicts The Releases view lists every serviceVersion your applications reported. Open one and it leads with a verdict whether the deploy made things worse, and whether anything behaves differently since, in one word and one sentence. Regression server errors (5xx) rose across the release boundary by more than noise. Changed server errors didn't rise, but the release does something new an error group first seen in it, a route that went quiet, or a change in what the code calls. Clean none of that. The sentence says what was compared, so a clean verdict over too little telemetry doesn't read as more than it is. Not enough data too few requests either side to judge. Under the verdict is the evidence it rests on the error groups first seen in the release, the routes that served steadily before the boundary and nothing after (requests are never sampled, so a route that went quiet really stopped), the outbound hosts, query shapes, and methods only one side of the boundary called, and caveats to read first sampled spans, or a rolling deploy whose numbers describe a mix of versions. What changed in the code then lists the queries, outbound calls, and methods whose behavior moved by more than noise New or Gone , a statement made 44× more often per request a new N+1 usually reads exactly like this, long before it moves a p95 or a method whose own time is 7.6× slower . A call the release added, or now makes more often, offers Pin as a rule , which starts a production rule that names the next release to break it. None of this collects anything extra it reads the same request rows and per method telemetry as the rest of the dashboard. An agent gets the same verdict over the MCP server with get release verdict . Status pages On Pro and above, an application can have a public status page its availability and p95 response time for each day your plan keeps, up to 90, at an address you can hand to the people who use it. On the Applications list, click the broadcast icon on the application's row, or choose Status page from its menu, and switch it on Write or Admin access is enough. Withdraw it from the same place; publishing it again brings back the same address. Show response times is on by default; with it off, the page shows availability alone. Availability is the share of requests that didn't fail with a server error (5xx); client errors (4xx) don't count against it. A day is Operational at 99.5% or more, shows Elevated errors from 95%, and Major errors below that; a day with fewer than 20 requests shows its figure without a state. The page never shows how much traffic the application gets, and it never calls an application down for something Observe did a day with no requests recorded says exactly that, and a day when overage collection was paused is marked partially recorded and left out of the figures. The page refreshes every minute and stays out of search engines. Handing a failure to a coding agent Reading a trace tells you what happened. The next step is always the same find that code and change it. The Copy agent prompt button does that handoff in one click. It copies the entire page as a self contained markdown prompt, ready to paste into Claude Code, Cursor, or any other tool that has your repository open. The button appears only where there is something to investigate a request or job that failed or ran slower than 95% of its peers, or a trace containing an error. The prompt carries the task framing, the operation context, the error with its trimmed stack trace and source lines (paths rewritten relative to your project root, so src/orders/orders.service.ts 35 rather than /var/app/current/dist/orders/orders.service.js 35 ), how the call compares to the operation's average and p95, the top spans by self time, up to 40 log lines chosen errors first, and closing instructions asking the agent to explain the root cause from the code and propose a fix as a diff with tests. For an agent that needs to keep asking questions (follow a trace into its logs, check whether an error is still firing), connect it to the MCP server instead. Alerts Alerts notify you when your telemetry crosses a threshold you care about, so you don't find out from a customer. A rule watches one metric from one of these families Family Metrics Scoped to Request Error rate, p95 latency, avg latency, throughput An application, and optionally one route + method Job Job failure rate, job throughput, p95 queue wait An application, and optionally one job name + queue Absence Telemetry silence, job silence An application, or one job name + queue Logs Matching log lines A pattern, and optionally levels + logger context Errors New error groups An application, or the whole project Runtime Event loop delay, CPU usage, memory usage An application (sampled per process) Custom Any custom metric your application reports A metric name, and optionally one label SLO SLO burn rate The SLO itself Production rules Production rule violations One rule, or every rule in a project or application Error rate counts server errors (5xx) alone. A 4xx is the client's a crawler's 404, an expired session's 401, a failed validation so it never trips an error rate rule, though it still shows on the Requests and Errors views. Every rule runs in one of two modes a fixed threshold ("error rate above 5%"), or anomaly detection , which fires when the metric deviates from its own recent baseline by more than a sensitivity you set. Anomaly mode is often the better choice for runtime metrics a fixed CPU threshold that's right for one service is wrong for the next, but "unlike its own recent baseline" applies to both. Two families depend directly on SDK instrumentation Absence detection. A Telemetry silence rule watches the runtime heartbeat the SDK's runtimeMetrics sampler emits even when the application is otherwise idle, and fires once it has been silent longer than a tolerance you set (2 minutes to 7 days). A Job silence rule does the same for one named job, e.g., a cron that didn't run. The same mechanism gives you both lightweight uptime monitoring without an external probe and cron monitoring. A scope that has never reported anything doesn't fire "not yet integrated" isn't "down". Log pattern alerts count log lines containing a substring within the window ("alert me when payment declined appears more than 10 times in 15 minutes"), and require forwardLogs to be on. A rule can notify through email , Slack (incoming webhook), a generic webhook , an in app notification, or by creating an issue pre filled with the rule's severity and scope. Rules can carry a recurring mute schedule for quiet hours, and every state transition (OK → Firing → Resolved) is recorded with per channel delivery status. Starter alerts. A paid plan doesn't start empty. When it begins, and whenever an application is added to a project it pays for, each application gets two rules that email the account's owner and show in app Unusual error rate an anomaly rule on the error rate over 15 minutes. It never fires on a baseline too thin to judge, and waits for 20 requests and 5 more server errors than the application usually has, so a single failed request isn't an alert. Went quiet a telemetry silence rule with a 15 minute tolerance, added once the application has reported around the clock for a week, so a laptop that sleeps overnight doesn't page anyone. They are ordinary rules edit their channels or thresholds, switch them off, or delete them. On Free, which has no alert rules, the same two are watched for you an application that runs around the clock is checked for an unusual error rate and for going quiet, with at most one alert email per account every 30 days. New errors. A new error groups rule fires when an error Observe has never seen before appears. It counts unhandled failures only a group whose first occurrence answered with a 5xx, or failed on an entry point with no HTTP status (an RPC handler, a gateway message). An error your code threw on purpose, such as a NotFoundException or a failed validation, still appears in the Errors view but doesn't count as a new bug. Every plan, Free included, also gets a built in new error email without creating a rule one email per project listing the new errors, at most six a day. Each person can switch it off under Settings → New error emails . SLOs SLOs turn "error rate above 5%" into "we promised 99.9% and we're spending the budget too fast". They're objectives over telemetry you already collect, so no new instrumentation is required. An SLO is built from three layered concepts SLI (service level indicator) a ratio of good events to total events over a window, measuring availability (requests without an unhandled error), latency (requests under a threshold you set), or job success. Objective the SLI plus a target percentage (90 99.999%) over a rolling compliance window of 7, 14, 28, or 30 days. Error budget how much room you have to miss the target ( 1 − target ), and burn rate , how fast that budget is being spent. A burn rate of 1.0 spends it exactly on schedule; 14.4 means a 28 day budget would be gone in about two days. An SLO can also be declared next to the handler it covers, with @Objective() , so it is reviewed and versioned with the route. A burn rate alert is a regular alert rule pointed at an SLO instead of a raw metric. Typical starting points are a fast burn rule (1 hour window, 14.4×), a slow burn rule (6 hours, 6×), and a trickle rule (3 days, 1×). A compliance window can't exceed how long your plan retains telemetry. Issues Issues are lightweight, project scoped tracking for the work that comes out of your telemetry, such as a recurring error worth fixing or a latency regression to investigate. Create them by hand from any execution page, promote an error group into one, or let a firing alert open one automatically. An issue links to the request, error, job, or trace it came from, so anyone opening it later has the telemetry in context, not only a description of it. Every issue linked to telemetry opens with its incident record what it was about (the error class, route, or job, and the alert rule that raised it), when it started and ended, the release it came in with, who it reached users, and the customer companies behind their email domains and the release that fixed it, on one timeline. Copy summary puts the whole record on your clipboard as plain text, for the postmortem, the status update, or the note to a customer. An issue promoted from an error group also answers Did a release fix this? Pick a release, and the answer is judged on that release's own requests, on the routes the error failed on, against how often it failed there before Fixed , Not fixed , Too early to tell , or Not enough data . It shows the error groups first seen in the release on the same routes too, because a fix that only moved where the error is thrown gives it a new fingerprint. The counts come from request rows, which are never sampled, so the answer is there as soon as the release has served enough of those routes. An agent asks the same question with verify fix . When you mark an issue resolved and it names something measurable (an operation, an alert rule's scope), the dashboard watches that operation's telemetry against its pre incident baseline and tells you whether the fix held. It moves the issue to Verifying , then either closes it on its own or moves it back to Open with the reading that broke it. After 7 days with nothing conclusive usually too little traffic to judge it says so with Unverified , and you close the issue by hand. If you name the release the fix shipped in (your serviceVersion ), verification waits until that release shows up in telemetry. A worked path through the dashboard The views are designed to be used in order. A typical investigation 1. An alert fires, or the Requests chart shows p95 climbing. 2. Sort the route list by duration or failure rate to find which operation moved. 3. Open the operation. Is it constant or spiky? Did it start at a deploy? Check Releases , and the release's verdict. 4. Open a single execution from the tail of the distribution, e.g., one the baseline card calls slower than 95% of calls . 5. Read the waterfall which span holds the self time? 6. If it failed, read the error card stack trace and the source lines around the throw. 7. Check the logs for that trace, hovering lines to line them up with the spans. 8. Copy the agent prompt and hand the whole thing to a coding agent, or open an issue linked to the execution so whoever picks it up starts where you stopped. The same path is available to an agent over the MCP server, one tool per step, when you'd rather ask questions than click through views.
observability/production-rules: Production rules A production rule says what one request or job may do, such as how many queries or model calls it makes, and NestJS Observe checks every kept trace against it. Some bugs never throw. A retry charges a card twice, a new relation loads one row per product, an agent loop calls the model forty times every request returns 200 , every test passes, and the dashboards stay green until the invoice, the latency, or a customer says otherwise. A production rule writes down what one request or job may do "checkout charges the payment provider exactly once", "the product list runs at most three queries", "no request makes more than five LLM calls" and every kept trace is checked against it as it arrives. The trace that breaks a rule, and the release it came from, are in front of you the moment it happens. When a coding agent wrote the change, a rule is the cheapest review there is one sentence of what production must keep doing, checked on every deploy without anyone re reading the diff. Rules need no new instrumentation they read the spans the SDK already records your methods, the agent's database query and outbound HTTP spans, and LLM calls. They are included in every paid plan, up to 25 per project, under Activity → Rules in the dashboard. Members with Write or Admin access create and edit them; Read members see them. If a plan lapses, its rules are kept but no longer checked, and checking resumes once the project is on a paid plan again. Rules worth writing What must hold The rule What breaking it usually means A payment is taken once POST /checkout/ orderId/pay calls POST api.stripe.com exactly once A retry or a duplicated handler charging twice, or a refactor that stopped charging The product list doesn't N+1 GET /products runs pg SELECT products at most 3 times A relation now loaded once per row An endpoint stays cheap to run Every request makes LLM calls at most 5 times A tool or agent loop that keeps calling the model Admin changes are audited PATCH /admin/users/ id calls AuditLogService.record at least once A new code path that skips the audit write A job sends one digest The send digest job calls POST api.postmarkapp.com exactly once A job retried after a partial failure, mailing everyone twice The best rules come from a change you just made what did it have to keep doing? A rule written while you still know the answer keeps holding production to it long after the diff is forgotten. What a rule says A rule reads as one sentence, and the dashboard's form shows that sentence as you write it The operation one route and method ( POST /checkout/ orderId/pay ), one job by name, or every request or every job. A route that hasn't been served yet is fine the rule reads Unchecked until a kept trace of it arrives. What it counts in each execution Calls to a class or method a provider method such as PaymentsService.charge , or a driver's statement such as pg SELECT orders , named the way the Services view names them. Outbound HTTP calls to a host api.stripe.com , optionally with one method. A host named without a port matches it on any port. LLM calls every model call, or one provider's (OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI and others, or a gateway you configured). The bound exactly, at most, or at least, a number of times per execution. An upper bound (exactly, at most) is held by every execution, failed ones included. A lower bound (exactly, at least) is held only by executions that succeeded no error, status below 400 because a request that failed halfway never got the chance to make its calls. Only spans the SDK records itself are counted; spans you open by hand with TracerService never are. When one method makes more than 20 identical calls, the SDK keeps the slowest few and folds the rest into a single span (see spanCollapse in the configuration reference). A rule counts the folded calls at their real number, so an N+1 of fifty queries counts as fifty. Writing one where the evidence is You can write a rule from scratch under Activity → Rules , but two shortcuts start one from the telemetry that suggests it Pin as a rule , on the Releases page. Each query, outbound call, or method a release added, or now makes more often, opens the form with the call and a starting bound taken from the release's numbers. The route is left for you to choose, because the release's numbers are averages over every request. Guard with a rule , in a trace's waterfall. A run of calls the SDK folded into one span the shape of an N+1 opens the form filled in with that trace's own route or job, the call, and a bound of at most 3. Neither saves anything until you press Create . Checked on kept traces Rules are checked by the trace worker on the traces it keeps, from the moment a rule is saved never on earlier ones. Edits and switches take effect within about 30 seconds. What that means for the numbers A violation is certain. It is an execution that happened, and its trace is a click away. A rule holding is evidence, not proof. When spend controls sample spans, server errors and traces slower than a second are always kept and the rest at the keep rate, so the traces checked lean towards slow and failing ones. Counts are traces checked, not requests. A share of checked traces is not a share of requests. A thinned window says so. On a day when fewer traces were kept than usual, rules were checked on those alone, and the rule's page warns above its numbers. Each rule shows its status for the window you pick (the last 24 hours or the last 7 days) Status Meaning Violated At least one checked trace broke the rule in the window Holding Checked, and never broken Unchecked No kept trace of the operation arrived, so the rule wasn't judged Disabled Switched off; the counts are from before A rule's own page lists the newest traces that broke it, each opening its waterfall, and its checks and violations per release, with when each version started and stopped breaking it which release broke a rule is usually the first question. Alerts on a rule Turn on Alert me when this rule breaks when you create a rule, and an alert is created with it more than 0 violations over an hour, severity High, in app and by email. It fires on the first violating trace and resolves an hour after the last one, once per episode rather than once per request. Any alert rule can also watch the Production rule violations metric, for one rule or for every rule in a project or application. From a coding agent Over the MCP server, on every paid plan, create production rule lets the agent that shipped a change pin what production must keep doing while it still knows, and list rule violations reads the same report the dashboard shows. Editing and deleting rules stay in the dashboard. An agent doesn't need to be told rules exist.
