The instructions the server sends when a client connects name create production rule as the write to reach for after shipping a change, get context pack lists the project's rules and how each held over the last day, and when a release added an outbound call or a statement, or makes one more often, get release verdict ends with a line saying what is worth pinning. info Hint A rule only reads the traces the SDK already sends. Neither the dashboard nor an agent can use one to widen what the SDK captures.
observability/mcp-server: MCP server NestJS Observe exposes an MCP server, so an MCP compatible client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, or an agent you wrote yourself) can query your projects directly instead of you copying dashboard data into a prompt. Regressions and what each release changed, slow operations, error groups, traces, jobs, alerts, and production rules are available the same data the dashboard shows, scoped to exactly what you can see. Two tools are made for an agent at work on your code a context pack to read before an edit, and a release verdict to read after a deploy. The MCP server is included in every paid plan (Pro and above). It follows the plan that pays for each project a member on a Free account who is invited into a paid team's projects can use it on those projects. info Hint MCP is one of two ways to get telemetry to an agent. The Copy agent prompt button (see Dashboard) packages one page as text for a single paste. MCP is for an agent that needs to keep asking questions (follow a trace, check whether the error is still firing) without you relaying each answer. The endpoint speaks Streamable HTTP at POST https //observe api.nestjs.com/mcp . It's stateless there's no session to open, nothing to keep alive, and no setup beyond the request itself. Connecting a client Give your client the URL and nothing else. The first time it calls, the server answers that it needs credentials and where to get them. A client that supports MCP's OAuth sign in Claude Code, Claude Desktop and claude.ai, Cursor, and VS Code all do then opens your browser on the dashboard, you approve the connection there, and the client carries on, with no token to copy, paste, or keep in a file. Claude Code Then run /mcp inside Claude Code, pick observe , and authenticate; your browser opens on the approval page. Claude Desktop and claude.ai under Settings → Connectors , add a custom connector with https //observe api.nestjs.com/mcp as its URL. Connecting it opens the approval page. Cursor add the URL to /.cursor/mcp.json (every project) or .cursor/mcp.json (one project), and log in when Cursor lists the server as needing it VS Code (Copilot agent mode) in .vscode/mcp.json for one workspace, or your user mcp.json for all of them. VS Code asks you to sign in when the server first starts The approval page shows the client's name (its own claim, so approve only a connection you just started yourself), the address your browser goes back to, and the account you're signed in as. A request lasts 10 minutes. Approving creates a personal MCP token named after the client, such as "Cursor (connected with OAuth)", and hands it to the client directly; it acts as you, with your exact project permissions, and lasts until you revoke it under MCP tokens . There's no refresh flow a client whose token was revoked gets a 401 and asks you to approve again. Connecting with a token For anything that can't open a browser CI, a script, an agent you wrote, a client without MCP's OAuth sign in create a token yourself and send it in an Authorization Bearer header. Getting a token Personal MCP tokens are minted in the dashboard under MCP tokens . Click Create token , give it a name, and optionally set an expiry. A token with no expiry never expires, because MCP clients have no refresh flow. The secret ( omcp ... ) is shown once , in the response to creating it. Copy it immediately; only its hash is stored, so it cannot be retrieved again. If you lose it, revoke the token and mint another. Tokens act as the user who created them , with their exact project permissions. There is nothing to scope if you can see it in the dashboard, the token can read it over MCP, and if you can't, neither can the token. Revoking a token from the same page cuts it off immediately. Token management itself is deliberately dashboard only an MCP token cannot mint or revoke MCP tokens, so a leaked credential can't extend its own life. Configuring a client with a token Any client that speaks Streamable HTTP connects with the URL and that one header. Clients differ only in where the config file lives and what its keys are called. Claude Code Claude Desktop, and other mcpServers clients Cursor uses the same mcpServers shape in /.cursor/mcp.json (every project) or .cursor/mcp.json (one project), and expands ${{ '{' }}env ...{{ '}' }} inside url and headers , which is how you keep the token out of a file you might commit VS Code (Copilot agent mode) uses servers rather than mcpServers , wants an explicit type , and can prompt for the token once and store it encrypted. In .vscode/mcp.json for one workspace, or your user mcp.json for all of them Your own agent. With the official TypeScript SDK, the endpoint is a StreamableHTTPClientTransport and the token goes in requestInit.headers Before debugging a client's config, confirm that the endpoint and token work. This command lists the tools the server advertises If you get a tool list back, the credential is valid and anything still broken is client side. A 401 means the token is missing, expired, or revoked, or the header is malformed. A 405 means the client sent GET or DELETE ; every MCP request to this endpoint must be a POST . An example investigation The tools are shaped around investigations rather than endpoints, so each answer carries the key the next question needs. Suppose a deploy went out and something seems wrong 1. "What regressed after the last deploy?" find regressions compares the server error rate (5xx) and latency either side of each release boundary (your serviceVersion values) and names the release that made things worse, along with the operations it degraded. 2. "Show me that operation." get operation details returns the route's latency and error summary plus recent individual requests, each with a traceId . 3. "What did that request actually do?" get trace resolves the trace id into the waterfall every execution under it, across services, with span trees. 4. "What did the code say while it happened?" get trace logs returns every log line emitted under the same trace id, in order. Errors and background jobs follow the same shape list error groups → get error details → get trace , and list jobs → get job details → get trace . In every case, start with list projects , since almost every diagnostic tool takes a projectId . Before an edit, and after a deploy An agent working on the code itself has two moments worth asking at Before editing , get context pack returns a brief of the project sized for an agent's context its hot paths and their latency, flaky dependencies, SLOs, and the production rules the code must keep. get method impact says how much weight a method carries how often it runs, its own time, its error rate, and which applications run it before it changes. After a deploy , get release verdict says what the release changed in how the code behaves and whether it regressed. When the release was meant to fix an error, verify fix says whether the error stopped on the release's own requests the evidence to cite before resolve issue . Then create production rule pins what the change must keep doing. The server names this order in the instructions it sends when a client connects, so a connected agent reaches for these tools without being told to. Available tools Almost every tool is read only; the ones that write are listed under Setting up a service. Most diagnostic tools share a scope a required projectId , an optional applicationId to narrow to one service, and an optional timeInterval look back window ( 1h , 3h , 12h , 1d , 3d , 7d , 30d ), defaulting to 1d . Tool What it answers list projects Every project you're a member of, with team and application counts. Start here to resolve project ids. get project One project by id, including your access level and subscription state. search Full text search over your projects, applications, alert rules, SLOs, and issues. get context pack A brief of one project to load before editing its code, about 2,500 tokens the busiest routes and jobs, the methods with the most own time, failing or slow outbound calls and statements, SLOs, routes that went quiet, and the production rules with how each held over the last day. Returned as JSON and again as markdown for an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md . get method impact The weight of one method before you change it calls per minute, own time per call, error rate, the last day against the rest of the week, and the applications that run it. It takes a method, an outbound METHOD host , or a statement such as pg SELECT orders . find regressions Releases that made things worse server error rate (5xx) and latency before vs. after each release boundary, with the specific operations each one degraded. get release verdict One release's verdict what it changed in how the code behaves (outbound hosts and statements added, calls made more or less often, new error groups, routes that went quiet) and whether it regressed. diff release The statement shapes, outbound calls, and NestJS methods whose calls per request or own time per call moved across one release boundary a new N+1, an external call added or dropped, a method whose own code got slower. verify fix Whether a release fixed an error group, judged on that release's own requests on the routes it failed on fixed, not fixed, too early to tell, or not enough data. Counts come from request rows, which are never sampled, and it writes nothing. list slow operations The slowest HTTP operations in the window, ranked by p95, with volume alongside, so effort goes to what's slow and hot. get operation details One route latency and error summary plus recent individual requests, each with duration, status, and traceId . get trace A traceId resolved to every execution that ran under it across services, requests, and jobs each with its span tree. get trace logs Every log line emitted under a traceId , in order. list error groups Errors grouped by fingerprint, ranked by occurrence count, with class, sample message and stack trace, first/last seen, and the introducing release. get error details Recent occurrences of one error class per occurrence message, status, user, and traceId , plus a summary. get error trend Whether errors are growing or decaying over the window, already classified as a direction. get affected users The blast radius of one error class which end users hit it and how often. list jobs Background job performance in the window, per job name and queue volume, duration, and failure counts. get job details One job name on one queue duration and wait time summaries plus recent individual executions, each with status and traceId . list classes , get class methods Where the time goes per NestJS class, as on the Services view (own time, total time, calls, errors), then which method of a hot class is the hot one. get service map Who calls whom across the project its applications, the queues they work, the databases they query, and the external hosts they call, each with calls, errors, and average duration. list issues , get issue Issues across your projects, and one issue with its comments and activity. get incident record The record an issue leaves behind what it was about, when it started, the release it came in with, who it reached, the release that fixed it, and how verification went, on one timeline. list slos A project's SLOs with current status and error budget burn. list rule violations A project's production rules, how each held over the window, and the traces that broke them. list alert rules , list alert events Alert rules across every project you can see, and their firing history. Apart from setting up a service, resolving an issue, and pinning a production rule, nothing can be created or changed through MCP, including alert rules, error group status, and existing production rules. Those stay in the dashboard. Tool results also omit the time bucketed chart series the dashboard endpoints return, because hundreds of bucket values cost context and say less than the summary derived from them. Setting up a service These are the tools that write. Each goes through the same service as the matching dashboard button, so your role on the project and your plan's limits apply exactly as they do there, and a refusal comes back as the tool's answer. Nothing can be deleted, renamed, or revoked over MCP. Tool What it does list applications The applications of one project. Check it before creating a duplicate. create project Creates a project, in an existing team (pass its id) or a new one named after the project. create application Registers one NestJS service in a project. The name can't be changed over MCP and should match the serviceId you give the SDK. create api key Issues the key pair the SDK authenticates with. The secret is returned once; a well behaved client writes it to your git ignored environment file and does not repeat it. resolve issue Marks an issue resolved after a fix ships, which starts verification against the pre incident baseline. create production rule Pins a production rule on one operation what each request or job may call, and how many times. It needs Write access and a paid plan; editing and deleting a rule stay in the dashboard. With these tools, an agent can take a repository from "not instrumented" to "reporting" in one request "Set up NestJS Observe for this service" becomes list projects → create application → create api key , followed by the install and the three code edits from the SDK guide.
observability/opentelemetry: OpenTelemetry OpenTelemetry is the vendor neutral standard for traces, metrics, and logs. You instrument an application once, send the data to any compatible backend Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, or one of the many vendors that accept the OpenTelemetry protocol (OTLP) and change backends later without touching application code. For the Nest services in your system, whether that's all of your backend or part of it, you don't have to choose between it and NestJS Observe Observe works on its own, or beside the OpenTelemetry you already have, and services written in other languages share its traces through OpenTelemetry. This page shows what each records for a Nest application, how to run the two together, and how to set OpenTelemetry up in one. What NestJS Observe adds OpenTelemetry instruments a Node.js application from the outside it patches the HTTP server, the router, and the database driver as they load. It has no way to see the structure Nest builds in between, so a trace reads in the vocabulary of libraries. A slow POST /orders in an OpenTelemetry backend looks roughly like this on NestJS 11 (on NestJS 12, the two Nest spans are missing too) NestJS Observe instruments the framework from the inside. Nest hands it every provider it creates, through the instrument option of NestFactory.create() , so every method call on a controller, service, repository, guard, interceptor, or pipe becomes a span named the way you named it. The same request in Observe Nobody wrote a span for PricingService.quote , and nobody had to guess in advance that it might matter. Because the tree is complete, Observe can compute the time each method spent on its own (self time) instead of leaving it to guesswork. With OpenTelemetry, getting the same tree means adding a span by hand to every method you care about code that has to be written, kept up to date, and only ever covers what someone already suspected (see Adding your own spans). The difference continues past the request Nothing to run. An OpenTelemetry pipeline is an SDK, an exporter, usually a collector, and a backend to store, query, and alert on the data. Observe is one command, npx @nestjs/observe link , which installs the SDK, wires it into your application, and writes the API key into .env . There is no collector and no backend to operate. Nest's building blocks, recorded as what they are. Queue consumers, @Cron() handlers, GraphQL resolvers, microservice handlers, and WebSocket gateways are each recorded as their own kind of operation, and a BullMQ or Bull job shares a trace with the request that enqueued it. Kept in step with the framework. Observe is built and maintained by the Nest team, alongside Nest itself. OpenTelemetry's Nest instrumentation, by contrast, doesn't support NestJS 12 yet (see What gets recorded for Nest). More than traces. Error monitoring with source context, queue wait times and retries, a per class breakdown of where time goes, runtime profiling, and releases come with the same SDK, on every plan, free tier included. OpenTelemetry covers ground that Observe deliberately doesn't It instruments NestJS on Node.js only. Services written in other languages share its traces through OpenTelemetry with the openTelemetry option, a Nest service joins the W3C traces they propagate in the traceparent header, and with OTLP export its spans land in the backend that holds theirs. Without the option, services are correlated through the x request id header (see Distributed tracing). It's a hosted service, and it doesn't ingest OTLP spans from an OpenTelemetry SDK don't appear in Observe. It can export its own spans to your OpenTelemetry backend over OTLP, beside what it sends to Observe (see Exporting spans over OTLP). Its library instrumentation records a client wherever it's called. Observe instruments database drivers and HTTP clients that way, and other clients as providers a Redis or Kafka client registered as one, as it almost always is in a Nest application, gets a span for each call, but a client created outside dependency injection isn't recorded. So the two fit together. OpenTelemetry is the foundation when vendor neutrality, keeping telemetry on your own infrastructure, or every service's spans in one backend is a requirement. NestJS Observe gives your Nest services the framework level view on its own, or beside OpenTelemetry, in the same traces as the rest of your system. For the full reasoning, see NestJS and OpenTelemetry why we instrument the framework itself. Running beside OpenTelemetry NestJS Observe can cover the Nest services in a system that otherwise runs OpenTelemetry, and it can run in a Nest application next to the OpenTelemetry SDK. For either, turn on the openTelemetry option With it on A request in a W3C trace keeps that trace's id. When a request arrives with a traceparent header from a service instrumented with OpenTelemetry, in any language, or from a mesh or load balancer that traces Observe reports it under that trace id, so it has the id the rest of the trace has in your OpenTelemetry backend. An x request id header is kept only when it names the same trace, which is what another service running Observe sends. An unrelated one, such as the id Envoy and Istio stamp on every request, gives way. Calls out of the service carry the trace on. Each outbound call sends a traceparent beside x request id , with the call's own span as the parent, and passes on the caller's tracestate and sampling decision, so the next service's spans nest under the call. This covers fetch and undici on every supported Node.js version, and clients built on node http on Node.js 22.12 and later. An OpenTelemetry SDK in the same process sets the trace. Observe reports each request under the trace id of the span the SDK opened for it, including a request that starts a trace, and leaves traceparent on outbound calls to the SDK. A request then has one trace id in both tools, and every call carries exactly one traceparent . The SDK keeps recording its spans, and Observe adds the provider level ones. If the SDK propagates B3 instead of W3C Trace Context, Observe follows its trace all the same, and adds a traceparent in that trace beside the B3 headers. Queue jobs and microservice messages stay in the request's trace in both tools. From @nestjs/observe 0.3.23, a BullMQ or Bull job added while a request is handled, and a message sent through a client registered with ClientsModule over a transport that carries the trace id (TCP and Redis on @nestjs/microservices 12.0.4 or later; NATS, Kafka, RabbitMQ, MQTT 5, and gRPC on 12.3.3 or later), carry the request's W3C trace context beside its trace id. A consumer instrumented with OpenTelemetry, in any language, continues the trace from it. In a Nest service that runs the OpenTelemetry SDK, Observe hands the context to the SDK, which has no instrumentation for BullMQ or for Nest's TCP and Redis transports the SDK's spans in the job or the handler, and the traceparent on the calls they make, belong to the request's trace, as the job and the handler do in Observe. Where an instrumentation does carry the trace BullMQ's own bullmq otel add on, or the SDK's gRPC instrumentation the job's or the handler's spans nest under the span it opens for them (with bullmq otel , from @nestjs/observe 0.3.24). The trace id is shared. With OTLP export on, the Nest service's spans are too your OpenTelemetry backend shows the whole trace, and Observe shows the Nest service's part. Without it, the backend shows the other services' part of a trace, and Observe the Nest service's. Observe writes a W3C trace id as a UUID, and either form works in Observe 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736 from Jaeger or Tempo finds the same trace as 4bf92f35 77b3 4da6 a3ce 929d0e0e4736 . Without the option, Observe reads and sends x request id alone, and leaves any OpenTelemetry SDK in the process alone. Jobs and messages still stay in the trace in Observe a BullMQ or Bull job added while a request is handled runs under that request's trace id, whether its worker runs in the same process or in another service, and so does a message sent over a microservice transport that carries the trace id on its own (Distributed tracing shows which transports do, from which version). info Hint The option works beside reporting to NestJS Observe. From @nestjs/observe 0.3.24, it's on from the moment the application starts, so a new instance's first requests stay in the traces around it; before 0.3.24, it turned on with the first batch the collector accepted. It stays on through outages and rate limits at the collector, so an outage at Observe doesn't split the traces running through your other services. It pauses, with a line in the log, only while the collector refuses the application's credentials or the SDK's worker is down. Requests handled in between are traced as with the option off. With enabled false , or without credentials, it never turns on. warning Warning NestJS Observe and the OpenTelemetry SDK both hook the database drivers. The combination is tested with pg ; try it with the drivers you use in a staging environment before production. Exporting spans over OTLP From @nestjs/observe 0.3.23, with the openTelemetry option on, Observe can also export the spans it records to your OpenTelemetry backend over OTLP/HTTP an OpenTelemetry Collector, Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, or any vendor that accepts OTLP. The Nest service's part of a trace, down to the provider methods, then sits in the same waterfall as the services around it. Point the otlp option at the backend's OTLP/HTTP endpoint otlp true reads the endpoint, headers, protocol, and service name from the standard OTEL EXPORTER OTLP , OTEL SERVICE NAME , and OTEL RESOURCE ATTRIBUTES variables instead; those variables never turn export on by themselves. The default encoding is http/protobuf , and protocol 'http/json' switches to JSON. gRPC isn't supported, so point the endpoint at the backend's HTTP port, 4318 by convention. Each request becomes a server span, under the caller's span when it arrived in a trace, and each queue job a consumer span. The controller, provider, and manual spans under it become internal spans, and database queries and outbound calls client spans; an outbound call's span is the parent of what the next service exports. Errors are recorded as the span's status and an exception event, redacted as they are for Observe. A request whose caller sampled its trace out isn't exported. Export runs beside reporting to NestJS Observe, never instead of it, and every plan includes it Paid plans export every trace the SDK records, whatever Observe then keeps of its own copy. Free exports what Observe keeps. Once your applications send 30,000 events in one UTC day, or the month's allowance is used, most waterfalls are paused, and the requests and jobs behind them are exported without the spans under them. Server errors, failed jobs, and anything over 1 s keep their full traces. While the collector can't be reached, what Observe keeps can't be known, so Free's export pauses a few minutes into the outage and resumes with the next batch the collector accepts. info Hint Export starts with the first batch the collector accepts, whose reply says what the application's plan includes, and the log says when it turns on. It pauses whenever the openTelemetry option does. Without the openTelemetry option, or without credentials, nothing is exported, and the SDK says why at startup. Zero code setup info Hint Much of OpenTelemetry's Node.js documentation assumes the compiled application runs as CommonJS. Applications generated by nest new on Nest 12 are ES modules, which need an extra loader flag. Both variants are shown below. On Nest 12 a CommonJS build needs that flag too, because the @nestjs/ packages are ES modules and import Express themselves. Without it Express isn't instrumented and the HTTP span is named without its route. The quickest way to get traces out of a Nest application is OpenTelemetry's zero code instrumentation. Install the API and the auto instrumentations bundle The instrumentation has to be loaded before Nest and the libraries it patches, so it goes on the node command line rather than into main.ts . For a CommonJS build For an ES module build, OpenTelemetry's loader hook is required as well If your platform starts the process for you and you can't change the command, put the same flags in the NODE OPTIONS environment variable. Spans are sent over OTLP to the endpoint you configure. To look at them locally, Jaeger runs in a single container and accepts OTLP on port 4318 Open http //localhost 16686 , send a request to your application, and the trace appears under the service name you set. Configuring the SDK in code To choose the exporter, sampler, or instrumentations yourself, start the SDK from a file of your own instead of the register entry point OTLPTraceExporter reads its endpoint from OTEL EXPORTER OTLP ENDPOINT and defaults to http //localhost 4318 . Load the file before anything else, the same way as the zero code entry point In a CommonJS build you can instead import the file on the very first line of main.ts , before @nestjs/core and your AppModule . In an ES module build, and for Express on Nest 12, that isn't enough, because the loader hook has to be registered on the command line. The SDK exports spans in batches. To send the last batch when the application stops, call otelSdk.shutdown() once Nest has finished shutting down, for example from an onApplicationShutdown() hook with shutdown hooks enabled. What gets recorded for Nest The auto instrumentations bundle records incoming and outgoing HTTP requests (including fetch ), Express, and the common database drivers such as pg , mysql2 , mongodb , and Mongoose. ORMs built on those drivers, such as TypeORM, MikroORM, and Drizzle, show up through the queries they run. Nest itself is covered by @opentelemetry/instrumentation nestjs core , which is part of the bundle. It emits three kinds of span Span name Type What it covers Create Nest App app creation The NestFactory.create() call at startup . request context The whole request, from Nest's point of view handler The controller method that handled the request warning Warning At the time of writing, @opentelemetry/instrumentation nestjs core supports @nestjs/core versions below 12. On NestJS 12 the three spans above aren't recorded, and a trace contains the HTTP and database spans only. Check the package's supported versions for the release you install. The spans stop at the controller. The providers it calls services, repositories, and the guards, interceptors, and pipes around it are not traced automatically, so the time spent in your own code shows up as one undivided span. On the Fastify adapter, route level spans come from @fastify/otel , maintained by the Fastify team, which isn't part of the auto instrumentations bundle. Adding your own spans To see inside your providers, create spans with the OpenTelemetry API. startActiveSpan() makes the new span the parent of everything that runs inside the callback, including database and HTTP spans Every span you start must be ended, including when the work fails, which is what the finally block is for. The API package is safe to import even when no SDK is running without one, the calls do nothing. This is the work NestJS Observe does for you with its SDK installed, every provider method is already a span, and the manual API is only needed for code that isn't a provider method.
observability/choosing-an-apm: Choosing an APM There's no single best APM for every NestJS application the right one depends on how much of your system is Nest, what you already run, and what you need to see besides the application itself. This chapter puts the tools people reach for side by side NestJS Observe, OpenTelemetry, Sentry, Datadog, New Relic and Elastic APM with the setup each one needs in a Nest application, what it can see of Nest once it's there, and when each one is the right call. The short answer NestJS Observe for the NestJS services in your system, whether that's all of your backend or part of it traces in your own vocabulary ( OrdersService.create , not express.middleware ) without running anything, joined through OpenTelemetry to the traces of services written in other languages. OpenTelemetry for the services that aren't Nest, or if you want one vendor neutral standard across every service, Nest ones included. Sentry if errors across a web or mobile frontend and a backend are the main concern. Datadog or New Relic if you want one platform for several languages and real infrastructure, and have the people to run it. Elastic APM if you already run the Elastic Stack, or the data has to stay on infrastructure you control. They aren't exclusive NestJS Observe works on its own, or beside the OpenTelemetry or platform APM you already have (see Using more than one). What every APM needs from a Nest application Most APM agents work by patching libraries as they load the HTTP server, the router, the database driver. So the agent has to start before your application imports any of them, which in a Nest application means before @nestjs/core and before your AppModule . There are two ways to get there a preload flag on the node command ( require for CommonJS, import plus a loader hook for ES modules), or an instrumentation file imported on the first line of main.ts . Starting an agent from inside a Nest module is fragile by then Nest and some of the libraries the agent patches may already be loaded, and whatever loaded first goes unrecorded. Every vendor below says the same thing in its documentation start it first. The module format matters more than it used to. Up to Nest 11, nest new generated a CommonJS project. Nest 12's nest new generates ES modules, and for most agents ES modules mean an extra loader flag, sometimes with fewer libraries instrumented. Both command lines are given below where the vendor documents them. NestJS Observe NestJS Observe is the observability platform built for Nest specifically, by the NestJS team. One command, run in your project, sets it up It prints a code that you approve in the dashboard (signing up first if you need to), then installs @nestjs/observe , registers ObserveModule in your root module, passes the instrument option to NestFactory.create() , and writes the API key into .env . Doing it by hand is the same three edits see Linking from the terminal and the Quick start. There's no preload flag Nest hands the SDK every provider it creates through the instrument hook, so your own classes don't depend on load order, and the setup is the same for CommonJS and ES modules. What it sees of Nest every provider. Each method call on a controller, service, repository, guard, interceptor or pipe during a request, job or message becomes a span named the way you named it, so PricingService.quote is in the trace without anybody adding it. Queue consumers, @Cron() handlers, GraphQL resolvers and WebSocket gateways are recorded as what they are, and a BullMQ or Bull job shares a trace with the request that enqueued it. Queries through pg , mysql2 , mssql and mongodb (so TypeORM, Drizzle, MikroORM, Mongoose and Prisma's pg and SQL Server adapters) and outbound HTTP calls show up under the method that made them. Where it's narrower than the rest it instruments NestJS on Node.js only. Services in other languages share its traces through OpenTelemetry (see Using more than one), but their spans stay in your OpenTelemetry backend, since Observe doesn't ingest OTLP. It's hosted only, and it doesn't monitor infrastructure beyond each Node.js process's own runtime. Driver level query detail covers pg , mysql2 , mssql and mongodb ; Redis and Kafka clients show up as spans when they're registered as Nest providers (the usual setup), and cloud SDK calls show up as the HTTP requests they make. It needs @nestjs/core 11.1.4 or later and Node.js 20.19 or later, with Express or Fastify. Pick it for your NestJS services, all of your backend or some of it, when the question you keep asking is which of your own classes is slow. The Free plan needs no payment details, and the live demo shows the dashboard over a busy service's data with no signup. OpenTelemetry OpenTelemetry is the vendor neutral standard you instrument once and send traces, metrics and logs to any backend that accepts OTLP Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, or one of the many vendors that ingest it, Datadog, New Relic and Elastic among them. Setting it up in a Nest application is covered in OpenTelemetry → Zero code setup. What it sees of Nest the HTTP server, the router, outbound calls and a wide range of drivers, through the Node.js auto instrumentations. Its Nest instrumentation, @opentelemetry/instrumentation nestjs core , adds three kinds of span on NestJS 11 and earlier application creation, the request context named Controller.method , and the route handler and nothing for the providers underneath. Its current release (0.71.0) supports @nestjs/core below 12, so on NestJS 12 it adds no Nest spans at all. Pick it for the services that aren't Nest, when you want to choose (and change) the backend yourself, or when the data has to stay on infrastructure you run. In a system with both, NestJS Observe joins its traces and can export the Nest services' spans to the same backend. Sentry Sentry is an error tracker first, with performance tracing built in. It has an official Nest SDK Then add SentryModule.forRoot() from @sentry/nestjs/setup to your root module's imports and, if you don't already have a catch all exception filter, register SentryGlobalFilter as an APP FILTER ahead of any other filters. What it sees of Nest more than any of the generic agents. Sentry's SDK creates spans for Nest's request pipeline middleware, guards, pipes, interceptors, filters and route handlers, as long as they're @Injectable() on top of HTTP and the common database drivers. Your service layer is still yours to instrument. Pick it when errors are the main concern, especially across a web or mobile frontend and a backend. Sentry can also be self hosted. Datadog Datadog's tracer, dd trace , sends traces to a Datadog Agent you run next to your application, which forwards them on For ES modules on Node.js 20.6 and later, there's a one flag shorthand What it sees of Nest NestJS isn't among the web frameworks Datadog's Node.js tracer lists; its documentation mentions it as a framework with a custom entry point, which is about load order, not instrumentation. You get Express or Fastify, outbound calls, a wide range of drivers, and BullMQ (5.66 and up) as a supported library. A community package, nestjs ddtrace , can wrap your controllers and providers in Datadog spans. Pick it when you have more than one language and real infrastructure to watch next to the application. New Relic New Relic's Node.js agent reports straight to New Relic, with no collector to run for APM For ES modules, New Relic documents a loader alongside the preload, and a newrelic.js config file has to become newrelic.cjs What it sees of Nest @nestjs/core is on New Relic's list of instrumented modules (version 10 and up), which names transactions after your Nest routes. Below that you get Express or Fastify, outbound HTTP, and drivers including pg , mysql2 , mongodb , ioredis and Prisma ( @prisma/client 5 and up). BullMQ and Bull aren't on the list, and your own providers aren't spans unless you add them. The current agent needs Node.js 22.16 or later. Pick it when you want a full platform APM, infrastructure, logs, browser with Node.js as one of several languages. Elastic APM The Elastic APM Node.js agent sends traces to an APM Server and on into Elasticsearch, where Kibana shows them For ES modules, the agent's support is described in its own documentation as incomplete and experimental you add a loader, still start the agent separately, and only a subset of modules ( http , Express, Fastify, pg , ioredis and a few others) is instrumented What it sees of Nest NestJS isn't in the agent's list of supported frameworks. It instruments the server underneath, so transactions are named after the route, and it records queries through pg , mysql2 , mongodb and ioredis . Your controllers, services and repositories aren't spans unless you add them with the agent's API, and BullMQ and Bull aren't on its list. Elastic's own documentation now also suggests EDOT, its OpenTelemetry distribution for Node.js, which sees roughly what OpenTelemetry does. Pick it when you already run the Elastic Stack, or when the data has to stay on infrastructure you control. Side by side NestJS Observe Sentry Datadog New Relic Elastic APM Setup npx @nestjs/observe link , or one module and one option Instrument file imported first, module, filter require dd trace/init , plus a Datadog Agent r newrelic and a license key r elastic apm node/start.js , plus APM Server and Elasticsearch ES modules (Nest 12's default) Same setup See Sentry's documentation import dd trace/initialize.mjs import newrelic/esm loader.mjs r newrelic Experimental loader, subset of modules Recognises Nest itself Built for it Pipeline spans (guards, pipes, interceptors, filters, handlers) Not listed @nestjs/core 10+ listed Not listed Your own providers as spans, automatically Yes No Community package ( nestjs ddtrace ) No No BullMQ jobs Yes, linked to the enqueuing request Check for your setup Supported (5.66+) Not listed Not listed Something to run besides the app Nothing Nothing (or self host) Datadog Agent Nothing APM Server, Elasticsearch, Kibana (or Elastic Cloud) Self hostable No Yes No No Yes Languages NestJS; other languages share its traces via OpenTelemetry Many Many Many Many Infrastructure monitoring No No Yes Yes Yes This chapter quotes no prices per host, per seat, per gigabyte and per event models don't convert cleanly, and they change. Price your own traffic on each before you decide. NestJS Observe's plans are listed under Subscribing. How to choose Already running Elastic, Datadog or New Relic for other services? Add the Nest application to it, and know that you'll see the router and the drivers, not your providers. If that's not enough, NestJS Observe can sit next to it for the application layer. Mainly worried about errors, especially on a frontend too? Sentry. Several languages in the request path that have to share one trace? OpenTelemetry on the services that aren't Nest, and NestJS Observe on the ones that are with openTelemetry and otlp , the Nest services join the same traces and export their spans, down to each provider method, to your OpenTelemetry backend, which shows the whole trace. A platform APM covers every service in one product, but sees the Nest services' router and drivers, not their providers. Data has to stay on your own infrastructure? Elastic, self hosted Sentry, or OpenTelemetry with a backend you run. A NestJS backend, no tracing today, and nobody has had the week to set it up? That's the case NestJS Observe was built for the setup above is the whole setup. Using more than one NestJS Observe beside OpenTelemetry with the SDK's openTelemetry option, a Nest service reads and sends W3C traceparent and joins the traces your other services share, and with otlp it also exports its spans down to each provider method to your OpenTelemetry backend. See Running beside OpenTelemetry. NestJS Observe beside Datadog or New Relic keep the platform for infrastructure and your other services, turn on openTelemetry , and point otlp at the platform's OTLP endpoint, so the Nest service's provider spans land in its traces too. NestJS Observe beside Sentry keep Sentry on the frontend and add NestJS Observe to the Nest backend.
reliability/resilience: Resilience @nestjs/resilience adds retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads and fallbacks to controllers, resolvers, message handlers and gateways, as decorators. Sooner or later, every application that calls another system meets one that is slow or down. Without a plan, a slow dependency ties up your request handlers, your clients wait until their own timeouts fire, and retries from every layer pile even more load onto the service that is already struggling. @nestjs/resilience gives you the usual tools as decorators retry , timeout , circuit breaker , bulkhead and fallback . They apply to your application's entrypoints , which are controllers, GraphQL resolvers, microservice message handlers and WebSocket gateways. For code inside services, the same settings are available as policy objects. A single global interceptor applies the decorators, so they behave the same on every transport, and each failure becomes that transport's native error. Over HTTP, for example, a timeout answers 504 Gateway Timeout and an open breaker answers 503 Service Unavailable with a Retry After header. In this tutorial you'll harden the order API of an online store for cat food and supplies. Checkout asks the shipping carrier for quotes, and the carrier's quotes API is slow at the best of times and occasionally down. By the end, a slow carrier costs checkout about three seconds at most. Once the carrier is known to be down, checkout stops waiting for it altogether customers see flat rate shipping instead of an error, and a background job stops calling the carrier until it recovers. Prerequisites This tutorial assumes an OrdersModule that exports an OrdersService . The service needs these methods findOne(id) (which throws NotFoundException for an unknown id), findAll() , update(id, changes) and exportCsv() . Orders look like this Install the package Retry a POST safely also uses @nestjs/idempotency (see Idempotency keys). Register the module Import ResilienceModule into the root module. Configure field defaults and one named preset, carrier , that describes how the application should treat the carrier The two options do different jobs defaults fills in the fields of any stage that a decorator or preset turns on. Defaults never turn a stage on themselves. Here, a retry first waits a random time between 0 and 200 ms (the delay ), then up to 400 ms, doubling each time up to 2 s (the maxDelay ). A bare @Timeout() means 5 seconds. presets holds named sets of stages, usually one per dependency. The carrier preset gives each attempt 2 seconds, makes at most 2 attempts, and adds a circuit breaker. That breaker is shared under the name carrier by every route, handler and service that uses the preset. The carrier is one dependency, so it gets one breaker. Every time valued option takes milliseconds or a string such as '200ms' , '2s' or '30s' . The module is global, so import it once, in the root module. It registers one app wide interceptor, which does nothing for handlers without resilience decorators apart from error mapping. It checks its configuration at bootstrap an unknown preset name, an invalid duration or number (such as the NaN of an unset environment variable), a missing fallback method or one breaker name configured in two different ways fails the boot instead of the first request. Use ResilienceModule.forRootAsync() to build the options from configuration. Put a time budget on the quotes route Start with a client for the carrier. Every method takes an AbortSignal and hands it to fetch() The service passes the signal through. It also has a flat rate price list and a booking method, which the circuit breaker and the retried POST use below Now the route. @Resilience('carrier') applies the preset, and @Signal() injects the current attempt's AbortSignal Register CarrierClient and ShippingService as providers, and ShippingController as a controller, of a ShippingModule that imports OrdersModule . Checkout can't wait long, so @Timeout('1.5s') gives this route a tighter budget than the preset's. Settings resolve stage by stage a decorator on the handler wins over the preset for its own stage, and the preset still supplies the retry and the breaker. A bare @Timeout() would take the preset's 2 seconds, and fall back to defaults.timeout only where no preset or class level @Timeout() sets a duration. When an attempt runs out of time, three things happen 1. The attempt is rejected with a ResilienceTimeoutError . 2. The signal is aborted with that same error. fetch() rejects and closes the connection, so nothing keeps waiting for an answer nobody will read. Cancellation is cooperative code that ignores the signal keeps running in the background, and its result is dropped. 3. Because GET is a safe method, the preset's retry makes a second attempt. Only the pipes, inner interceptors and handler run again. Guards and middleware run once per request. If the second attempt times out as well, the client gets a 504 The timeout applies per attempt , so a carrier that hangs costs this route about 3.2 seconds two attempts of 1.5 s plus up to 200 ms of backoff. The status is 504 rather than 408 on purpose. A 408 claims that the client was too slow to send its request, and some clients and proxies repeat 408s automatically, even for POST requests. Client errors are not failures. A request for an unknown order throws NotFoundException before the carrier is called. It answers 404, and it is neither retried nor counted by the breaker. info Hint Code that can't take the signal as a parameter can inject ResilienceContext and read its signal and attempt . It reads the current attempt from AsyncLocalStorage , so it works in any service the handler calls, on every transport. A policy object used inside the attempt inherits its signal too, so the route's timeout also stops that policy's retries. Fail fast with a circuit breaker The preset's breaker records the outcome of every attempt. The carrier breaker opens once it has seen at least minimumCalls (10) calls, and at least failureRateThreshold (50%) of them failed. By default it looks at the last 20 calls. Every error counts as a failure, timeouts included, except client errors and rejections from other policies. A client error is a 4xx HttpException , or any other error with a 4xx status or statusCode property. That covers CarrierError when the carrier answers 422 to a malformed request, it isn't down, so the breaker ignores the error and the retry doesn't repeat it. A 408 or 429 from the carrier is the exception, because it means the carrier is pushing back, so it counts like a 5xx . An HttpException with one of those statuses is still a client error the handler threw it to answer its own caller, and that says nothing about the carrier. To change what counts, pass a recordIf function in the breaker options. While the breaker is open , calls fail immediately and the carrier is not called at all. The client gets a 503 with a Retry After header the number of seconds until the breaker lets a probe call through. The retry wraps the breaker, so a rejection is never retried. After openDuration (30 s), the breaker is half open . It lets one probe call through (see halfOpenMaxCalls ). If the probe succeeds, the breaker closes and starts over with an empty window. If it fails, the breaker opens for another 30 seconds. The breaker doesn't use a timer for this. It checks the state on the next call. A 503 is correct, but checkout can do better. Add a fallback that serves flat rate quotes while the carrier is known to be down (import Fallback and CircuitOpenError from @nestjs/resilience ) @Fallback() takes the name of a method on the same class, or a function. TypeScript checks that the class has a method with that name. The fallback is called with the error and the ExecutionContext , and whatever it returns becomes the response. It can be a value, a Promise or an Observable . Fallback is the outermost stage, so it also sees the breaker's rejections. By default, a fallback replaces every error except client errors. The handleIf option narrows that down. Flat rates cost the store money on heavy parcels, such as bags of litter, so here they're a last resort they're served only when the breaker says the carrier is down, and a single slow answer still gets a 504. info Hint To look at a breaker from your own code, inject ResilienceService and call circuitBreaker('carrier') . The breaker exposes state and stats , and you can force it open or closed with trip() and reset() . Cap concurrent CSV exports with a bulkhead The back office downloads all orders as a CSV file. Building the file reads every order and is heavy on both the database and the CPU. Two exports at a time are fine, but twenty would slow checkout down for everyone. A bulkhead caps how many run at the same time Two exports run at a time. Up to three more wait for a slot, for at most 10 seconds each. A sixth request gets a 503 right away, and so does a waiting request once its 10 seconds are up This 503 has no Retry After header, because nobody knows when a slot will free up. The status is 503 rather than 429 because a 429 blames the client's request rate, while a full bulkhead means the server is at capacity for everyone. A slot stays taken until the handler finishes, or until a timeout on the route gives up on the attempt. A handler that ignores its signal then keeps running in the background, outside the bulkhead's count, which is one more reason to pass the signal to every call that takes one. A bulkhead without a name belongs to its handler, and is registered under the handler's name. To read its load, inject ResilienceService and look at bulkhead('OrdersController.export') , which has active and queued counts. Give the bulkhead a name to share one pool of slots between several handlers. Retry a POST safely So far, retries have only happened on GET . That's deliberate. On HTTP, a retry applies only to the safe methods GET , HEAD and OPTIONS , and on GraphQL only to queries. Running a POST twice might create two shipments, and the package can't know whether that's harmless. So a preset's retry is simply skipped on a POST . A @Retry() decorator placed directly on a POST handler is skipped too, and bootstrap warns about it Booking a shipment is safe to repeat, because the carrier deduplicates shipments by reference , which is the order id. That matters for another reason too a booking that timed out may still have gone through on the carrier's side, so the retry has to be safe anyway. Setting idempotent true on @Retry() is how you state that running the handler twice within one request is fine A handler level @Retry() merges into the preset's retry, field by field. The fields you set win, and the rest come from the preset, then from defaults.retry . So this route keeps the preset's 2 attempts and adds only idempotent true . The preset's 2 second timeout and its breaker still apply. Only a decorator can say idempotent true a preset can't declare every handler that uses it safe to repeat. idempotent true and @Idempotent() solve two different problems idempotent true lets the server re run the handler within one request. @Idempotent() deduplicates the client's retries of the whole request. When a client repeats a request with the same Idempotency Key header, it gets the stored response back and the handler doesn't run again. Register IdempotencyModule before ResilienceModule Both modules register a global interceptor, and the one imported first runs outermost. With this order A replay, or a 409 for a key that is still in flight, is answered before any retry, breaker or timeout runs. A booking that already succeeded replays even while the breaker is open. All the retries of one request happen under a single claimed key. The stored response is the final outcome, after retries and any fallback. A 503 or 504 is a 5xx response, so the key is released and the client can try again later with the same key. Releasing the key on a 504 has a catch. The key is released as soon as the timeout answers, but the timed out run may still be in progress, or may already have reached the carrier, so a retry with the same key can overlap it. That's why the side effect has to be safe to repeat downstream, as the carrier makes it with reference . Passing the signal on, as createShipment() does, stops the local work sooner. Use the same policies inside services Pending orders include a shipping estimate in their total . Every 15 minutes, a background job re quotes them. The job isn't an entrypoint, so it uses a policy object , which you get from ResilienceService Add RepricingService to the providers of ShippingModule , and call repricePendingOrders() from a scheduled job (see Task scheduling). resilience.preset('carrier') returns the preset as one policy. Its breaker is the same instance that the routes use, so the job and checkout share what they learn about the carrier in both directions While the breaker is open, the job gets a CircuitOpenError immediately and stops, instead of spending a timeout on every order. If the job is the first to find the carrier failing, its failures open the breaker, and checkout serves flat rates without waiting on timeouts first. A few details differ from entrypoints execute() passes your function the attempt's signal and attempt number. The source option labels the events this call emits. A policy object has no GET or POST to look at, so the preset's retry always applies. Only wrap calls that are safe to repeat (a quote is). The route's @Timeout('1.5s') belongs to the route. The job gets the preset's 2 seconds. Create the policy once, for example in the constructor, not on every call. For options that aren't a preset, use resilience.create(options, name) . Why not put @Retry() on repricePendingOrders() ? Resilience decorators are metadata that the global interceptor reads, and interceptors only run around entrypoints. On a provider method, a decorator would do nothing, so bootstrap warns instead This is a deliberate choice, for three reasons Wrapping arbitrary provider methods would miss request scoped and transient instances, which Nest creates after bootstrap. Retries hidden deep inside services multiply. A route that makes 3 attempts, calling a service that makes 3 attempts, calling an SDK that makes 3 attempts, sends up to 27 requests to a dependency that is already struggling. A policy object is visible at the call site, where you can see what it does. info Hint An entrypoint without decorators still maps resilience errors. If a service throws a CircuitOpenError inside a plain route, the client gets a 503 with Retry After . Set mapErrors false in the module options to turn this off. Other transports The same decorators work on microservice handlers. The warehouse service asks for quotes over TCP when it re packs an order Add ShippingHandlers to the controllers of ShippingModule . A message has no GET or POST to tell whether it's safe to repeat, so on message, event and WebSocket handlers, only a @Retry() on the handler itself turns retries on. A preset's retry, or a class level @Retry() without idempotent true , doesn't apply there on its own, so reusing the carrier preset can't silently re run a handler with side effects. Here the handler's @Retry() opts in, and its attempts 3 raises the preset's 2 attempts to 3. Only use it on handlers that are safe to run twice. Errors reach the caller as an RpcException with a structured payload A timeout has "code" "TIMEOUT" and "statusCode" 504 , and no retryAfter . In a hybrid application, connect the microservice with inheritAppConfig true , or the global interceptor won't reach its handlers (see Hybrid application) GraphQL resolvers work the same way. If your application serves GraphQL, add a resolver to ShippingModule 's providers Queries are retried, while mutations need idempotent true , just like POST requests. A failure fails only its own field. The response still has status 200, and the error carries the code in extensions An open breaker reports "code" "CIRCUIT OPEN" , "httpStatus" 503 and "retryAfter" in seconds. The package sets httpStatus rather than Apollo's extensions.http , because Apollo would apply extensions.http to the whole response, although only one field failed. Observe breaker transitions Every policy emits typed events retry , timeout , circuit open , circuit half open , circuit closed , circuit rejected , bulkhead rejected , rate limited and fallback . Each event carries the policy name, and its source when there is one the entrypoint (such as ShippingController.getQuotes ) or the label passed to execute() . Inject ResilienceEvents to get them its events$ is an RxJS stream of every event from this application's policies. Log the ones someone should see Add ResilienceLogger to the providers array of AppModule . Every policy also publishes each event on a diagnostics channel of its own, such as nestjs resilience timeout or nestjs resilience circuit open , including policies created without the module. Metrics and tracing tools can subscribe without any dependency on this package. ResilienceTimeoutEvent is the type of one channel's messages, and ResilienceEvent the union of them all NestJS Observe already reads outbound HTTP from Node's diagnostics channels (see Database queries and outbound HTTP). It doesn't subscribe to the nestjs resilience channels yet. Once it does, it can attach retries and timeouts to the request's span, chart breaker state per name, and alert on bulkhead rejections, with no code in either package that depends on the other. Try it Start the application with CARRIER URL pointing at a carrier stub you control, such as a mock server or a few lines of node http . While the carrier answers, checkout gets live quotes Now make the stub hang. The same request answers 504 after about 3 seconds, and the stub sees both of its requests cancelled Keep sending it. Each request records two failed attempts. On the fifth slow request, the breaker has 10 calls in its window and 9 of them failed. The breaker opens, the request's second attempt is rejected, and the fallback answers. The application logs From now on, booking a shipment fails fast without calling the carrier Quotes, meanwhile, answer immediately with the flat rate Let the stub answer again and wait 30 seconds. The next quote request is the probe. It succeeds, so the breaker closes and checkout shows live quotes again Repeating the booking with the same Idempotency Key now creates the shipment and returns 201 . The earlier 503 released the key. Testing Resilience behavior is worth testing, but not by waiting 30 seconds for a breaker. Replace CarrierClient with a fake, and use Vitest's fake timers for the clock. Fake only setTimeout , clearTimeout and Date , so that the HTTP server and supertest keep working with real I/O A few things make this work vi.waitFor() waits until the request has actually reached the carrier. Only then are there timers to advance. With fake timers enabled, vi.waitFor() also moves the clock by its polling interval (50 ms), which stays well within the 1.5 second budget. vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync() fires the timeouts and the backoff in order, and lets the promises in between settle. trip() opens the breaker directly, so you don't have to produce ten failures to test the open state. Because the breaker checks openDuration against Date on the next call, moving the fake clock forward is enough to make that call a probe. Breakers, bulkheads and outbound rate limits belong to the application that created them, so every test application starts with fresh state. To test with different settings, such as a shorter openDuration , override the module's options with overrideProvider(RESILIENCE MODULE OPTIONS) . See End to end testing for the testing basics. Production checklist Budget time end to end. Time per attempt times the number of attempts, plus backoff, must fit inside your client's timeout and your load balancer's. For the quotes route, that's about 3.2 seconds. Retry only what is safe. Set idempotent true only when a second run within the same request is harmless. Pair it with @Idempotent() to handle client retries. Pass the signal to every I/O call. Without it, timed out work keeps running in the background, unseen by the bulkhead that admitted it. Retry at one layer. Retry at the entrypoint or in the service policy, not both, and turn off retries in SDKs and HTTP clients underneath. Tune each breaker to its dependency. Make minimumCalls high enough that two errors at night don't open it, set openDuration close to how long the dependency usually takes to recover, and use recordIf to leave out errors that aren't outages. Give every breaker a timeout. A breaker learns only from calls that finish. A call that hangs is never counted, and a hanging probe keeps a half open breaker rejecting everything else. Remember that state is per process. With several instances, each one has its own breakers, bulkheads and outbound rate limits, and a restart starts them fresh. Each breaker opens on its own, bulkhead limits apply per instance, and an outbound rate limit allows limit calls per instance. Keep fallbacks cheap and independent. A fallback must never call the dependency it stands in for. Alert on transitions. A breaker opening and bulkheads rejecting requests are the signals to page on. Register an idempotency store. Without one, @Idempotent() keeps its records in each process's memory, lost on every restart or deploy, and production refuses to start. See Store keys in PostgreSQL in the idempotency tutorial. Wire the modules correctly. Import ResilienceModule once, in the root module, and IdempotencyModule before it. Use inheritAppConfig true for hybrid applications. Honor Retry After in your clients. It tells them when trying again can succeed. reliability/idempotency: Idempotency keys @nestjs/idempotency makes routes, GraphQL mutations and message handlers safe to retry each Idempotency Key runs the handler once, and retries get its result. A customer of an online store for cat food and supplies pays for salmon kibble and cat litter in the store's mobile app, on a phone on a train. The app sends POST /orders/ord 1001/pay . The server charges the card through the payment provider, but the response never reaches the phone. The app can't tell a lost request from a lost response, so it retries. Without protection, the retry goes wrong in one of two ways It arrives after the first request finished. The order is already paid , so the customer gets an error for a payment that went through. It arrives while the first request is still waiting for the payment provider. Both requests pass the "is the order still pending?" check, and the card is charged twice. An idempotency key fixes both. The client generates a unique key for each payment attempt and sends it in the Idempotency Key header with every retry. The server runs the handler once per key, stores the result, and answers every retry with that result. @nestjs/idempotency implements this for HTTP routes, GraphQL mutations and microservice handlers with one decorator, @Idempotent() . Its HTTP behavior follows the IETF Idempotency Key header draft. In this tutorial, you'll make the payment endpoint idempotent, teach the mobile app to retry safely, move the keys to PostgreSQL (or to Redis), encrypt the stored receipts, protect the GraphQL mutation, and deduplicate the order.paid events that the shipping service consumes. Prerequisites This tutorial starts from the store's order API, which already has An OrdersModule with an OrdersService and an OrdersController . An Order has an id , a userId , items , a total in cents, and a status of 'pending' , 'paid' , 'shipped' or 'refunded' . A PaymentProviderClient that wraps the payment provider's SDK. It throws a 402 HttpException when a card is declined, and a ServiceUnavailableException (503) when the provider is down. An AuthGuard that validates the bearer token and sets req.user (see Authentication), plus a @CurrentUser() parameter decorator that reads it. A global ValidationPipe , and a TCP client for the shipping service, registered as SHIPPING SERVICE . Its data in PostgreSQL, through Drizzle, with the database registered by @nestjs/drizzle (see Drizzle). Using TypeORM? Store keys in PostgreSQL ends with the store for TypeORM. This is the method we need to protect The status check can't stop a double charge on its own two requests that arrive together both see pending before either one reaches markPaid() . Install the package Make the payment endpoint idempotent Register IdempotencyModule once, in the root module The module is global. It registers one app wide interceptor, which does nothing for handlers that aren't marked with @Idempotent() , so no other route changes behavior. scope gives every user's keys their own namespace. Without it, all clients share one namespace, and a key that one user picks could replay another user's receipt. With it, Alice and Bob can both send Idempotency Key 1 without ever seeing each other's results. Because guards run before interceptors, req.user is already set when scope runs, and an unauthenticated request is rejected before it can use up a key. If a signed in user calls an @Idempotent() handler that has no scope , the module logs a warning, once for each handler. Where one shared namespace is deliberate, such as a webhook keyed by the provider's event ids, set scope false . Now mark the handler required true rejects a request without a key with a 400 IDEMPOTENCY KEY REQUIRED error, before the handler runs. A payment without a key can't be retried safely, so it's better to refuse it than to charge the card unprotected. Here's what happens to a request that carries a key 1. The interceptor computes a fingerprint of the request a SHA 256 hash of the scope, the method, the URL (which includes the order id) and the body, with object keys sorted. 2. It atomically takes a lock on the record key , for example usr alice 5e0f6d0e … . If a record already exists, the handler doesn't run (see the table below). While the handler runs, the interceptor keeps renewing the lock, so a slow handler never loses it to a retry. 3. The handler runs. When it finishes, the lock becomes a completed record that holds the response the status code, the body, and the headers from a short allowlist ( Location , Content Type , Content Language , Content Location , ETag and Last Modified ) if the handler or a middleware set them. They describe the stored body, so a retry sent with another Accept Language still gets the stored body's Content Language . Cookies, CORS and rate limit headers belong to the original request and are never replayed. Every later request with the same key gets one of these answers Situation Response The first request is still running 409 IDEMPOTENCY KEY IN USE , with a Retry After header The first request completed The stored status and body, plus Idempotent Replayed true . The handler doesn't run. Same key, but a different body or URL 422 IDEMPOTENCY KEY REUSED Errors can be stored too. Tune TTLs and failure handling covers which ones. Because the interceptor is global, it runs outside the interceptors of your controllers and handlers. The stored body is exactly what the client received, after serializers and other interceptors ran, and a replay skips all of them. Pipes run inside it, so a ValidationPipe 400 is stored like any other client error. Other global interceptors are a different matter, as the production checklist explains. Until you store keys in PostgreSQL, records live in memory, in the default InMemoryIdempotencyStore . That's fine for a single instance in development, but every instance of the API has its own records, and they're lost on restart. When NODE ENV is production , the app refuses to start this way, with an error that says how to register a store. Send keys from the mobile app The server can only deduplicate what the client sends consistently. The app follows two rules It creates the key when the customer taps Pay , not once per request. Every retry of that payment sends the same key, even after the app is killed and restarted, so the key is saved with the pending payment. It creates a new key only for a new decision by the customer, such as choosing another card after a decline. Sending an old key with a different body is a 422. crypto.randomUUID() is available in browsers and Node.js. In React Native, use a UUID library, such as randomUUID() from expo crypto . These are the responses the app can get, and what they mean for a retry Response Meaning Retry with the same key? No response (network error, timeout) The card may or may not have been charged Yes 2xx Done. With Idempotent Replayed true , it's the first attempt's result No, show the receipt 409 with the code IDEMPOTENCY KEY IN USE The first attempt is still running Yes, after Retry After seconds 5xx The attempt failed, and the server released the key Yes, with backoff 429 Rate limited before the handler ran Yes, after Retry After seconds 422 IDEMPOTENCY KEY REUSED A bug the key was reused for a different request No Any other 4xx 400, 402 (declined), 404, 409 (already paid) Final. Every retry with this key gets the same answer No. Show the error; a new attempt gets a new key Check code , not just the status. A 409 can also mean that the order is already paid, and that one is final. Store keys in PostgreSQL The in memory store isn't enough in production. Its records vanish whenever the process stops, on every deploy or replaced container, so a retry that arrives afterwards runs the payment again. And once the API runs on more than one instance, a retry that lands on another instance wouldn't find the record, and two instances could both take the lock. The records need a shared store that can "create unless it exists" atomically. @nestjs/idempotency doesn't ship one. It defines the contract, the IdempotencyStore interface, and you implement it in a provider of your app, with the database or the Redis client it already has. The interface has four methods. Each one takes the record key and an owner first, and durations arrive in whole milliseconds acquire(key, owner, fingerprint, lockTtl) creates the lock, or returns the existing record in flight, or completed with its response. It must be atomic of any number of concurrent calls for a free key, exactly one may win. complete(key, owner, response, ttl) turns the lock into a completed record, if owner still holds it. release(key, owner) deletes the lock, if owner still holds it, so a retry can run the handler again. extend(key, owner, lockTtl) resets the lock's expiry to lockTtl from now, if owner still holds it. The interceptor calls it every lockTtl / 3 while the handler runs and its result is being stored. owner is a random id for each attempt, known as a fencing token. If an attempt stops renewing its lock (its instance crashed, say) and a retry takes over after lockTtl , the old attempt's extend() , complete() or release() does nothing, instead of overwriting the retry's record. So "if owner still holds it" has to be checked in the same atomic operation that writes checked in a separate read first, a takeover could slip in between. This section shows that store twice first with Drizzle, which is the tutorial's path, and then, under "With TypeORM" at the end of the section, the same store for an application whose ORM is TypeORM. Take one of the two. The store keeps its data in PostgreSQL, with Drizzle, so the records get a table in its Drizzle schema The primary key is a SHA 256 hash of the record key, because record keys (a scope, the client's key and, for GraphQL, the field's path) can be longer than PostgreSQL allows in an index entry. The response is json rather than jsonb , because jsonb rejects a \u0000 inside a string, and a response body can contain one. Generate the migration with drizzle kit, and apply it with npx drizzle kit migrate as usual The store implements each method with Drizzle's query builder. It injects the database with @InjectDrizzle() from @nestjs/drizzle , and the constructor registers the store with IdempotencyStorage , a registry that IdempotencyModule exports The database is typed as NodePgDatabase , and the tests below cast their PGlite database to it, since the store only uses the query builder both drivers share. Each method is a single statement that PostgreSQL runs atomically, without a transaction acquire() inserts the lock, or takes over an expired row, with one INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... WHERE expires at info Hint The app reads DATABASE URL , and, once receipts are encrypted, IDEMPOTENCY KEYS , from process.env . An application loads its environment through @nestjs/config , with a validation schema that stops startup when a variable is missing, and injects ConfigService into these factories instead. At startup, the module logs the store it uses, IdempotencyStorage DrizzleIdempotencyStore , and then it stops taking registrations An app has one store. A second registerSource() call throws, naming both classes. Register from the constructor of a singleton provider. The registry locks when IdempotencyModule initializes, so a store that registers later (from a lifecycle hook, per request, or in a lazy loaded module) throws instead of being silently ignored. Without a registered store, the module keeps records in memory. In production ( NODE ENV=production ), it refuses to start that way, unless you set allowInMemoryStorage true , which accepts that every restart or deploy forgets the records. Every store is tested with the same contract suite, which @nestjs/idempotency/testing exports as plain test cases for any test runner. It covers each method, the owner checks, expiry, and, with concurrent , the races that a store that reads and then writes gets wrong. The example project runs it against this store on PGlite, and on PostgreSQL through a pg pool, where 32 callers race for each key on up to 16 connections With TypeORM. The same store for an application whose ORM is TypeORM, on the same table. Drizzle stays the tutorial's path take this store instead of the one above, not next to it. The table is an entity, and every column states its type, so that the TypeORM CLI, which loads it without decorator metadata, sees the same schema as the application TypeORM returns a bigint column as a string, so a transformer reads expiresAt back as a number. The response column is typed object rather than IdempotencyStoredPayload , because the payload's unknown body doesn't fit TypeORM's insert types; the store casts it when it reads a record. The TypeORM CLI and TypeOrmModule share one set of options, in a data source file Generate the migration from the entity, apply it, and check that the entity and the database agree. The CLI needs a TypeScript loader for the data source file; this uses tsx The migration it wrote, 1790321611502 Idempotency.ts , is the CREATE TABLE and CREATE INDEX statements of the Drizzle migration, and migrations in the data source lists it. Now the store, under the same rules as the Drizzle one acquire() is the same INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... WHERE expires at info Hint Using Prisma? The store contract, after the tutorial, shows how Prisma expresses these statements. Check your store with the same suite. Store keys in Redis instead If your API already runs Redis, it can keep the records there instead of in PostgreSQL. Redis suits this store well a record is a small hash that Redis expires on its own, so there's no pruning job, and a hot key, such as a client retrying one payment every second, costs a round trip to memory instead of a row lock in the primary database. The price is a second store to run, protect and back up, and Redis has to be configured never to evict the records (see the production checklist). Each method is one Lua script, which Redis runs atomically Each record is a hash at idem , with the fields state , fp (the fingerprint), owner and resp (the stored response as JSON). The hash expires on its own lockTtl after the last renewal while it's in flight, and after ttl once it's completed, so no cleanup job is needed. Each script touches a single key, so the store also works with Redis Cluster. Redis runs a script atomically, but it doesn't undo the script's writes when a later command fails. PEXPIRE , for one, rejects a fraction of a millisecond, and failing after the HSET , it would leave a lock that never expires. That's why the interceptor hands the store whole milliseconds. Nest injects the Redis client, and the constructor registers the store, as in the PostgreSQL store. An app has one store, so RedisIdempotencyStore takes the place of the other one in AppModule RedisModule stands for your app's Redis module a global module that provides an ioredis client under the REDIS token, for example with useFactory () = new Redis(process.env.REDIS URL!) , and closes it with quit() in its onApplicationShutdown() , after the package has finished the requests in flight. RedisClient asks for nothing but eval() , which an ioredis Redis instance provides as is. At startup, the log line reads IdempotencyStorage RedisIdempotencyStore , and the registry's rules from the PostgreSQL store apply one store, registered from a constructor. The example project runs the contract suite against this store too info Hint This tutorial's example project has no Redis server, so its tests run the store against an in process fake that implements the same four scripts in JavaScript. That covers the store's logic and the way it reads replies, but not the Lua itself. Run the contract suite against a real Redis, for example in a container, before you rely on the store. Without advanceTime , the suite waits for real expiry, which takes about ten seconds. The remaining steps show DrizzleIdempotencyStore in their module listings.
