mcp/overview: Model Context Protocol (MCP) @nestjs/mcp turns a Nest application into a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, whose tools, resources and prompts are methods of your providers. The online store for cat food and supplies answers a lot of email "where is my order?", "can I change the delivery address?", "is the salmon kibble back in stock?". The support team works in an AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, an agent in their help desk), and the assistant can only answer when it can see what the order API sees. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is how an assistant reaches an application. The application runs an MCP server , and exposes three kinds of things to the assistant, the MCP client Tools , actions the model calls with arguments look up an order, change its address. Resources , data the client reads by URI the catalog, one order. Prompts , templates the user picks "draft a reply about this order". @nestjs/mcp turns methods of your providers into tools, resources and prompts with a decorator each. They run through the guards, interceptors, pipes and exception filters your routes use, and the server is served from the Nest application you already have over Streamable HTTP for remote assistants, and over stdio for one that launches it as a local process. In this tutorial, you'll give the store's order API an MCP server Tools to find an order and to change its delivery address, with schemas the model sees and the server validates. The catalog as a resource, and each order as a resource template. A prompt for drafting a reply. A guard that lets only the support team change orders, and an interceptor that logs each call. OAuth 2.1 on the HTTP endpoint, with the store's identity provider, and a scope for changing orders. The same server over stdio, and tests that call it in memory. Installation Install the package, the MCP TypeScript SDK it builds on, and Zod, for the schemas info Hint The schemas can come from any Standard Schema library that produces JSON Schema Zod 4.2 or later and ArkType as they are, Valibot through toStandardJsonSchema() from @valibot/to json schema , and a JSON Schema document you already have through fromJsonSchema() from @modelcontextprotocol/server . Zod 3 schemas are refused at startup the SDK cannot turn them into JSON Schema. Register the module Import McpModule in the root module. name and version identify the server to clients; instructions tells the model how to use it The module looks for tools, resources and prompts on every provider of the application, at startup. include [OrdersModule] limits the search to the modules you list. Start the application as usual The MCP endpoint is served at http //localhost 3000/mcp , next to the application's own routes. The same module can also be served over stdio, to an assistant that launches the application as a local process see Transports. How a call is served When the application starts, the module looks through its providers for methods decorated with @Tool() , @Resource() , @ResourceTemplate() and @Prompt() . It turns each schema into JSON Schema once, and fails at startup on what would otherwise only break later two tools with one name, a tool name outside the MCP naming rules, a request scoped provider, scopes without auth . Each HTTP request to the endpoint is then served on its own. The module builds an MCP server for it from what it found at startup, the MCP TypeScript SDK speaks the protocol, and a call goes through these steps 1. With auth , the access token is verified, and the call's scopes are checked. 2. The SDK validates the arguments against the schema. Arguments it refuses never reach your method the model is told what's wrong, and can try again. 3. Your guards run, then your interceptors and pipes, as around a route handler. 4. The method runs, with the arguments and the call's context. 5. What it returns becomes the MCP result. What it throws goes through your exception filters, and becomes an error the client understands. Nothing is kept between requests, so the server runs on as many instances as you like, behind any load balancer. Over stdio, one server serves the connection for as long as the process lives. Async configuration forRootAsync() takes the options from a factory, a useClass or a useExisting provider. path , endpointVersion , decorators and imports stay at the top level, because the module's routes are known when it is defined; a verifier from the factory is an instance Module options Option Default Description name , version Required. The server's identity, sent to clients title , description , websiteUrl , icons More of it, for clients to show instructions How the model should use the server include every module The modules whose providers are searched for tools, resources and prompts path 'mcp' The HTTP endpoint's route. false for none. Top level of forRootAsync() endpointVersion The endpoint's version, with versioning enabled. Top level of forRootAsync() decorators [] Class decorators applied to the endpoint's controller. Top level of forRootAsync() imports [] Modules whose exports a verifier class injects. Top level of forRootAsync() http.legacy 'stateless' 'reject' serves the 2026 07 28 revision only http.responseMode 'auto' 'json' or 'sse' pin the response shape of 2026 07 28 requests http.allowedOrigins localhost , 127.0.0.1 , [ 1] The hostnames a request's Origin header may name; requests without one pass. A list replaces the default, false turns the check off http.allowedHosts not checked The hostnames the Host header must name http.maxRequestBodySize 4 MiB For bodies the platform did not parse auth.verifier A class or an instance with verifyAccessToken(token) auth.resource The server's canonical URL, and the audience of its tokens auth.authorizationServers The issuers whose tokens are accepted auth.scopesSupported , auth.requiredScopes Scopes advertised, and scopes every request needs auth.resourceName , auth.resourceDocumentation More protected resource metadata stdio.legacy 'serve' 'reject' refuses connections that open with the 2025 handshake Example A working example is available here.
mcp/primitives: Primitives An MCP server exposes three primitives tools , actions the model calls, resources , data the client reads, and prompts , templates the user picks. Each is a method of one of your providers, with a decorator, and runs through the same guards, interceptors, pipes and exception filters as your routes. Tools A tool is a method decorated with @Tool() . inputSchema describes its arguments the SDK advertises it to the client as JSON Schema, and validates every call against it before the method runs. .describe() texts reach the model, which reads them to fill the arguments in Register the class as a provider, as any other The method is called with the validated arguments and the call's context. What it returns becomes the tool's result The method returns The client gets A string One text block Another value, with an outputSchema The value as structuredContent (validated against the schema), and as a JSON text block Another value, without one A JSON text block A CallToolResult ( {{ '{' }} content, structuredContent?, isError? {{ '}' }} ) It, as it is, for images, audio, embedded resources and links undefined An empty result The name defaults to the method's ( find ); tool names have 1 to 128 characters out of A Z a z 0 9 . , and two tools with one name fail at startup. annotations are hints for the client, such as readOnlyHint true , which lets it run the tool without asking the user first. To return something other than text, such as a picture the model should look at, return a CallToolResult (from @modelcontextprotocol/server ) yourself info Hint The model picks a tool by its name and description, and fills the arguments in from their .describe() texts, so write them for the model what the tool does and when to use it, what each argument means, with an example value. Say when a tool changes something. Resources A resource is data the client reads, and shows the user or hands the model. @Resource() serves a fixed URI, @ResourceTemplate() every URI that matches an RFC 6570 template, whose variables the method receives A string is sent as text of the mimeType , a Uint8Array or Buffer as a binary blob, a ReadResourceResult ( {{ '{' }} contents [...] {{ '}' }} ) as it is, and anything else as JSON. A NotFoundException is answered with the spec's resource not found error. Resources suit content the client loads into the conversation as it is the catalog, an order, the return policy. Clients decide when to read them, often when the user attaches one. To let the model look something up, with arguments, give it a tool. Prompts A prompt is a message template the user picks in the client. Its arguments are a schema too, and the client asks the user for each one A string is one user message; an array of messages, or a GetPromptResult ( {{ '{' }} messages [...] {{ '}' }} ), is sent as it is. A prompt can also open the conversation with more than one message. This one attaches the order as an embedded resource, then asks the question PromptMessage is a type from @modelcontextprotocol/server . Try it Start the application, and the endpoint is at http //localhost 3000/mcp . The MCP Inspector lists and calls everything the server exposes Choose Streamable HTTP , enter the URL, and Connect . Assistants that connect to remote MCP servers take the same URL. The call context The second argument of every MCP method is an McpContext Property What it is kind , name , uri 'tool' , 'resource' or 'prompt' ; the tool's or prompt's name, or the resource's; the URI being read authInfo The verified access token, with authorization clientId , scopes , expiresAt , extra request The HTTP platform's request (Express, Fastify, the Node adapter), with its headers and whatever middleware set on it; for the in memory test client, a plain {{ '{' }} method, url, headers {{ '}' }} object; undefined over stdio requestInfo The web standard Request the SDK served transport , era 'http' or 'stdio' ; 'modern' (protocol revision 2026 07 28) or 'legacy' (the 2025 revisions) signal An AbortSignal , aborted when the client cancels the call or goes away pass it on to fetch() and your database reportProgress(progress, total?, message?) Sends a progress notification, when the client asked for them server The SDK's own request context, for the rest ( mcpReq.envelope , mcpReq.inputResponses ) Asking the user. A tool that needs the user's confirmation, or a missing value, returns inputRequired() from @modelcontextprotocol/server the client asks the user, and calls the tool again with the answer, which acceptedContent() reads and validates warning Warning Over HTTP, this works with clients of the 2026 07 28 revision. A client of a 2025 revision is asked through a request from the server, which needs a session, and the endpoint keeps none the call ends with a tool error. Over stdio, both work. Guards, interceptors, pipes and filters Every call runs through Nest's enhancers, bound on the class, on the method or globally, as for a route. The execution context's type is 'mcp' , and McpExecutionContext reads the call, as GqlExecutionContext does for a GraphQL resolver. Only the support team may change an order McpExecutionContext.create(context) has getInput() (the arguments), getContext() (the McpContext ), getKind() , getName() , getRequest() and getAuthInfo() . Interceptors see the method's return value before it becomes the result, and can time, log or transform it. Pipes see the input as the call's body , so a global ValidationPipe({{ '{' }} transform true {{ '}' }}) validates a DTO class you type the input with, as it does for a route. Custom parameter decorators made with createParamDecorator() work after the input and the context, as on GraphQL resolvers add(input, ctx, @CurrentUser() user) . Interceptors work the same way. This one logs how long each call takes, with its kind and name @UseInterceptors(CallLoggingInterceptor) on the OrdersTools class logs every tool, resource and prompt of the class. warning Warning Global guards, interceptors and filters ( app.useGlobalGuards() , APP GUARD ) run on MCP calls too, as they do on GraphQL resolvers, and on the HTTP request that carries them. An enhancer written for HTTP routes that reads context.switchToHttp().getRequest() should check context.getType() === 'http' first. Errors What a tool throws becomes a result with isError true , which the model reads and can recover from the message of an HttpException (a BadRequestException('The address has no postcode') ), and Internal server error for any other error, which Nest's exception handler logs and whose message never reaches the client. Resources and prompts answer with JSON RPC errors a NotFoundException as resource not found, a BadRequestException as invalid params, another HttpException as an internal error carrying its message and status. An exception filter can answer instead what it returns is the result, and a ProtocolError (from @modelcontextprotocol/server ) it throws is the JSON RPC error. Authorization The order API's MCP server answers questions about customers, so it requires a signed in user. In MCP, the server is an OAuth 2.1 resource server the client gets an access token from the store's identity provider (Auth0, Keycloak, Entra ID, WorkOS, your own), and sends it with every request. The server verifies it, and never issues tokens. Configure auth resource is the canonical URL of the MCP server. Clients ask the identity provider for a token for it, and the server accepts only tokens issued for it (their audience), as the spec requires. authorizationServers are the issuers whose tokens it accepts. The module serves them, with scopesSupported , as the protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) at /.well known/oauth protected resource/mcp , where clients discover how to sign in. A request without a valid token gets 401 with a WWW Authenticate Bearer challenge that points at the metadata. That challenge is what starts the client's sign in. The verifier decides which tokens are valid. It's a class of yours with verifyAccessToken(token) , which returns the token's AuthInfo , or null to refuse it. Nest instantiates it, so it injects what it needs. For JWT access tokens, JwtVerifier from @nestjs/authentication checks the signature against the identity provider's keys, the issuer, the audience and the expiry An error with status 401 ( JwtError , UnauthorizedException ) refuses the token; any other error (the keys could not be fetched) is answered with 500. Opaque tokens go through your identity provider's introspection endpoint instead, behind the same method. For opaque tokens, the verifier asks the identity provider's introspection endpoint (RFC 7662) instead Whichever verifier you write, the module checks two things in what it returns resource must be the auth.resource URL, and expiresAt must be set and in the future. A token that fails either is refused with 401. Scopes. scopes on a tool, a resource or a prompt names what the token must carry for it. A call without them is answered, before the method runs, with 403 and the missing scopes in the challenge, and the client asks the user to grant them (step up authorization). requiredScopes in auth requires scopes on every request Declaring scopes without auth fails at startup, because nothing would check them. The token is ctx.authInfo in methods, and McpExecutionContext.create(context).getAuthInfo() in guards, for decisions scopes don't express. With @nestjs/authentication and @nestjs/authorization . Their global guards run on every MCP call. The authentication guard authenticates the call with your providers, from the HTTP request it arrived in a JwtBearerProvider that accepts the identity provider's tokens accepts the MCP client's. @CurrentUser() and AuthenticationContext then work in tools, and @Can() policies decide each call Exempt the endpoint's route from the authentication guard with decorators [Public()] , and let auth answer its unauthenticated requests the guard's own challenge doesn't point MCP clients at the metadata. A refusal on a call is a tool error, Unauthorized or Forbidden , and a tool that declares no @Can() is denied, as a route is. Over stdio there is no request, so a call is anonymous unless a provider of your own authenticates it from the environment. info Hint This needs @nestjs/authentication 0.1.3 and @nestjs/authorization 0.1.1 or later, the first versions that know MCP calls (context type 'mcp' ). With earlier ones, the global guard finds no credentials on a call mark the providers of your tools @Public() . Decorators Decorator Options The method is called with @Tool() name , title , description , inputSchema , outputSchema , annotations , icons , meta , scopes The validated arguments, the context @Resource() uri , name , title , description , mimeType , size , annotations , icons , meta , cacheHint , scopes {{ '{' }}{{ '}' }} , the context ( ctx.uri ) @ResourceTemplate() uriTemplate , and the same The template's variables, the context @Prompt() name , title , description , argsSchema , icons , meta , scopes The validated arguments, the context
mcp/transports: Transports The server is served over two transports Streamable HTTP, from the Nest application you already have, for assistants that connect over the network, and stdio, from a standalone application context, for an assistant that launches the server as a local process. Both serve the same tools, resources and prompts. The HTTP endpoint The endpoint is a controller the module adds, at path (default 'mcp' ) the global prefix, versioning, middleware, CORS and HTTP guards apply to it as to any route, so with app.setGlobalPrefix('api') it's at /api/mcp , and app.setGlobalPrefix('api', {{ '{' }} exclude ['mcp'] {{ '}' }}) keeps it at /mcp . endpointVersion sets its version when versioning is on ( VERSION NEUTRAL keeps it at /mcp despite a defaultVersion ), and decorators applies class decorators to it, such as [Public()] to exempt it from a global authentication guard, or [UseGuards(ApiKeyGuard)] . A server that only your own agents call, rather than users through an assistant, can do without OAuth. A guard on the endpoint's route checks an API key instead, which clients that connect to remote servers let you send as a request header A request without the key gets 403 before any MCP message is read. It serves every request statelessly each request gets a server instance of its own, and nothing is kept between requests. Several instances of the application behind a load balancer need no session affinity and share nothing. Clients of the 2026 07 28 protocol revision and of the 2025 ones are served on the same endpoint; http {{ '{' }} legacy 'reject' {{ '}' }} makes it 2026 07 28 only. A 2026 07 28 request is answered with a JSON body, or with a stream of server sent events when the method sends something before its result, such as progress notifications. http {{ '{' }} responseMode 'json' {{ '}' }} never streams, and drops progress notifications; 'sse' always streams. A few settings matter in production Pages from other sites. The endpoint checks the Origin header a request from a web page on another site, made by a user's browser, gets 403. A request without an Origin header passes, so assistants, CLIs and hosted connectors, which aren't browsers and send none, are unaffected. By default, only pages on localhost , 127.0.0.1 and [ 1] are let through. To serve a browser based client, list its hostname, http {{ '{' }} allowedOrigins ['support.catstore.example'] {{ '}' }} (the list replaces the default), or turn the check off with allowedOrigins false . DNS rebinding. A server bound to localhost can also be reached by a page whose own domain resolves to 127.0.0.1 its requests name that domain as their Host . Name the hosts the server answers to, http {{ '{' }} allowedHosts ['localhost', '127.0.0.1', '[ 1]'] {{ '}' }} , and requests with another Host header get 403. The Host header isn't checked unless you set allowedHosts . Body size. Tool arguments arrive in the request body, which your platform's body parser reads first Express's default limit is 100 KB. Raise it with app.useBodyParser('json', {{ '{' }} limit '4mb' {{ '}' }}) . CORS. A browser based client on another origin needs it listed in both places in allowedOrigins , by hostname, and in your CORS configuration, which also allows the Authorization , Content Type , Mcp Protocol Version , Mcp Method and Mcp Name request headers and exposes WWW Authenticate app.enableCors({{ '{' }} origin ['https //support.catstore.example'], exposedHeaders ['WWW Authenticate'] {{ '}' }}) . For a support dashboard at https //support.catstore.example that calls the server from the browser, with larger tool arguments than Express allows by default Over stdio An assistant on the user's machine (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, an IDE) can launch the server as a local process, and talk to it over its stdin and stdout. Serve the same module from a standalone application context stdout carries the protocol, and Nest's default logger writes to it McpStdioLogger writes every level to stderr, which clients show as the server's log. listen() resolves when the client closes stdin, and app.close() then lets the process exit. Over stdio, the spec takes credentials from the environment, not from OAuth, so scopes aren't checked there; guards still run. Set path false in an application that serves stdio only. The client starts the process from a command. Desktop assistants and IDEs take it in a configuration like this one, here with an environment variable for the server The process belongs to one user, on their machine, for as long as the client runs it. There is no OAuth there what the server needs, such as an API key, comes from the environment the client passes, and your providers read it from process.env . Clients of both protocol eras are served; stdio {{ '{' }} legacy 'reject' {{ '}' }} refuses a connection that opens with the 2025 handshake. One build can serve both transports main.ts starts the HTTP application, and clients that launch the server run stdio.ts . NestJS Observe With NestJS Observe ( @nestjs/observe ) in the application, every MCP call names its operation, tools/call find order or resources/read orders //{{ '{' }}orderId{{ '}' }} , instead of all of them being POST /mcp . There is nothing to configure. Production checklist auth configured on a server reachable from the network, with resource its public URL. allowedHosts on a server bound to localhost . The browser based clients that call the server, if any, in allowedOrigins and in your CORS origins by default, only pages on localhost get through. The body parser's limit above your largest tool arguments. Tool descriptions and .describe() texts written for the model they're all it knows about your tools. annotations.readOnlyHint on the tools that change nothing, so clients don't ask the user before each call. McpStdioLogger in the stdio entry point anything else written to stdout breaks the protocol.
mcp/testing: Testing Tools, resources and prompts are methods of providers, so their logic is tested like any provider's call the method. What MCP adds around it, the schemas, guards, scopes and the shape of the results, is tested through a real MCP client, which @nestjs/mcp/testing connects to the application in memory. Unit tests A unit test calls the method with the arguments and the context it needs A direct call skips everything the module adds the arguments aren't validated, guards and interceptors don't run, and the return value isn't turned into an MCP result. The client tests those. The in memory client connectMcpClient() connects a client of the official MCP SDK to the application, through the same handler as the HTTP endpoint the token check, the schemas, and every guard, interceptor, pipe and filter. It starts no HTTP server. The client comes from @modelcontextprotocol/client , a dev dependency The order API requires a token, so the tests replace its verifier with one that knows a few test tokens Like a real token, a test token needs an expiresAt in the future and the server's resource . The tests override the verifier class, and connect with a token The client is the SDK's own Client listTools() , callTool() , readResource() , getPrompt() and the rest are what an assistant calls. Results and errors What goes wrong in a tool is a result the model reads, not an exception in the test. isError and the text say what the model was told Resources and prompts answer with JSON RPC errors instead, which the client throws Tokens and scopes Connect a client for each token a test needs. A call without the scopes its tool declares fails before the method runs, with the error that tells a real client to ask the user for more access. A client without a token can't connect at all Headers and protocol revisions headers sends request headers with every request, which guards read from ctx.request.headers , in lowercase. era 'legacy' connects as a client of the 2025 protocol revisions, to check that the server works for both info Hint The in memory client starts where the endpoint's route ends middleware, and guards given in the module's decorators , don't run, and ctx.request is a plain {{ '{' }} method, url, headers {{ '}' }} object. Test what happens on the route over HTTP. Every primitive at once McpRegistry holds what the module found at startup. A test can hold every tool to rules of your own, such as a description the model can work with The registry is filled when the application initializes, which connectMcpClient() does; without it, call moduleRef.init() first. Over HTTP The route itself, the global prefix, middleware, CORS and the Origin check, is tested over a socket. Start the application on a free port, and send requests to it The stdio entry point To test stdio.ts the way a client launches it, build the application, and start it with the SDK's stdio transport Closing the client closes the process's stdin, and the application shuts down, as it does when the assistant quits.
mcp/migration: Migration An MCP server built with the community package @rekog/mcp nest moves to @nestjs/mcp with mostly mechanical changes the decorators keep their names, and tools, resources and prompts stay methods of your classes. This page maps both of its APIs, the McpModule.forRoot() one of its 1.x releases and the McpStrategy one of 2.x, to @nestjs/mcp . Packages @nestjs/mcp is built on version 2 of the MCP TypeScript SDK, @modelcontextprotocol/server . Replace the packages From 2.x, also uninstall @modelcontextprotocol/core and @modelcontextprotocol/node , @rekog/mcp nest auth if you used its authorization server, and @nestjs/microservices if nothing else in the application uses it. Types you imported from @modelcontextprotocol/sdk , such as CallToolResult , come from @modelcontextprotocol/server . The module From 1.x, McpModule.forRoot() stays, with fewer options @rekog/mcp nest 1.x @nestjs/mcp name , version The same transport Streamable HTTP is served unless path false ; stdio is served by McpStdioServer (see Transports) mcpEndpoint , apiPrefix path , under the application's global prefix guards decorators [UseGuards(...)] streamableHttp Nothing to set every request is served on its own, and http.responseMode shapes the answers to 2026 07 28 requests forRootAsync() forRootAsync() , with path , decorators and imports at its top level forFeature() One MCP server per application From 2.x, the strategy and its bootstrap code go away. McpModule.forRoot() takes the strategy's name and version , and the endpoint is a route of the application, served by app.listen() @McpController() classes become ordinary @Injectable() providers, listed in a module's providers instead of its controllers , and the MCP STRATEGY provider goes. A stdio server that NestFactory.createMicroservice() started is served from an application context with McpStdioServer instead, as Transports shows. Tools, resources and prompts The decorators keep their names and most of their options. The method's arguments change @rekog/mcp nest @nestjs/mcp parameters inputSchema on a tool, argsSchema on a prompt outputSchema , annotations The same (args, context, request) in 1.x, @Payload() and @Ctx() in 2.x (input, ctx) the request is ctx.request , the verified token ctx.authInfo context.reportProgress({{ '{' }} progress, total {{ '}' }}) ctx.reportProgress(progress, total) context.mcpServer.server.elicitInput() Return inputRequired() see asking the user A resource's ({{ '{' }} uri {{ '}' }}) ctx.uri . A resource template's method receives its variables as the input {{ '{' }} content {{ '}' }} , {{ '{' }} contents {{ '}' }} and {{ '{' }} messages {{ '}' }} results Returned as they are, or return the value itself and let the module build the result @Injectable({{ '{' }} scope Scope.REQUEST {{ '}' }}) A singleton provider read what belongs to the call from ctx McpRegistryService.registerTool() , strategy.registerTool() Not supported declare tools with decorators A resource template, for example A request scoped provider fails at startup with @nestjs/mcp every request is served by the same singleton instances, and what differs between calls, the request, the token and the client, is in ctx . Guards and errors Guards, interceptors, pipes and filters keep working, with McpExecutionContext.create(context) in place of context.switchToRpc().getContext () . The context's type is 'mcp' , not 'rpc' . A tool's errors still reach the model as tool results. An HttpException carries its message to the client, where 2.x needed an RpcException ; any other error is answered with Internal server error . Authorization @nestjs/mcp is a resource server, as the MCP spec asks of a server the tokens come from an identity provider, and the module verifies them (see Authorization). @rekog/mcp nest @nestjs/mcp McpAuthModule , the built in authorization server An identity provider (Auth0, Keycloak, Entra ID, WorkOS, your own) that issues the tokens, and auth pointing at it McpAuthJwtGuard in guards auth.verifier @ToolScopes(['orders write']) scopes ['orders write'] on the decorator. Scoped tools stay listed to every client @ToolRoles(['admin']) A guard, or a @Can() policy with @nestjs/authorization @PublicTool() , allowUnauthenticatedAccess Not supported with auth , every request needs a token ctx.getUser() in 2.x ctx.authInfo , or @CurrentUser() with @nestjs/authentication What's not there The HTTP+SSE transport of the 2024 11 05 protocol revision isn't served. Clients connect over Streamable HTTP, the transport current clients use. Sessions aren't kept every HTTP request is served on its own, which is what lets the server run on many instances. A 2025 client can't be asked for input mid call over HTTP; the call ends with a tool error. Registering tools at runtime , several MCP servers in one application and request scoped providers aren't supported in this version.
ai/overview: AI @nestjs/ai brings language models into a Nest application models registered by name and injected, calls with timeouts, retries and fallback models, answers validated by a schema, and the methods of your providers as agent functions, which the model calls as tools. The online store for cat food and supplies gets a hundred support emails a day, and its customers would rather ask the website about their orders than write one. Both are jobs for a language model, inside the order API sort an email and draft a reply, or answer a customer in a chat with what the API knows about their orders. The package builds on the AI SDK ( ai ) and its provider packages, so any model they support works Claude, GPT, Gemini, Mistral, or a model behind a gateway. Model calls run on the policies of @nestjs/resilience . You write an agent function, a method with @AgentFunction() , and the model is offered it as a tool every call of one goes through the guards, interceptors, pipes and exception filters your routes use, as the user the model acts for. In this chapter, you'll give the store's order API A triage of support emails into a typed object, and a drafted reply, with a fast and cheap model. Retries, timeouts and a fallback model around every call, a budget per call, and a record of what each one cost. Agent functions the model calls as the signed in customer, among them find order , which the store's MCP server serves too one method, two consumers. A chat assistant whose answer streams to the browser as it's written. A refund agent that waits for the support team's approval, as a durable workflow. Embeddings of its product descriptions, for a search that finds products by what they mean. Tests that run without a model provider. Installation Install the package, @nestjs/resilience , whose policies model calls run on, the AI SDK, a provider package, and Zod, for the schemas info Hint Every @ai sdk/ provider package works the same way @ai sdk/openai , @ai sdk/google , @ai sdk/mistral , @ai sdk/amazon bedrock and the others. Schemas can come from any Standard Schema library that produces JSON Schema, as for @nestjs/mcp Zod 4.2 or later and ArkType as they are, Valibot through toStandardJsonSchema() . Each major version of @nestjs/ai supports one major version of the AI SDK, ai 7 for this one, and it needs Node.js 22 or later, as the AI SDK does. Register the models Import AiModule in the root module, with the models the application uses, by name. Calls that name no model use default A model is what a provider package returns, such as anthropic('claude opus 5 5') , or a definition with it as model and settings of its own fallback , the models tried when it fails, pricing , timeout , retry , and generation settings such as maxOutputTokens . defaults apply to every call here, an attempt may take 30 seconds, and each model gets three attempts. Models describes every setting. The provider package reads its API key from the environment, ANTHROPIC API KEY for @ai sdk/anthropic . To pass it from ConfigService instead, create the provider in a factory see Async configuration. isGlobal true lets every module of the application inject AiService . Without it, the module isn't global AiService is injected only in the module that imports AiModule.forRoot() . To share one configuration with some modules only, import it in a module of your own that exports it, and import that module where models are called Calling a model AiService makes the calls. generateText() sends a prompt, with instructions (the system prompt), and resolves with the answer model names one of the module's models, default when it's left out, and label names the call in usage events and in the events of its policies. prompt is the user's message; messages takes a whole conversation instead, as the AI SDK's ModelMessage objects (see Conversations). The result has more than the text Property What it is text The answer the text of the last model call finishReason Why the model stopped 'stop' , 'length' when it reached maxOutputTokens , or 'tool calls' when it still asked for tools after maxSteps model calls usage The tokens of every model call, summed inputTokens , outputTokens , totalTokens , cachedInputTokens and reasoningTokens cost What the call cost, for models with pricing steps One per model call, with its text, tool calls, usage, and the attempts it took toolCalls , toolResults The tools the model called, with their input, and what each returned or why it failed responseMessages The assistant and tool messages of the call, to append to a conversation model The model that answered its name , provider and modelId A call that names a model the module doesn't configure, an agent function that doesn't exist, or both prompt and messages , is refused with an AiConfigurationError before anything is sent. Structured output Sorting an email is a job for generateObject() . The model is sent the schema's JSON Schema, and its answer is parsed and validated by the schema, so object is typed by it The model reads the .describe() texts, as it reads an agent function's say what each field means, with an example value. schemaName and schemaDescription name and describe the object, for providers that pass them on to the model. Besides object , the result has everything generateText() 's has usage , cost , steps and the rest. An answer that isn't JSON, or doesn't match the schema, rejects with AiOutputError , which carries the model's text . It isn't retried, and no fallback model is tried the model did answer. The schema's transforms run on the answer, while the model is sent the JSON Schema of its input side. The store also extracts the lines of its suppliers' invoices, and wants the due date as a Date ; the model is asked for an ISO date string The same call works in a queue job, where the store reads its suppliers' mailbox the code that calls the model doesn't change with where it runs. With tools, the model can look things up before it answers, and the object is the answer of its last model call. A model that is still calling tools after maxSteps model calls has given no object, so the call rejects with AiOutputError too. Async configuration forRootAsync() takes the options from a factory, a useClass or a useExisting provider. Here, the factory creates the provider with the API key from ConfigService A useClass provider implements AiOptionsFactory , whose createAiOptions() returns the options. isGlobal stays at the top level, and so do modelNames and embeddingModelNames . @InjectModel() (see Models) needs a provider for each model name it injects, and forRootAsync() creates them before its factory has run for the names @InjectModel() was seen asking for when the module was defined, in the classes the application had imported by then. A class loaded later, such as one of a lazily loaded module, lists its names in modelNames ['fast'] . A name nothing configures fails at startup, with the name of the class that asked for it. One package for many providers Each @ai sdk/ provider package is one more dependency to install and keep in step with ai . Most providers and gateways (OpenAI, Groq, Together, Fireworks, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, LiteLLM, Ollama, vLLM and others) also serve the OpenAI API, so a single package, @ai sdk/openai compatible , can reach all of them The providers then become data rather than dependencies keep their base URLs, API keys and model IDs in a database table or your configuration, and build the models in the forRootAsync() factory The factory runs once, at startup, so a new row takes effect when the application restarts. One row has to be named default , for the calls that name no model, and an empty table fails the startup. To use a row without a restart, build the model when you call it and pass it as the call's model , which has no settings of its own. createOpenAICompatible() assumes the least of a server. Set supportsStructuredOutputs true for a model that accepts a JSON schema, or structured output won't send it the schema, and includeUsage true to ask for usage on streamed calls, which budgets rely on. Use a dedicated @ai sdk/ package when you need a feature the OpenAI API does not expose, such as Anthropic's prompt caching or Google's grounding settings. Module options Option Default Description models The models, by name a LanguageModel , or {{ '{' }} model, ... {{ '}' }} with the settings below. Required unless embeddingModels names a model models. .fallback The names of the models tried, in order, when this one fails models. .pricing input , output and cachedInput prices per million tokens models. .timeout , retry , resilience The model's own policies, which win over defaults , as its generation settings do defaults.timeout '60s' How long an attempt may take; false for no limit defaults.retry 3 attempts, from '1s' The options of RetryPolicy attempts , backoff ( delay , factor , maxDelay , jitter , or a function), retryIf ; false for none defaults.resilience A policy, or the name of a ResilienceService preset, in place of retry and timeout defaults.maxSteps 10 The model calls one call makes while the model asks for tools, and one durable run (whose own default is 25 ) defaults.budget maxTokens and maxCost , per call and per durable run defaults.maxOutputTokens , temperature , providerOptions , headers Passed to the model onUsage Called after every model call that answered embeddingModels The embedding models, by name an EmbeddingModel , or {{ '{' }} model, ... {{ '}' }} with settings of its own embeddingDefaults The settings of embedding calls, which defaults don't reach onEmbeddingUsage Called after every embedding call that succeeded include every module The modules whose providers are searched for agent functions isGlobal false Whether the module is global. Top level of forRootAsync() modelNames More model names @InjectModel() may inject, for classes loaded after the module is defined. Top level of forRootAsync() embeddingModelNames The same for @InjectEmbeddingModel() . Top level of forRootAsync() Every option of defaults is also an option of each call, which wins. timeout , retry , resilience and the generation settings are also settings of a model's definition, which win over defaults . ai/models: Models Every model call runs under a timeout, retries and fallback models, built from the settings of the call, of its model and of the module, and reports the tokens it used and what they cost. Model settings A model in forRoot({{ '{' }} models {{ '}' }}) is a LanguageModel from a provider package, or a definition with the LanguageModel as its model and settings of its own. The store's Claude models have their prices, and the default one a fallback from another provider Each setting comes from the call, else from the model's definition, else from the module's defaults . A call to default above is sent maxOutputTokens 4000 , and one to fast or backup maxOutputTokens 1000 ; a call that sets maxOutputTokens 200 sends that, whichever model answers it. fast gives an attempt 15 seconds, the others 45. Settings Set on timeout , retry , resilience The call, the model, defaults maxOutputTokens , temperature , providerOptions , headers The call, the model, defaults maxSteps , budget The call, defaults fallback The call, the model pricing The model onUsage The call, and the module both are called topP , topK , seed , stopSequences , presencePenalty , frequencyPenalty , toolChoice , fallbackIf , abortSignal The call providerOptions are the provider package's own options, keyed by the provider's name, and headers are HTTP headers sent with each request to the provider. In models , a model can also be a model id string such as 'openai/gpt 5' , which the AI SDK sends through the AI Gateway. In a call, a string is always the name of one of the module's models. A call can also take a LanguageModel as its model , or in its fallback it has no settings of its own, and the result's model.name is undefined . Calling the AI SDK yourself To call the AI SDK yourself, inject the model. @InjectModel('fast') injects the LanguageModel that fast names, and @InjectModel() the default one A name the module doesn't configure fails at startup, naming the class that asked for it SummariesService @InjectModel('fats') asks for a model AiModule does not configure. The model is the provider's LanguageModel as it is, so a call made with it gets none of what AiService adds no timeouts, fallback models, budgets or usage events, and the AI SDK's own retries ( maxRetries , 2 by default) instead of the policies below. AiModels lists the configured models, with names() , has(name) and get(name) . Retries, timeouts and fallback Model providers fail they answer 429 when you send too much, 529 when they are overloaded, and now and then take a minute to answer. Every model call runs under the policies of @nestjs/resilience , built from three settings timeout a TimeoutPolicy , '60s' by default, per attempt until the whole answer for generateText() and generateObject() , until the first chunk for streamText() . The time tools take doesn't count, since the model has answered by then. false turns it off. retry a RetryPolicy , with its options attempts (3 by default, the first included), backoff (from '1s' , doubling up to '30s' , with full jitter) and retryIf . What the provider marks retryable is retried, 408, 409, 429 and 5xx responses and failed connections, and so are timeouts. A retry after header is honored, and one that asks for longer than backoff.maxDelay moves on to the fallback instead. retry false turns retries off. fallback the models tried, in order, once the model's retries have run out, each under its own policies. A call sets its own with fallback ['default'] , or none with fallback false , and fallbackIf narrows which failures move on. A call can change any of them Only the call's own model has its fallback followed a fallback model's fallback isn't, so a call that should go on to a third model lists both, as above. APICallError is the AI SDK's error for a provider's response, from ai . Some failures never move on, whatever fallbackIf says the call's abort, an answer that doesn't match the schema of generateObject() , and the AI SDK's errors for a call it can't send, such as an invalid prompt. Every fallback is logged as a warning through Nest's Logger , with the model that failed, the model the call moves on to, and the cause the error's class, its HTTP status and its message. A revoked API key or a refused request can't hide behind a fallback that works The model "default" failed (APICallError, 401 Invalid API key); falling back to "backup". Once a chunk has reached the browser, or the tools of a model call have started, its outcome is committed no timeout, retry or fallback replaces it, so no answer is sent twice and no tool runs twice. An abortSignal passed to the call cancels it at once, without a retry or a fallback, and the call rejects with the signal's reason. Inside a resilient route, such as one with @Timeout() from @nestjs/resilience , the route's attempt stops the model calls it makes in the same way. When a call fails When every attempt fails, on every model tried, the call rejects with AiModelError . Its attempts list each model, attempt and error (a ResilienceTimeoutError for an attempt that ran out of time), and its cause is the last error. The package's errors extend AiError Error When AiModelError Every attempt failed, on every model tried attempts , cause AiOutputError generateObject() 's answer isn't JSON or doesn't match the schema, or the model still called tools after maxSteps text AiBudgetExceededError The call has spent its budget, before its next model call usage , cost , limit AiConfigurationError A model, an agent function or an option the package can't use at startup, or when the call is made, before anything is sent AiToolError What the model is told about a tool call that failed toolName , the agent function's name A route that calls a model answers an AiModelError with 500, as any other error. An exception filter can say the assistant is unavailable instead Policies of your own resilience takes a policy, or the name of a preset of ResilienceService , in place of retry and timeout a circuit breaker or a bulkhead shared with the rest of the application, say. Fallback models are still tried around it, so a call to a model whose breaker is open goes on to the next one A preset replaces the model's retry and timeout with its own a preset without a timeout leaves the model's calls without one, and a preset's retries honor retry after only if its backoff does. A rejection of such a policy ( CircuitOpenError , BulkheadFullError ) that no fallback takes reaches the caller as it is an error of @nestjs/resilience , which ResilienceModule answers with 503 on an HTTP route. Naming a preset without importing ResilienceModule fails with an AiConfigurationError . The policies publish the events of @nestjs/resilience on the nestjs resilience diagnostics channels retry , timeout and fallback , named after the model ( ai fast retry , ai fast fallback ), with the call's label as their source ( AiService for a call without one). To log the retries of every model call Usage, cost and budgets Every model call that answers emits a usage event. With a model's pricing , in a unit of your choice per million tokens, it also has a cost , in the same unit. onUsage receives them Property What it is label The call's label , to tell calls apart model The model that answered name , provider , modelId step , attempt The model call's step in the call (from 0), and the attempt of this model for it (from 1) fallback , stream Whether a fallback model answered, and whether the call was streamed usage inputTokens (cached ones included), outputTokens , totalTokens , cachedInputTokens , reasoningTokens cost The input tokens not read from the cache at input , the cached ones at cachedInput (default input ), and the output tokens at output ; undefined without pricing durationMs , finishReason How long the model call took, and why the model stopped A call can take its own onUsage too, which is called after the module's. What a listener throws is logged, and never fails the call. The store meters the assistant's tokens per customer A budget limits one call maxTokens and maxCost , over all its model calls. A call that uses tools makes several, and the budget is checked before each one a call that has spent it rejects, before its next model call, with AiBudgetExceededError , which carries what was spent ( usage , cost ) and the limit . The check can't stop a model call halfway, so the last one can take a call over its budget. A model without pricing counts as free. defaults.budget applies a budget to every call info Hint Since @nestjs/observe 0.3.20, NestJS Observe records the model and the tokens of every model call on its outbound span, as it does for any AI SDK call see Model calls. A model named by a gateway id, such as 'openai/gpt 5' , is called through the AI Gateway's host, ai gateway.vercel.sh add it to outgoing.llm.hosts for Observe to read those calls too.
ai/tools: Tools An agent function is a method of one of your providers that the model may call, with arguments it fills in, to look something up or to change something the model reads what the method returns, then calls more functions or answers. You write an agent function; the model is offered it as a tool. The store's assistant answers questions about orders, so its model must look orders up. In @nestjs/ai , the method that does it is decorated with @AgentFunction() , and it runs through the guards, interceptors, pipes and exception filters of its class and method, as the user the model acts for. It needs nothing beyond @nestjs/ai . Define an agent function inputSchema describes the function's arguments the model is sent its JSON Schema, and every call is validated against it before the method runs. The model picks a function by its name and description, and fills the arguments in from their .describe() texts @AgentFunction() takes four options, all of them optional name what calls list the function by, and what the model calls it by. It defaults to the method's name, and must be 1 to 64 characters out of A Z a z 0 9 , which is what model providers accept as a tool name. description what the function does, for the model. inputSchema its arguments, as an object schema. Without one, the function takes none. scopes the scopes the caller must hold see Who the agent acts for. Register the class as a provider, as any other AiModule finds the agent functions of every module of the application; its own include option limits the search to the modules it lists. Give a call its tools A call lists, in tools , the agent functions its model may use, by name or by provider class (every agent function of the class), and says who it acts for with caller The model is offered the functions the call lists, as tools, and no other. When it calls one, the arguments are validated against the function's schema, the method runs, and what it returns is sent back to the model, which calls more functions or answers. Each of the model's answers is one model call, and maxSteps , 10 by default, caps how many a call makes see The agent loop. Arguments the schema refuses never reach the method, nor its guards the model is told what's wrong, and can try again. Mistakes fail early A call that lists an agent function that doesn't exist, or a class without any, is refused before anything is sent There is no agent function named "find orders". Agent functions find order, change address. A name model providers refuse fails at startup, naming the method. So do two agent functions with one name, and an agent function on a request scoped provider pass what a call needs through caller instead. So does a schema that isn't a Standard Schema with JSON Schema, or doesn't describe an object. The model reads what the method returns as JSON a Date as its ISO string, and undefined as null . A method that also serves MCP clients may return an MCP CallToolResult the model reads its structuredContent , or else its text blocks, joined. Images, audio and other blocks don't reach the model, and a warning in the log says so. A result with isError true is a tool error, with its text. The call context An agent function is called with its arguments and an AgentFunctionContext , from @nestjs/ai Property What it is name The agent function's name request The HTTP request the call runs in, caller.request , with its headers and the user your authentication set on it user , scopes caller.user and caller.scopes who the call acts for where there is no request, as in a queue job toolCallId The model's id for this tool call, to tie the function's logs to the conversation idempotencyKey In a durable run, the same for every attempt of this call; undefined elsewhere messages The conversation the model had read when it called the function, without the system prompt signal An AbortSignal , aborted when the call is pass it on to fetch() and your database reportProgress(progress, total?, message?) In a streamed answer, sends the browser the call's progress; elsewhere, does nothing change address lets the assistant change the delivery address of an order. It passes the call's signal on to the database, and a guard checks that the order is the customer's Who the agent acts for caller says who a call acts for, and the agent functions, their guards and the authentication packages read it from the context request in a route, the HTTP request of Express, Fastify or the Node adapter, as @Req() injects it. The functions see it as ctx.request , with the user your authentication set on it, as a route's guards do. user and scopes where there is no request, as in a queue job or a scheduled task, who the call acts for and what they may do. They are ctx.user and ctx.scopes . An agent function whose @AgentFunction() declares scopes runs only for a caller that holds them in caller.scopes otherwise, the call is refused before any guard runs, and the model reads Forbidden this tool needs the scope(s) orders refund . A nightly job reviews the refund requests nobody answered, as the store's refund bot Nothing a caller lacks is made up a call without caller runs its agent functions with no request, no user and no scopes. Guards, interceptors, pipes and filters Every agent function call runs through Nest's enhancers, bound on the class, on the method or globally, as for a route. Its execution context's type is 'ai' , and AiExecutionContext reads the call. A customer may change their own orders only AiExecutionContext.create(context) has getType() , getInput() (the arguments, also switchToRpc().getData() ), getContext() (the AgentFunctionContext ), getName() and getRequest() . An agent function call goes through these, in order 1. The arguments are validated against the function's schema. 2. The function's scopes are checked against the caller's. 3. The guards run, global ones first, then the interceptors and the pipes, as around a route handler. 4. The method runs, with the arguments and the context. Pipes see the arguments as the call's body , so a ValidationPipe validates a DTO class you type them with, after the function's schema has, and they see the context as a custom parameter, which ValidationPipe skips. Custom parameter decorators made with createParamDecorator() work after the arguments and the context changeAddress(input, ctx, @CurrentUser() user) . Interceptors see the method's return value before the model does. This one logs each call, with the id of the model's tool call What an agent function throws reaches the model as an error it can recover from, and tell the user about a guard's refusal as Forbidden resource , the message of an HttpException (a BadRequestException('The address has no postcode') ), and Internal server error for any other error, which Nest's exception handler logs and whose message never reaches the model. An exception filter can answer instead what it returns is the function's result. warning Warning Global guards, interceptors and filters ( APP GUARD , app.useGlobalGuards() ) run on agent function calls too, as they do on MCP calls. An enhancer written for HTTP routes that reads context.switchToHttp() should check context.getType() === 'http' first. Serving MCP clients too The order API already has an MCP server, whose clients, the support team's assistants, call find order too. One method serves both consumers it carries @Tool() from @nestjs/mcp , for MCP clients, and @AgentFunction() , for the application's agents, each with options of its own. Neither decorator reads the other's a method with @Tool() alone is no agent function, and one with @AgentFunction() alone is no MCP tool. A schema constant saves writing the schema twice Each consumer finds its own decorator McpModule serves the @Tool() methods of the modules its include lists, and AiModule finds the @AgentFunction() methods MCP clients get find order , and the assistant may call find order and change address , which has no @Tool() . The two kinds of call have context types of their own 'mcp' for an MCP client's call, which McpExecutionContext reads, and 'ai' for an agent's, which AiExecutionContext reads. The guards, interceptors and filters of a method that serves both see both, and tell them apart with context.getType() . find order shows a customer only their own orders through the assistant, and the support team's MCP clients every order The method's second argument is an McpContext for an MCP client's call, and an AgentFunctionContext for an agent's. Custom parameter decorators, made with createParamDecorator() , run for both kinds of call as well, and the ExecutionContext they receive has the type of the call they run for. With @nestjs/authentication and @nestjs/authorization @nestjs/authentication and @nestjs/authorization read agent function calls as they read MCP clients' calls from their arguments, with the request the call runs in. In a route, the global authentication guard authenticates each call from the request it runs in (once the route's result is reused), @CurrentUser() and AuthenticationContext work in agent functions, and @Can() policies decide each call. An agent function that declares no @Can() is denied, as a route is, and the model reads Forbidden In a job, there is no request. @Can() finds the caller's user on the context, and the authentication guard treats the call as anonymous, as it does over stdio, so mark the providers of the agent functions that jobs call @Public() A refusal is Nest's UnauthorizedException or ForbiddenException , as on a route, and the model reads it as the tool's error Unauthorized , or Forbidden . info Hint This needs @nestjs/authentication 0.1.4 and @nestjs/authorization 0.1.2 or later, the first versions that know the 'ai' context type. Tools in your own AI SDK calls AiTools turns agent functions into the AI SDK's tools select() takes the same list a call's tools does, and the caller their calls run as, for code that calls the AI SDK itself. The functions keep their schemas, scopes and enhancers stopWhen and stepCountIs() are the AI SDK's it runs its own loop here, as it does any of its calls.
ai/agents: Agents An agent is a model that calls tools in a loop it reads what each tool returns, then calls more tools or answers, until it has answered or reached its limit of model calls. Every AiService call with tools, your agent functions, runs that loop, inside your process there is nothing else to deploy. This page covers what comes with it the loop and its limits, conversations, answers streamed to the browser as they are written, and durable runs that survive restarts and wait for a person's approval. The agent loop A call with tools makes a model call, runs the tools the model asked for, and makes the next model call with their results, until the model answers without asking for a tool. Each model call is a step , and the result lists them Each step has its text , toolCalls , toolResults (what each tool returned as output , or the error the model was told), finishReason , usage , cost , the model that answered and the attempts it took. maxSteps caps the model calls of one call, 10 by default ( defaults.maxSteps changes it for every call). When it runs out while the model still asks for tools, generateText() resolves with what it has, and its finishReason is 'tool calls' ; generateObject() rejects with AiOutputError , since it has no object to give. Tools run inside their step their time doesn't count against the model's timeout , and a step whose tools have started is never retried, so no tool runs twice. toolChoice is passed to the model as the AI SDK's 'auto' , the default, lets the model choose, and 'none' offers the tools but lets it call none. 'required' and {{ '{' }} type 'tool', toolName {{ '}' }} make it call one, which not every model accepts. An abortSignal cancels a call the model call in flight, the wait before a retry, and the agent functions running, through their context's signal . A job that must not take more than two minutes passes abortSignal AbortSignal.timeout(120 000) , and the call rejects with the signal's reason, without a retry or a fallback. Conversations messages takes a whole conversation, as the AI SDK's ModelMessage objects, in place of prompt . A call's responseMessages are the messages it added the model's answers and tool calls, and the tools' results. Append them to the conversation, and send it with the customer's next message The instructions aren't part of the conversation each call sends its own. A chat in the browser keeps the conversation itself, and sends it with each message see Streaming to the browser. Streaming to the browser The assistant answers as it thinks, so the browser shows the answer as it's written. streamText() starts the call and returns its stream at once, and pipeUIMessageStreamToResponse() sends it, as server sent events in the AI SDK's UI message stream protocol, on the response that @Res() injects The route works the same on Fastify and on the Node adapter pipeUIMessageStreamToResponse() takes the platform's response, a FastifyReply on Fastify, whose headers set before the stream starts, such as CORS headers, are kept. convertToModelMessages() , from ai , turns the UIMessage objects the browser posts into the model messages the call takes. In the browser, useChat() from @ai sdk/react , or the AI SDK's packages for Vue, Svelte and Angular, posts the conversation to the route and builds the answer as it arrives Each message's parts hold its text ( type 'text' ) and the tool calls the model made, as tool find order parts with their state , input and output . The answer of every model call of the call streams as one message, its tool calls and their results included. Errors. A call that fails before its first chunk rejects, with nothing sent, so the route's exception filters answer it. Until then, the stream is retried, and falls back to another model, as any call. A failure after it ends the stream with an error chunk that says An error occurred. , so that no detail of the server leaks the errorText option says more. Keep alive. When 15 seconds pass without a chunk, as while a tool works, a comment line ( keep alive ) goes out, so that proxies and load balancers don't close the connection as idle. useChat() skips it. The keepAlive option sets the interval, or false turns it off. A browser that goes away. When the browser closes the connection, the model call is aborted, and so is the signal of the agent functions running. Headers. The response is text/event stream with x accel buffering no , which tells nginx not to buffer it. status and headers add your own. An agent function's ctx.reportProgress() reaches the browser as a transient data tool progress chunk, which useChat() hands to its onData callback without adding it to the message The stream has other readers. pipeTextStreamToResponse(response) sends the text alone, as text/plain ; textStream iterates it; toUIMessageStream() is the UI message stream as a ReadableStream , and toUIMessageStreamResponse() as a web standard Response . text , usage , steps , finishReason and responseMessages are promises that settle when the call ends, and result has all of them; they reject with the call's error. The call runs once, whatever reads it, and each reader gets the whole stream from its start. abort() cancels it. Mistakes in the options, such as an agent function that doesn't exist, throw from streamText() at once. Durable agent runs A refund request takes a person the agent looks the order up and asks to refund it, and someone in the support team approves, maybe the next morning, maybe after a deploy. @nestjs/ai/workflows runs the agent loop on @nestjs/workflows , with each model call as a step and each tool call as another. A run that a restart interrupts resumes where it was, and what its journal holds is read back, not done again. Install the package Import AiWorkflowsModule in the module of your workflows. The application imports WorkflowsModule , with a store in your database as Durable workflows describes, and AiModule , as usual Run the agent from a workflow of your own, with AiAgents Start it as any workflow, with an id from the ticket, which makes starting it again for the same ticket return the run that exists A call of an agent function named in approve waits for a person before it runs, for as long as it takes; approvalTimeout bounds the wait. pendingApprovals(runId) lists the calls waiting, each with its key , toolName and input , and approve(key) or reject(key, {{ '{' }} reason {{ '}' }}) answers one, from wherever the support team works A rejected call doesn't run the model is told it was rejected, and why, and answers the customer. A call nobody answered within approvalTimeout doesn't run either. The first answer for a call counts, and approve() and reject() take by , who answered, which is kept with the answer. While a run waits, its workflow instance is suspended, and holds no process. What a run needs to resume is stored with it, so its options are data models by name, agent functions by name or by provider class, which the run stores as names, and the caller as the user and scopes the agent functions need, since there is no request to read after a restart. The agent functions get them as ctx.user and ctx.scopes ; with @nestjs/authentication , their providers are @Public() , as for any call without a request. A run's model calls use their model's and the module's timeout , retry and generation settings, and its maxSteps and budget fall back to the module's defaults , as a call's do. An agent function call runs at least once a process that dies while it runs makes it again after the restart, with the same ctx.idempotencyKey . A function that changes something passes the key on, so the change happens once An agent function's failure is a result the model reads, as in any call, not the failure of its step. A model call keeps its retries, timeouts and fallback models; one that still fails is retried as a step of the workflow, which waits durably between attempts (three attempts by default). After stepsPerInstance model calls (10), a run goes on in a child workflow, so that no instance's journal grows long each resume replays it in full, and it is capped. maxSteps (25) caps the model calls of a run. The run resolves with what generateText() resolves with, text , steps , toolResults and the rest, as JSON it is the workflow's output, which WorkflowClient 's getStatus(runId) reads too. ai/embeddings: Embeddings An embedding model turns a text into a vector, so that an application can compare texts by what they mean AiService calls embedding models registered by name, with timeouts, retries and usage events, as it calls language models. A customer of the store searches for "my cat won't eat", and the search finds nothing no product says that, and the one they want is a "gentle appetite support for picky eaters". Compared as vectors, the two are close. The store embeds the descriptions of its products once, keeps the vectors next to the products, and embeds each search as it comes in. The package stops at the vectors. Your application stores them, in PostgreSQL with pgvector or in a vector database, and splits long documents into chunks if it needs to. Register the models Embedding models have a registry of their own, embeddingModels , next to models . The store's come from OpenAI, through its provider package An embedding model is what a provider package returns, as above, or a definition with it as model and settings of its own. A model id string, such as 'openai/text embedding 3 small' , is sent through the AI Gateway, as it is in models . Calls that name no model use default , and the first model registered is never picked in its place. The two registries don't share names default above is one model for generateText() and another for embed() . An application that only embeds leaves models out, and one with no model in either fails at startup. Calling an embedding model embed() embeds one text, and embedMany() a list of them model names one of embeddingModels , default when it's left out, and label names the call in usage events and in the events of its policies. A call can also take an EmbeddingModel as its model it has no settings of its own, and the result's model.name is undefined . The result has more than the vectors Property What it is embedding , embeddings The vector of embed() , and the vectors of embedMany() , in the order of values value , values The texts that were embedded usage The tokens the provider reported, summed over its requests tokens cost What the call cost, for a model with pricing attempts The provider requests the call made, retries included model The model that answered its name , provider and modelId warnings , providerMetadata What the provider added to its answers response , responses The provider's HTTP response to embed() , and one for each request of embedMany() A value that isn't a string, or a model the module doesn't configure, is refused with an AiConfigurationError before anything is sent. To compare two vectors in memory, cosineSimilarity() from ai takes them and answers a number from 1 to 1. Beyond a few hundred texts, let the database find the nearest ones, with an index. Embedding settings A definition gives a model settings of its own, and embeddingDefaults applies settings to every embedding call. Each setting comes from the call, else from the model's definition, else from embeddingDefaults Settings Set on timeout , retry , resilience The call, the model, embeddingDefaults maxParallelCalls , providerOptions , headers The call, the model, embeddingDefaults pricing The model onEmbeddingUsage The call, and the module both are called abortSignal , label The call The module's defaults are for language models, and nothing in them reaches an embedding call not their timeouts, their headers or their provider options. budget and fallback are settings of language models only. providerOptions are the provider package's own options, keyed by the provider's name, and headers are HTTP headers sent with each request to the provider. The number of dimensions of a vector is such an option, for the models that let you choose it, as documents does above. Batches embedMany() takes as many values as you have. The AI SDK splits them into provider requests, with as many values in each as the provider allows, and sends maxParallelCalls of those at a time 4 by default, or one at a time for a model that can't take parallel calls. Whichever request answers first, embeddings keeps the order of values . Retries, timeouts and cancellation Every provider request runs under the policies of @nestjs/resilience , built from the same settings as a language model's timeout , '60s' by default, and retry , 3 attempts by default, which retries what the provider marks retryable and timeouts, and honors a retry after header. They apply to each request, not to the whole call. timeout is how long one request may take, so a call with 20,000 values can run for as long as it needs, and a request that fails is retried alone, without sending the others again. When a request runs out of attempts, the call rejects with AiModelError , whose attempts are that request's, and the requests still running are aborted. embedMany() returns every vector or none, so what the finished requests embedded is lost with them. To keep the progress of a big job, send it in groups and save each one, in a queue job or a step of a workflow An abortSignal passed to the call cancels the requests in flight and the backoff of a retry, and the call rejects with the signal's reason. Since timeout covers one request, this is also how to give the whole call a deadline Inside a resilient route, such as one with @Timeout() from @nestjs/resilience , the route's attempt stops the requests in the same way. An embedding call has no fallback models. Vectors of different models can't be compared, even when they have the same number of dimensions, so a search index written with one model can't be read with another. Policies of your own resilience takes a policy, or the name of a preset of ResilienceService , in place of retry and timeout , as it does for a language model. It runs around each provider request, so an outbound rate limit or a bulkhead counts requests, across every call that shares it. The store keeps its embedding requests within its quota at the provider Give such a policy room for the requests of a call to wait. A request that finds no token rejects the whole call with OutboundRateLimitError once it has waited maxWait , which is 0 by default, and one that finds a full bulkhead rejects it with BulkheadFullError unless the bulkhead has a maxQueue to hold it. The policies publish the events of @nestjs/resilience on the nestjs resilience diagnostics channels, named after the model ( ai embedding default retry ), with the call's label as their source . Usage and cost A call that succeeds emits one usage event, with the tokens its requests reported. With a model's pricing , its price per million input tokens in a unit of your choice, the event also has a cost , in the same unit. onEmbeddingUsage receives them Property What it is operation 'embed' or 'embedMany' label The call's label , to tell calls apart model The model that answered name , provider , modelId inputCount How many values the call embedded usage The tokens the provider reported tokens attempts The provider requests the call made, retries included durationMs How long the call took, with its retries and backoff cost The tokens at pricing.input ; undefined without pricing A call can take its own onEmbeddingUsage too, which is called after the module's. onUsage is for language models, and isn't called. What a listener throws is logged, and never fails the call. The event carries neither the texts nor the vectors, so it's safe to log. The events aren't a billing ledger a provider may bill a request that timed out, and a call that fails emits nothing, even for the requests it completed. Calling the AI SDK yourself To call the AI SDK yourself, inject the model. @InjectEmbeddingModel('documents') injects the EmbeddingModel that documents names, and @InjectEmbeddingModel() the default one A name the module doesn't configure fails at startup, naming the class that asked for it. The model is the provider's EmbeddingModel as it is, so a call made with it gets none of what AiService adds no policies or usage events, and the AI SDK's own retries ( maxRetries , 2 by default). AiEmbeddingModels lists the configured models, with names() , has(name) and get(name) . Under forRootAsync() , its factory returns embeddingModels as it returns models , and @InjectEmbeddingModel() needs what @InjectModel() does a class loaded after the module is defined lists its names in embeddingModelNames , at the top level. info Hint Testing describes FakeEmbeddingModel , an embedding model for tests that calls no provider.
