recipes/router-module: Router module info Hint This chapter is only relevant to HTTP based applications. In an HTTP application (e.g., a REST API), the route path for a handler is determined by concatenating the (optional) prefix declared for the controller (inside the @Controller() decorator) and any path specified in the method's decorator (e.g., @Get('users') ). You can learn more about this in the routing section of the controllers chapter. Additionally, you can define a global prefix for all routes registered in your application, or enable versioning. In some cases, it's useful to define a prefix at the module level, which then applies to all controllers registered inside that module. For example, imagine a REST application that exposes several endpoints used by a specific part of your application called "Dashboard". Instead of repeating the /dashboard prefix in each controller, you can use the RouterModule , as follows info Hint The RouterModule class is exported from the @nestjs/core package. You can also define hierarchical structures, in which each module has children modules. The child modules inherit their parent's prefix. In the following example, the AdminModule is registered as the parent module of DashboardModule and MetricsModule info Hint Use this feature carefully, as overusing it can make code difficult to maintain over time. In the example above, every controller registered inside the DashboardModule gets an extra /admin/dashboard prefix, because the module concatenates paths recursively from top to bottom, parent to children. Likewise, every controller defined inside the MetricsModule gets the additional module level prefix /admin/metrics .
recipes/fastify-migration: Migrating from Fastify A Fastify application can move to Nest and stay on Fastify your plugins keep working, and routes move one at a time or all at once. Nest runs on Fastify through the FastifyAdapter , so this isn't a change of server. The router, the plugins, the JSON schemas and the serialization stay the same, including how paths match, how query strings parse and how large a body may be. What you add is the structure around them modules, dependency injection, and guards and pipes in place of hooks registered route by route. Choose an approach Question One route at a time All at once How does it work? Nest runs on your Fastify instance, and routes move to it one by one A new Nest application replaces the Fastify app in one release What gets deployed? Each moved route, on its own Everything, once What happens to feature work? It continues, and new endpoints go into Nest It waits, or gets written twice, until the switch How do you go back? Restore one route Deploy the last Fastify release Which Fastify version? Fastify 5, so upgrade first Any, since the Fastify app isn't touched What about existing plugins? They keep running, for Nest's routes too You register them again on the Nest application How long are there two styles in the code? Until the last route moves Never Move one route at a time when the application is large, when several people work on it, or when it can't wait. Move it all at once when it's small enough to review as one change and you can pin what it does with tests. That also suits a coding agent. One route at a time The Fastify app keeps its routes, plugins and error handler, new endpoints are written in Nest, and existing ones move over when you next change them. Both answer on the same port, so clients don't notice, and every step can be deployed on its own. Requirements Fastify 5. Nest's FastifyAdapter registers plugins that require it, so a Fastify 4 instance fails as soon as Nest starts. Upgrade the app first. TypeScript. The Nest code on this page is TypeScript. If the Fastify app is written in JavaScript, its files can stay as they are TypeScript's allowJs option compiles them with the rest. Install Nest next to Fastify Run Nest on the Fastify app Nest normally creates its own Fastify instance. Give it yours instead. Stop the app from listening, and have a function return it. Nest sets the instance's own error and not found handlers, so two things have to change Move setErrorHandler() into a plugin that holds your routes. It keeps handling their errors, and Fastify won't warn about it being overridden. Remove setNotFoundHandler() . Nest refuses to start with Not found handler already set , and it answers unknown routes itself. Then pass it to the FastifyAdapter , and let Nest listen Both now serve requests from one Fastify instance The Fastify routes answer as they did before, and their errors reach their own error handler. Plugins and hooks registered on the root instance apply to Nest's routes too, so helmet and the onRequest hook above run for them, and request.jwtVerify() works inside a Nest guard. Hooks registered inside an encapsulated plugin stay inside it, as they always do, so they don't run for Nest's routes. Errors in Nest's routes go through its exception filters, and a request for a route neither has gets Nest's 404 response. Move a route Write the route in Nest, and delete it from Fastify in the same change. Fastify's router refuses duplicates, so with both in the code the application stops at startup with Method 'GET' already declared for route . A plugin you already use can back a guard, and @RouteSchema() takes the JSON schema the route already has Read Keep what would change without an error as you go. It applies to every moved route, and the response schema above is there because of it. Finish the migration When the Fastify routes are gone, register the plugins on the Nest application with app.register() , turn the error handler into an exception filter, delete the legacy folder, and create the application with new FastifyAdapter() . All at once A new Nest application replaces the Fastify app in one release. Until then the Fastify app stays as it is, and it's the reference for what the new application must do. Stay on the FastifyAdapter for the migration, even if you plan to change adapters later that keeps the router, query parsing, body limits and path syntax as they are, so fewer things can change at once. Pin the API with tests Write tests that know only URLs, so that the same tests run against both applications. Go through every plugin and route, and cover each route's status code, body and important headers, for failures as well as successes. Check that fields a response schema removes stay removed Run them against the Fastify app until they all pass, before writing any Nest code Translate the application Create the Nest application with nest new next to the Fastify one, switch it to the FastifyAdapter , and move each routes plugin to a controller Fastify Nest app.register(routes, {{ '{' }} prefix {{ '}' }}) A controller, @Controller('api/orders') , in a module app.get('/ id', handler) @Get(' id') on a method request.params , request.query , request.body @Param() , @Query() , @Body() schema {{ '{' }} querystring, body, response {{ '}' }} @RouteSchema() from @nestjs/platform fastify , with the same JSON schemas onRequest app.authenticate A guard preHandler app.requireRole('admin') Metadata on the route, read by a guard A decorator such as request.jwtVerify() The same call on @Req() , with the plugin registered reply.code(201).send(x) return x , with @HttpCode() when the status isn't the default reply.code(204).send() @HttpCode(204) , and return nothing reply.redirect(url, 301) @Redirect(url, 301) reply.setCookie() @Res({{ '{' }} passthrough true {{ '}' }}) reply , then reply.setCookie() and return as usual reply.type('application/json') @Header('content type', 'application/json') reply.send(stream) new StreamableFile(stream, {{ '{' }} type {{ '}' }}) await request.file() The same call on @Req() , with @fastify/multipart registered app.register(plugin, options) app.register(plugin, options) app.addHook('onRequest', fn) app.getHttpAdapter().getInstance().addHook('onRequest', fn) setErrorHandler() and setNotFoundHandler() One global exception filter A plugin that decorates the instance with a database pool A provider Route paths stay as they are, since the same router reads them search/ term? , items/ id(^\\d+$) , and assets/ , with @Param(' ') . Keep what would change without an error Two of these expose data without any error at all, so check them first In Fastify In a Nest application To keep the old behavior A response schema removes every field it doesn't list, so handlers can return whole records Without the schema, every field is sent, passwordHash included @RouteSchema({{ '{' }} response {{ '}' }}) on each route that had one A POST answers 200 , and response {{ '{' }} 200 schema {{ '}' }} applies A POST answers 201 , so a schema keyed on 200 no longer applies, and the fields come back too @HttpCode(200) , or key the schema on 201 Authentication in onRequest runs before validation, so an invalid request with no token gets a 401 @RouteSchema({{ '{' }} body {{ '}' }}) validates before any guard, so that request gets a validation error Validate with a pipe, @Body({{ '{' }} schema {{ '}' }}) , which runs after guards, on routes where it matters Errors have the shape your handler gives them {{ '{' }} statusCode, message, error {{ '}' }} A global exception filter A validation error reaches your handler with err.validation It reaches the filter the same way, with exception.validation The same filter An unknown route gets your not found handler NotFoundException , with Nest's body The same filter The filter must keep your error shape for every error, including the ones Nest and Fastify raise themselves. Body errors such as malformed JSON and a body over the limit arrive as an HttpException Switch over Run the same tests against the Nest application, and fix the application rather than the tests When they pass, deploy it in place of the Fastify app, and keep the last Fastify release deployable until the new one has served real traffic. Give it to a coding agent Either approach works with a coding agent, and all at once is the better fit when the application is small enough to review in one change. Point the agent at this page and hold it to the tests, so that it can't declare success on code that merely compiles
recipes/cqrs: CQRS The flow of simple CRUD (Create, Read, Update and Delete) applications can be described as follows 1. The controllers layer handles HTTP requests and delegates tasks to the services layer. 2. The services layer is where most of the business logic lives. 3. Services use repositories or DAOs to change and persist entities. 4. Entities act as containers for values, with setters and getters. While this pattern is usually sufficient for small and medium sized applications, it may not be the best choice for larger, more complex ones. In such cases, the CQRS (Command and Query Responsibility Segregation) model may be more appropriate and scalable, depending on the application's requirements. Benefits of this model include Separation of concerns . Read and write operations are handled by separate models. Scalability . Read and write operations can be scaled independently. Flexibility . Reads and writes can use different data stores. Performance . Each data store can be optimized for its workload (reads or writes). To support this model, Nest provides a lightweight CQRS module. This chapter describes how to use it. Installation First, install the required package Once the installation is complete, open the root module of your application (usually AppModule ) and import CqrsModule.forRoot() forRoot() accepts an optional configuration object. To provide the options asynchronously (e.g., from a configuration service), use CqrsModule.forRootAsync() instead. The following options are available Attribute Description Default commandPublisher The publisher responsible for dispatching commands to the system. DefaultCommandPubSub eventPublisher The publisher used to publish events, allowing them to be broadcasted or processed. DefaultPubSub queryPublisher The publisher used for publishing queries, which can trigger data retrieval operations. DefaultQueryPubSub unhandledExceptionPublisher The publisher used to publish unhandled exceptions to the UnhandledExceptionBus . DefaultUnhandledExceptionPubSub eventIdProvider Service that retrieves unique event IDs from event instances. DefaultEventIdProvider rethrowUnhandled Whether exceptions thrown by event handlers and sagas are rethrown instead of being published to the UnhandledExceptionBus . false Commands Commands change the application state. They should be task based rather than data centric. When a command is dispatched, it is handled by a corresponding command handler , which is responsible for updating the application state. The code above instantiates the KillDragonCommand class and passes it to the execute() method of the CommandBus . Here is the command class The KillDragonCommand class extends the Command class, a utility class exported from the @nestjs/cqrs package that lets you define the command's return type. In this case, the return type is an object with an actionId property. Whenever the KillDragonCommand command is dispatched, the return type of the CommandBus execute() method is inferred as Promise . This is useful when the command handler returns data to the caller. info Hint Extending the Command class is optional. You only need it to define the command's return type. The CommandBus represents a stream of commands. It dispatches commands to the appropriate handlers. The execute() method returns a promise that resolves to the value returned by the handler. Let's create a handler for the KillDragonCommand command. This handler retrieves the Hero entity from the repository, calls its killEnemy() method, and then persists the changes. The KillDragonHandler class implements the ICommandHandler interface, which requires an execute() method. The execute() method receives the command object as an argument. ICommandHandler requires execute() to return a value that matches the command's return type (here, an object with an actionId property). This only applies to commands that extend the Command class. For other commands, the return type isn't constrained. Finally, register the KillDragonHandler as a provider in a module Queries Queries retrieve data from the application state. They should be data centric rather than task based. When a query is dispatched, it is handled by a corresponding query handler , which is responsible for retrieving the data. The QueryBus follows the same pattern as the CommandBus . Query handlers implement the IQueryHandler interface and are annotated with the @QueryHandler() decorator. Start with the query class Like the Command class, the Query class is a utility class exported from the @nestjs/cqrs package that lets you define the query's return type. In this case, the return type is a Hero object. Whenever the GetHeroQuery query is dispatched, the return type of the QueryBus execute() method is inferred as Promise . To retrieve the hero, create a query handler The GetHeroHandler class implements the IQueryHandler interface, which requires an execute() method. The execute() method receives the query object as an argument and must return data that matches the query's return type (in this case, a Hero object). Finally, register the GetHeroHandler as a provider in a module To dispatch the query, use the QueryBus Events Events notify other parts of the application about changes in the application state. They are dispatched by models or directly through the EventBus . When an event is dispatched, it is handled by the corresponding event handlers , which can, for example, update the read model. For demonstration purposes, let's create an event class While you can dispatch events directly with the EventBus.publish() method, you can also dispatch them from the model. Let's update the Hero model to dispatch the HeroKilledDragonEvent event when the killEnemy() method is called. The apply() method dispatches events. It accepts an event object as an argument. However, the model isn't aware of the EventBus , so you need to connect the two. The EventPublisher class does that The EventPublisher mergeObjectContext method merges the event publisher into the provided object. This object must implement the IAggregateRoot interface (or extend the AggregateRoot class). Once merged, the object can publish events to the event stream. Events applied with apply() are queued until you call the model's commit() method, which dispatches all outstanding events. To dispatch events as soon as they are applied, set the autoCommit property to true To merge the event publisher into a class rather than into an existing object, use the EventPublisher mergeClassContext method Every instance of the HeroModel class can now publish events without calling the mergeObjectContext() method. As of @nestjs/cqrs 12.1, a model's commit() , publish() and publishAll() return what the event bus returns, which is whatever the event publisher returns. The default in memory publisher returns nothing, as it doesn't wait for the event handlers. With an asynchronous publisher, such as one that writes to a message broker, await hero.commit() waits for it and throws when it fails. All three also accept a dispatcher context, which the event publisher receives in place of the model. A command handler can pass its transaction this way, for a publisher that writes through it commit() clears the model's events as soon as it hands them to the event bus, without waiting for the publisher, so calling it again never publishes the same events twice. If an awaited commit() fails, roll back and run the command again with a freshly loaded model. Flexible Aggregate Roots The AggregateRoot class is a base class that you can extend to add event driven capabilities to your domain models. However, this approach requires domain entities to extend AggregateRoot directly, which can be a limitation if your application already has an established entity inheritance hierarchy (e.g., a base Entity class or domain specific base classes such as Monster or Vehicle ). For more flexibility, the @nestjs/cqrs package supports three approaches to implementing aggregate roots Approach 1 Traditional (Class Inheritance) This is the standard approach shown in the previous examples. It works well for simple scenarios and greenfield projects. Approach 2 Mixin (For existing hierarchies) If you already have a base class and can't extend AggregateRoot directly, use the WithAggregateRoot () mixin function. It applies aggregate root behavior to any existing base class. Approach 3 Custom Implementation For maximum control, or to keep your domain layer completely framework agnostic, implement the IAggregateRoot interface directly All three approaches work with EventPublisher , which accepts any object that implements the IAggregateRoot interface. As of @nestjs/cqrs 12.1, mergeObjectContext() and mergeClassContext() give the model publish() and publishAll() methods that pass a dispatcher context on to the event bus and return its result. A custom commit() supports the dispatcher context by passing it on to publishAll() . The parameters are optional an implementation without them, whose methods return nothing, still satisfies the interface. Manual event publishing To publish an event without going through a model, call the EventBus publish() method directly info Hint The EventBus is an injectable class. Each event can have multiple event handlers . info Hint Event handlers run outside the traditional HTTP request context Errors thrown in command handlers can still be caught by the built in exception filters. Errors thrown in event handlers can't be caught by exception filters, so you have to handle them yourself with a try/catch block, with a saga that triggers a compensating event, or with another approach of your choice. The value returned by a command handler can still be sent back to the client in the HTTP response. Event handlers can't send HTTP responses. To send information to the client, use WebSockets, server sent events, or another mechanism. As with commands and queries, register the HeroKilledDragonHandler as a provider in a module Sagas A saga is a long running process that listens to events and may trigger new commands. Sagas are typically used to manage complex workflows. For example, when a user signs up, a saga may listen to the UserRegisteredEvent and send the user a welcome email. A single saga may listen for 1..\ events. With the RxJS library, you can filter, map, fork, and merge event streams to build sophisticated workflows. Each saga returns an Observable that emits command instances. Each emitted command is then dispatched asynchronously by the CommandBus . info Hint Sagas run in memory. For processes that must survive restarts, see Durable sagas. Let's create a saga that listens to the HeroKilledDragonEvent and dispatches the DropAncientItemCommand command. info Hint The ofType operator and the @Saga() decorator are exported from the @nestjs/cqrs package. The @Saga() decorator marks the property as a saga. The events$ argument is an Observable stream of all events. The ofType operator filters the stream by the specified event type, and the map operator maps each event to a new command instance. In this example, each HeroKilledDragonEvent is mapped to a DropAncientItemCommand command, which the CommandBus then dispatches automatically. As with query, command, and event handlers, register the HeroesGameSagas as a provider in a module Durable sagas Sagas and event handlers run in memory. If the process stops between an event and the command a saga dispatches, the command is never dispatched. A saga that combines several events, such as one that waits for the payment after an order and gives up after an hour, loses the events it has seen on a restart. An event published just before the transaction behind it rolls back still reaches them. When a process must survive restarts and deploys, let the events start and signal a durable workflow instead. The @nestjs/workflows/cqrs entry point maps events to workflows, so your code keeps executing commands and publishing events Until you register a store, WorkflowsModule keeps the workflows in memory. On PostgreSQL or MySQL, register the package's PostgresWorkflowStore or MySqlWorkflowStore as a provider, on the database client you already use, as Keep workflows in your database shows the workflows then live in your database, and their starts and signals can join your transactions. @StartOn() starts the workflow when an event is published, and @SignalOn() wakes the instance that waits for another one The command handler passes its transaction as the second argument of publish() , CQRS's dispatcher context. The workflow is then created in that transaction, so it exists if and only if the order was saved An aggregate's events go the same way. As of @nestjs/cqrs 12.1, pass the transaction to the aggregate's commit() in the same callback, and await it it resolves once the workflows are started and signalled. The workflow's state lives in your database, so it outlives restarts and deploys. A completed step never runs again, and a step the process died in runs again with the same idempotency key, which the command hands to the payment provider. A repeated event finds the instance the first one started. Your event handlers and sagas still receive every event, after the workflows. See Durable workflows with CQRS for the guarantees of each way of publishing, and aggregates. Unhandled exceptions Event handlers are executed asynchronously, so they must always handle exceptions properly to prevent the application from entering an inconsistent state. If an exception isn't handled, the EventBus logs it, creates an UnhandledExceptionInfo object, and pushes it to the UnhandledExceptionBus stream. The same applies to exceptions thrown by sagas and by command handlers executing commands that sagas dispatched. The UnhandledExceptionBus is an Observable that you can subscribe to in order to process unhandled exceptions. If the rethrowUnhandled option is set to true , these exceptions are rethrown instead of being published to the UnhandledExceptionBus . To handle only specific exception types, use the UnhandledExceptionBus.ofType() operator, which filters exceptions with instanceof Here, only exceptions that are instances of TransactionNotAllowedException reach the subscriber. The UnhandledExceptionInfo object contains the following properties Subscribing to all events CommandBus , QueryBus , and EventBus are all Observables . This means you can subscribe to the entire stream and, for example, process all events log them to the console or save them to an event store. Request scoping If you're coming from other programming languages, you may be surprised that in Nest, most things are shared across incoming requests a connection pool to the database, singleton services with global state, and more. Node.js doesn't follow the request/response multi threaded stateless model, in which each request is processed by a separate thread. As a result, using singleton instances is safe for your applications. However, there are edge cases where a request based lifetime for a handler is desirable, such as per request caching in GraphQL applications, request tracking, or multi tenancy. See the injection scopes chapter to learn how to control scopes. Using request scoped providers alongside CQRS can be complex because the CommandBus , QueryBus , and EventBus are singletons. The @nestjs/cqrs package handles this by automatically creating a new instance of a request scoped handler for each processed command, query, or event. To make a handler request scoped, either 1. Depend on a request scoped provider. 2. Explicitly set its scope to REQUEST in the @CommandHandler() , @QueryHandler() , or @EventsHandler() decorator, as shown To inject the request payload into a request scoped provider, use the @Inject(REQUEST) decorator ( REQUEST is exported from @nestjs/core ). In CQRS, however, the request payload depends on the context it could be an HTTP request, a scheduled job, or any other operation that triggers a command. The payload must be an instance of AsyncContext (exported from @nestjs/cqrs ) or of a class that extends it. It acts as the request context and holds data that is accessible throughout the request lifecycle. When executing a command, pass the custom request context as the second argument to the CommandBus execute() method This makes the MyRequest instance available as the REQUEST provider to the corresponding handler Queries work the same way And in the query handler For events, you can pass the request context to EventBus publish() , but this is less common. Instead, use EventPublisher to merge the request context into a model Request scoped event handlers that handle these events have access to the request context. Sagas are always singletons because they manage long running processes (registering a saga in a non singleton provider throws an exception). However, you can retrieve the request context from event objects Alternatively, call the request.attachTo(command) method to attach the request context to the command. Example A working example is available in the nest cqrs example repository.
recipes/serve-static: Serve Static To serve static content, such as a single page application (SPA), use the ServeStaticModule from the @nestjs/serve static package. Installation First, install the required package Bootstrap Once the installation is complete, import the ServeStaticModule into the root AppModule and configure it by passing a configuration object to the forRoot() method With this in place, build the static website and place its content in the location specified by the rootPath property. Configuration The ServeStaticModule accepts a variety of options to customize its behavior. For example, you can set the path at which the static app is rendered, exclude specific paths, or enable or disable the Cache Control response header. See the ServeStaticModuleOptions interface for the full list of options. warning Notice By default, renderPath matches all paths, and the module responds with the index.html file. This enables client side routing for your SPA, while routes declared in your controllers are still handled by the server. You can change this behavior by combining the serveRoot and renderPath options with the other options. With the Fastify adapter, set serveStaticOptions.fallthrough to true to mimic the Express fallthrough behavior, i.e., to send index.html instead of a 404 error for routes that don't exist. Example A working example is available in the serve static sample on GitHub.
recipes/nextjs: Next.js A Next.js application can use Nest as its backend one repository, one origin for the browser, and request schemas shared by both applications. Route handlers and Server Actions are enough for a small backend. As it grows, with background jobs, webhooks, a public API, a mobile client or a team of its own, it needs the structure that Nest gives it modules, dependency injection, guards, and validation on every route. Next.js keeps rendering, and Nest takes over everything behind it Next.js Nest Pages, layouts and Server Components The API, and the business rules behind it Forms, and the state of the browser Validating what the forms send Fetching data to render it The database, and every other data source Sign in, permissions, webhooks, queues, scheduled jobs Other clients, such as a mobile app This page sets up a Nest application next to a Next.js one, and then moves a backend from one to the other Both live in one repository, as npm workspaces. The browser calls /api on the Next.js origin, and Next.js passes the request on to Nest, so cookies work without CORS. Zod schemas in a shared package validate a form in the browser and the same request in Nest. The route handlers you already have keep answering, and move to Nest one at a time. Project layout The root package.json declares the workspaces Create both applications without installing their packages, then install everything once, from the root skip git also leaves the Nest application without a .gitignore , so add one at the root of the repository The Next.js development server takes port 3000 , so give Nest another one in apps/api/src/main.ts , and put its routes under /api , the path the browser will call Send /api to Nest Next.js rewrites pass a request on to another server and return its response, without the browser seeing a redirect. In apps/web/next.config.ts , send every /api request that the Next.js app doesn't answer itself to Nest The browser talks to one origin, the Next.js one. A cookie that Nest sets, such as a session, is stored for that origin and sent back with every request to it, so it reaches Nest and Next.js alike, and Nest needs no CORS configuration. fallback rewrites run after Next.js has checked all of its pages and route handlers, dynamic ones included. So an existing route handler, such as src/app/api/orders/[id]/route.ts , keeps answering its requests, and only the rest reach Nest. An /api path that neither app has gets Nest's 404 response. An afterFiles rewrite would run before dynamic routes, and pass that route handler's requests to Nest. Set API URL for development in apps/web/.env.development warning Warning Next.js reads rewrites() when it builds the application, so API URL must also be set for next build a different value when the application starts doesn't change where its rewrites go. Everything an API does goes through the rewrite untouched cookies, raw request bodies for webhook signatures, server sent events as they're written, and WebSockets with the ws adapter. Two limits fail badly, with a 500 and no useful error a request body over 10 MB, and a response that takes more than 30 seconds to start, such as a call to a language model. Raise them with two experimental options of Next.js Nest also sees the Next.js server as the client, so req.ip is its address, and anything that limits requests per IP address, such as @nestjs/throttler , treats all your visitors as one. Next.js doesn't add X Forwarded For itself, but it passes on the one set by a load balancer in front of it. If you have one, call app.set('trust proxy', 1) on the NestExpressApplication . Without one, leave it off, or a visitor can claim any address. Share schemas between the apps Nest validates a request body against any Standard Schema schema, such as a Zod one (see Schema based validation). Put the schemas in a package of their own, packages/contracts , and the Next.js app validates its forms with the very schema that Nest checks the request against, and both use the types inferred from it. The package is compiled, so that both applications import plain JavaScript and its type declarations. Add it to both applications, and build it ( npm run dev w @acme/contracts rebuilds it on every change) In Nest, bind the StandardSchemaValidationPipe and pass the schema to @Body() In Next.js, a form checks its input with the same schema before it sends anything A request that doesn't come from your form, from a script or an older version of the app, is still checked, by Nest To run everything with one command, add concurrently to the root, and two scripts to its package.json . The shared package has to be built before the applications that import it Sign users in Sign in belongs to Nest, since the API is what it protects. @nestjs/authentication keeps the session in an HttpOnly cookie, and a form signs in by posting to /api/auth/sign in through the rewrite, like any other request from the browser. That chapter builds it, and one setting is specific to running behind Next.js. The module ignores a session cookie on a POST from another origin, and refuses sign ins from one, to stop cross site request forgery. Behind a rewrite, Nest's own host is localhost 3001 while the browser's Origin is http //localhost 3000 . Browsers that send Sec Fetch Site pass anyway, but a client that sends only Origin gets a 403 . So name the Next.js origin as trusted Requests from any other origin are still refused. Call Nest from the Next.js server Server Components and Server Actions run on the Next.js server, so they call Nest directly, without the rewrite. The browser's cookies don't go with those requests unless you forward them, so put that in one helper warning Warning A page that fetches without reading cookies may be rendered during next build , so Nest has to be reachable from the build, or it fails with fetch failed . Migrate a Next.js backend to Nest Next.js's own backend guide says that its backend capabilities "are not a full backend replacement". A Next.js backend works well until it has to be one, and past that point a separate backend can be the simpler of the two. Why it can be simpler It isn't less code. The same four endpoints (list, create, read and cancel an order, for a signed in user) came to about the same number of lines in route handlers as in a Nest controller and service. What changes is what you have to remember Route handlers Nest Checking the session In every handler, four times here. A handler that forgets is public Once, in a global guard. A new route answers 401 until you mark it @Public() Validating a body Each handler parses it and builds its own 400 @Body({{ '{' }} schema {{ '}' }}) , and the handler only runs with valid input A missing record Each handler builds its own 404 , and a helper can't end the request for it throw new NotFoundException() from anywhere, such as a service Testing the logic Handlers read cookies() , which throws was called outside a request scope , so a test has to mock next/headers A service is a class new OrdersService() , with no HTTP and no mocks of the framework Finding an endpoint One file per path, with the path in the folder names One controller per resource Scheduled jobs Nothing built in, so a platform has to call a URL @Cron() , in the same process as the rest of the application WebSockets Won't work where handlers are deployed as lambda functions, says the same guide Gateways Here's one of those four endpoints in both. As a route handler The other handlers repeat its first lines. In Nest, the guard has already checked the session, and the service holds the rule, where the other methods can reuse it and a test can reach it You can get part of the way with helpers a withSession() wrapper, then one for validation, then one that turns errors into responses. That's a reasonable step, and it's also writing your own guards, pipes and exception filters. It does cost something. There's a second application to deploy, a rewrite to configure, and a network hop between a Server Component and its data. If your backend is a few handlers with one client and no background work, stay on route handlers. What goes where Write new endpoints in Nest, and move the existing ones when you next change them. Each piece of a Next.js backend has a place to go In Next.js In Nest A route handler A controller method A database query in a Server Component or a Server Action A service behind an endpoint, called through api() getSession() at the top of every handler The global guard of @nestjs/authentication , and @CurrentUser() Checking request.json() by hand @Body({{ '{' }} schema {{ '}' }}) Role checks inside handlers @nestjs/authorization A webhook route handler that reads request.text() @VerifyWebhook() from @nestjs/webhooks A cron route called by the platform @Cron() from @nestjs/schedule Work started with after() , such as sending email A queue, and @nestjs/mail Move one route Write the endpoint in Nest under the same path, and delete the route handler. The URL doesn't change, so neither does any client. Because route handlers come before the rewrite, both can be in the code until you delete the route handler. Then check what a client can see The status code. NextResponse.json() answers 200 on a POST , and a Nest POST answers 201 unless you add @HttpCode(200) . The shape of an error , which is now {{ '{' }} statusCode, message, error {{ '}' }} . A global exception filter keeps the old shape if clients depend on it. Dynamic segments. [id] becomes id , and a catch all [...path] becomes path , whose @Param('path') is an array of segments. Move queries out of pages A Server Component or a Server Action that queries the database directly makes a request instead, and the query moves to a Nest service When nothing in apps/web imports the database client any more, remove it from the Next.js application, so that a page can't go around the API. Deployment The two applications deploy separately. Whatever the platform, the order is the same build @acme/contracts , then the applications, with API URL set for next build . Nest runs anywhere Node.js does (see Deployment). If you deploy the Next.js application on Vercel, set API URL in its environment to Nest's address. Vercel can deploy Nest too, as a project of its own. Other clients, such as a mobile app, call Nest's address directly, and need a CORS configuration only if they run in a browser on another origin.
recipes/supabase: Supabase Supabase gives an application a Postgres database, sign in, file storage and an API that the browser can call directly, which covers a lot without a backend. What it leaves out is the work that needs a secret, a retry or a clock Stripe webhooks, scheduled jobs, queues, an admin API. Nest takes on that work next to Supabase, on the same database and for the same users. Stays in Supabase Goes in Nest Sign up, sign in and password resets Checking who is calling, and what they may do Postgres, its migrations and row level security Business rules, and queries that span many tables Browser reads and writes that row level security covers Anything that needs a secret payments, email, other APIs Storage and Realtime Stripe webhooks, scheduled jobs, queues and an admin API The browser keeps calling Supabase directly for what row level security covers, and calls Nest with the same access token for the rest. If a short function or two is all you need, Edge Functions may be enough, with no server to run. They have limits on CPU time and duration and nowhere to run a queue's worker, so Nest fits better once you have jobs, queues or many routes that share code. This recipe builds such an application on the local Supabase stack, so that you can run each step as you read. The finished module shows how the pieces are wired together. Create the projects The local stack needs Docker. npx supabase status o env prints the stack's URLs and keys. Put API URL , PUBLISHABLE KEY , SECRET KEY and DB URL in .env , under the names this recipe reads warning Warning The secret key bypasses row level security. It belongs on the server only, and never in anything you ship to a browser or a mobile app. info Hint A hosted project has the same keys in its dashboard. Supabase is deprecating the older anon and service role keys by the end of 2026, so use these two. Load .env with @nestjs/config Keep it first in imports , as the modules you'll add after it read process.env as they're declared. A module declared in another file reads it earlier, when the file is imported, so use forRootAsync() for what you register there. Define a table The schema stays in Supabase's migrations Write the table in the file this creates under supabase/migrations , with a policy that lets users reach only their own rows. auth.uid() is the user the request's access token belongs to Apply it to the local database warning Warning Supabase's API serves the tables in the public schema to anyone with the publishable key, and that key is in your browser code. Enable row level security on every table you create there, including those only Nest uses. With it enabled and no policy, the key reads nothing. Verify Supabase tokens Supabase Auth signs an access token for each signed in user, and publishes the public keys that verify it. @nestjs/authentication can verify tokens from another issuer, so Nest needs no secret from Supabase to know who is calling The role comes from app metadata , which only your server can change. A signed in user can change their own user metadata with supabase.auth.updateUser() , so never base a decision on it. Register the module and the provider The module registers a global guard, so every route now answers 401 Unauthorized without a valid token, including one with a bad signature, another issuer or audience, or an expired one. Mark a route that stays open with @Public() , and read the user with @CurrentUser() info Hint A project still on the legacy JWT secret signs tokens with it and publishes no keys. Pass key process.env.SUPABASE JWT SECRET instead of jwks , until you migrate to signing keys. Call Nest from the browser The browser sends the access token that Supabase gave it. getSession() refreshes the token when it has expired If the browser calls Nest on another origin, allow that origin when the application starts Query as the user, or as the server @supabase/supabase js is a client for your database's REST API. Generate types from your schema, so that a query on a table or a column that doesn't exist fails to compile, and run this again after each migration Create one client for the server, and one per request for the user. A client holds no database connection, so that's cheap A small decorator reads the token that the guard has already verified Prefer forUser() in a route that acts for a user. Your policies keep applying, so a query that forgets a filter still returns only that user's rows, and an insert for someone else is refused Use admin for what the server does on its own behalf, where no user is involved, as in a job or a webhook. Query Postgres directly For transactions and for queries that the REST API can't express, connect to the database with @nestjs/drizzle or another database integration. The webhooks and jobs below use this connection too Locally, DATABASE URL is the stack's DB URL . On a hosted project, Nest is a persistent backend, so use the direct connection string, or the shared pooler in session mode if your host only has IPv4. The pooler's transaction mode doesn't support prepared statements, nor the LISTEN that BullMQ's PostgreSQL backend uses. Supabase's migrations stay the source of truth, so the Drizzle schema only describes the tables to query warning Warning Row level security doesn't protect these queries. The postgres role bypasses it, so a query with no filter returns every user's rows, and each query has to check the owner itself. To keep your policies on a direct query instead, run it in a transaction as the authenticated role, with the claims that auth.uid() reads Both settings end with the transaction, so they never reach the next query on that connection. Here's each way side by side, with @CurrentSession() giving a route the verified claims Protect an admin API An admin API is what the browser can't do itself, as it needs the secret key. Keep a user's role in app metadata , which SupabaseAuth already reads, and set it from the server The role is in the user's next token, so someone already signed in gets it when their token refreshes, within an hour by default. Check it with @nestjs/authorization Register the module with AuthorizationModule.forRoot({{ '{' }} globalGuard false {{ '}' }}) , and AdminPolicy in providers . Its global guard is on by default and denies every route that has no @Can() , which would also close the routes above. A guest gets 401 , a user without the role 403 . Receive Stripe webhooks @nestjs/webhooks verifies a webhook's signature and remembers which events it has processed. It keeps its state in your database, through @nestjs/outbox , in schemas of their own. Supabase's API doesn't serve those schemas, so they stay private The signature covers the exact bytes that Stripe sent, so create the application with rawBody Name the sender in the module's receivers , with the signing secret from the Stripe dashboard or from stripe listen . This application only receives webhooks, so it needs neither of the background workers Register the two stores in providers . migrate true creates their schemas at startup, which suits development (see Deployment for production) Add a table for what the webhook changes. Only Nest reads it, and the policy less row level security keeps it from the browser. Add it to a new migration The route is @Public() , as the signature is what authenticates it, and an invalid one gets 401 . processInTransaction() records the event's id in the same transaction as your change, so a redelivery changes nothing To try it, forward events to your application with the Stripe CLI, which prints the signing secret to put in STRIPE WEBHOOK SECRET Run scheduled jobs There are two ways to run a job in Nest. Both work on any number of instances, and each run happens on one of them @nestjs/schedule with @nestjs/locks BullMQ Where it runs In the instance that holds the lease In a worker that picks it up If a run fails It waits for the next tick It retries, with a backoff If every instance is down The tick is missed The job waits in the queue What it adds to Postgres One table A schema of its own What else it does Nothing else Jobs enqueued from your code, priorities and flows Choose it for A job that's safe to skip, as the next tick catches up A job that mustn't be lost, or runs for long Both can call the same code info Hint Supabase Cron schedules SQL inside Postgres, with no application involved. It's a good fit for a job that's only SQL, such as deleting old rows. With @nestjs/schedule and @nestjs/locks @nestjs/schedule runs a job inside the application, next to the code it calls. On its own, it runs the job on every instance. @nestjs/locks adds @OnOneInstance() the first instance to fire takes a lease and runs every tick while it's up, and the others skip them. When it stops, another takes over, about a second after a clean shutdown and within 30 seconds after a crash The lease has to live somewhere that all instances share, and in production the application refuses to start with only the default in memory store. Keep it in your database, with a table in a new migration Then copy the Drizzle table and DrizzleLockStore from Keep locks in your database, and add the store to providers . With BullMQ BullMQ keeps jobs in a queue, with retries and a backoff. It usually runs on Redis, and it also has a PostgreSQL backend, so on Supabase it can use the database you already have migrate true creates the bullmq schema at startup, which Supabase's API doesn't serve. The migration takes an advisory lock, so several instances starting together apply it once. info Hint To use Redis, install ioredis and replace those options with connection {{ '{' }} host, port {{ '}' }} . Nothing else changes. A job scheduler creates the job on each tick. The id makes it one schedule, however many instances declare it The processor runs it, on whichever instance is free The same queue takes jobs from your own code, such as a route that shouldn't wait for an email. Inject it with @InjectQueue('billing') , and add a case for the job to the processor Hand out file uploads A browser can upload to Supabase Storage directly, under policies on the storage.objects table. When the decision belongs on the server, such as a quota or a paid plan, keep the bucket private and let Nest sign each upload. Create the bucket in a migration The browser then uploads straight to Supabase, so the file never passes through your application To hand a file back, createSignedUrl(path, 60) on the admin client makes a link that works for 60 seconds. Test against the local stack An end to end test can use real tokens and your real policies, as the stack gives you both. Put it in test/ , and run npx supabase start and npx supabase db reset before it Move an Edge Function to Nest Most of a function has a direct counterpart, and you can move them one at a time, as both use the same tokens and database In an Edge Function In Nest Reading the Authorization header and calling supabase.auth.getUser() SupabaseAuth and @CurrentUser() A client created with the caller's header SupabaseService.forUser() A client created with the secret key SupabaseService.admin Verifying Stripe's signature by hand @VerifyWebhook('stripe') pg cron calling the function over HTTP @Cron() , or a BullMQ job scheduler supabase secrets set Your host's environment variables supabase.functions.invoke('name') in the browser fetch() with the access token The finished module Here's everything above wired together, with both ways of running a job, of which you'll keep one enableShutdownHooks() lets a running job finish and passes its lease on when a deploy stops an instance. Deployment Nest deploys separately from Supabase, on anything that runs Node.js (see Deployment). Host it close to your database's region, as every query crosses that distance. Apply your migrations to the hosted project Set the same environment variables on your host, with the hosted project's values and the connection string from Query Postgres directly. Each instance opens its own connections, for Drizzle and for BullMQ, so count them against your project's connection limit. The webhook stores shouldn't change a schema while a new version boots, in the middle of a rolling deploy. Remove migrate true from those two, and apply their migrations as a step before the new version starts, with DATABASE URL set. BullMQ's can stay, as it runs in one transaction under an advisory lock
recipes/nest-commander: Nest Commander Expanding on the standalone applications chapter, the nest commander package lets you write command line applications with a structure similar to a typical Nest application. info Note nest commander is a third party package and is not managed by the NestJS core team. Please report any issues with the library in the nest commander repository. Installation First, install the package A Command file nest commander lets you write command line applications with decorators the @Command() decorator for classes and the @Option() decorator for methods of those classes. Every command class should extend the CommandRunner abstract class and be decorated with the @Command() decorator. Nest treats every command as an @Injectable() , so dependency injection works as usual. The CommandRunner abstract class ensures that every command has a run() method that returns a Promise and takes the parameters string[], Record . The run() method is where your command's logic starts. Its first argument is an array of all parameters that didn't match an option flag, in case you need to work with multiple parameters. In the second argument, the options object, the property names match the name property given to the @Option() decorators, and their values are the return values of the corresponding option handlers. For better type safety, you can also create an interface for your options. Running the Command In a NestJS application, you use the NestFactory to create a server and run it with listen() . Similarly, the nest commander package exposes an API to run your command line application import the CommandFactory , call its static run() method, and pass in the root module of your application By default, Nest's logger is disabled when using the CommandFactory . To enable it, pass a logger as the second argument to the run() method. You can provide either a custom NestJS logger or an array of the log levels you want to keep. For example, pass ['error'] to print only Nest's error logs. Under the hood, CommandFactory calls NestFactory for you and calls app.close() when the command finishes, so you don't need to worry about memory leaks. To add error handling, wrap the run() call in a try/catch block, or chain a .catch() call to the bootstrap() call. Testing nest commander provides testing utilities that fit in with the rest of the NestJS ecosystem. Instead of using the CommandFactory to build the command in test mode, use the CommandTestFactory from the nest commander testing package and pass in your module metadata, similarly to how Test.createTestingModule() from @nestjs/testing works. In fact, it uses @nestjs/testing under the hood. You can still chain overrideProvider() calls before calling compile() to swap out providers in the test. Putting it all together The following class defines a CLI command that can take the subcommand basic or be called directly. It supports the n , s , and b flags (along with their long forms), with a custom parser for each option. The help flag is also supported, as is customary with commander. Make sure the command class is added to a module Then, to run the CLI, add the following to your main.ts file You now have a command line application. More Information Visit the nest commander docs site for more information, examples, and API documentation.
recipes/async-local-storage: Async Local Storage AsyncLocalStorage is a Node.js API (based on the async hooks API) that provides an alternative way of propagating local state through the application without explicitly passing it as a function parameter. It's similar to thread local storage in other languages. The main idea of Async Local Storage is that you can wrap a function call with the AsyncLocalStorage run call. All code invoked within the wrapped call gets access to the same store , which is unique to each call chain. In the context of NestJS, this means that if you find a place within the request's lifecycle to wrap the rest of the request's code, you can access and modify state visible only to that request. This can serve as an alternative to REQUEST scoped providers, avoiding some of their limitations. Alternatively, you can use ALS to propagate context for only a part of the system (e.g., the transaction object) without passing it around explicitly across services, which can increase isolation and encapsulation. If your application is instrumented with NestJS Observe, you already have a request scoped store and don't need to build one. See the NestJS Observe section below. Custom implementation The NestJS core framework doesn't provide a built in abstraction for AsyncLocalStorage , so let's walk through how to implement it yourself for the simplest HTTP case, to get a better understanding of the whole concept info Hint For ready made solutions, see the @nestjs/observe and nestjs cls sections below. 1. First, create a new instance of AsyncLocalStorage in a shared source file. Since we're using NestJS, let's also turn it into a module with a custom provider. info Hint AsyncLocalStorage is imported from node async hooks . 2. We're only concerned with HTTP, so let's use a middleware to wrap the next function with AsyncLocalStorage run . Since middleware is the first thing a request hits, this makes the store available in all enhancers and the rest of the system. 3. Now you can access the local store instance anywhere within the lifecycle of a request. 4. You now have a way to share request related state without injecting the whole REQUEST object. warning Warning While this technique is useful for many use cases, it inherently obscures the code flow (by creating implicit context), so use it responsibly, and especially avoid creating contextual "God objects". NestJS Observe If you run NestJS Observe, the @nestjs/observe SDK already maintains an AsyncLocalStorage store for every request, job, and message it instruments. This store carries the trace context through your call stack. TracerService exposes it, so request scoped state is something you read and write rather than something you set up there's no module to write, no middleware to mount, and nothing to re wire per transport. info Hint This is the same TracerService documented in Manual instrumentation. This section covers only its async local storage side; spans, handled errors, and custom metrics are described there. Setup No setup is needed beyond the standard SDK integration described in Observability → SDK install the package, import ObserveModule.forRoot() , and pass ObserveInstrument to NestFactory.create() . ObserveModule exports TracerService , so you can inject it anywhere in your application Reading and writing the store setAttribute(key, value) writes to the current context store, and getAttribute(key) reads the value back from anywhere downstream on the same request (a different service, a guard, or an interceptor) without threading it through every function signature getAttribute() returns undefined for a key that was never set. Both methods throw when called outside a traced context, since there's no store to read from or write to. If a value may legitimately be read before any request exists, guard the call accordingly. Typing the store Pass the shape of your store as the first type argument of TracerService to have keys and values type checked, including nested paths Beyond HTTP Because the store is created by the instrumentation rather than by a middleware, it exists wherever the SDK traces an operation HTTP and GraphQL requests, gRPC and @nestjs/microservices messages, and background work such as BullMQ consumers and cron runs. The pattern above is identical in all of them. This is the practical difference from a hand rolled, middleware based implementation, which only covers HTTP. The store also holds the current trace ID, so it doubles as the correlation key for logs and downstream services. currentTraceId() returns it. Unlike getAttribute() , it returns null outside a traced context instead of throwing info Hint ObserveModule also exports the underlying AsyncLocalStorage instance. setAttribute() and getAttribute() are the supported way to access the store; inject the instance directly only if you need something they don't expose. NestJS CLS The nestjs cls package provides several developer experience improvements over plain AsyncLocalStorage ( CLS is an abbreviation of continuation local storage ). It abstracts the implementation into a ClsModule that offers various ways of initializing the store for different transports (not only HTTP), as well as strong typing support. You can then access the store with an injectable ClsService , or abstract it away from the business logic entirely by using Proxy Providers. info Note nestjs cls is a third party package and is not managed by the NestJS core team. Please report any issues with the library in the nestjs cls repository. Installation Apart from peer dependencies on the @nestjs packages, it uses only built in Node.js APIs. Install it like any other package Usage You can implement functionality similar to the custom implementation above using nestjs cls , as follows 1. Import the ClsModule in the root module. 2. Then use the ClsService to access the store values. 3. To get strong typing of the store values managed by the ClsService (and auto suggestions for the string keys), use the optional type parameter ClsService when injecting it. info Hint You can also let the package automatically generate a request ID and access it later with cls.getId() , or get the whole request object using cls.get(CLS REQ) . Testing Since the ClsService is just another injectable provider, you can mock it out entirely in unit tests. However, in certain integration tests, you might still want to use the real ClsService implementation. In that case, wrap the context aware piece of code with a call to ClsService run or ClsService runWith More information Visit the nestjs cls GitHub page for the full API documentation and more code examples.
recipes/socket-activation: Socket activation With socket activation, the service manager opens the listening socket for your application. systemd listens on the port, starts the application when the first connection arrives, and hands the socket over to it. Connections that arrive while the application starts or restarts wait in the kernel's queue instead of being refused. This is useful for services that are called rarely, such as internal tools, admin panels, or the many services of a development or staging machine. If the application also exits after some time without requests, such a service holds no memory while nobody uses it. The cost is a cold start the first request after a pause waits until Node.js loads the application and Nest bootstraps it. info Hint Listening on a socket passed by the service manager is a feature of Node.js's server.listen() . It is not supported on Windows. systemd units Create a socket unit, for example /etc/systemd/system/my app.socket Next to it, create a service unit with the same name, /etc/systemd/system/my app.service Then enable the socket only. systemd starts my app.service on the first connection warning Warning Start node directly in ExecStart . systemd passes the socket as file descriptor 3 and sets the LISTEN FDS and LISTEN PID environment variables, where LISTEN PID is the ID of the process it started. With npm start , nest start , or a shell script in between, LISTEN PID doesn't match your application's process. The bootstrap below then falls back to listening on the port, which fails with EADDRINUSE because systemd already holds it. info Hint To try it without unit files, run systemd socket activate listen=3000 node dist/main.js . It passes the socket the same way, but starts the application only once. It also doesn't forward variables such as NODE ENV unless you name them with setenv=NODE ENV . Bootstrap In your main.ts file, listen on the passed socket when the application was started this way, and on a port otherwise The Express and Node adapters pass the options object to Node.js's server.listen() as is, but their listen() typings accept only a port, hence the cast. The Fastify adapter accepts fd in its typed listen options Exiting when idle systemd doesn't stop the application on its own. To free its memory, let the application exit after some time without requests, and systemd starts it again on the next connection. The following helper counts in flight requests on the underlying HTTP server, so it works with every adapter and also sees requests that never reach a route handler Call it once the application listens on the passed socket app.close() runs the same shutdown hooks as enableShutdownHooks() does when systemd stops the service with SIGTERM . Exit code 0 tells systemd that the service stopped cleanly, so Restart=on failure doesn't start it again. systemd keeps its own copy of the socket open, so a connection that arrives while the application exits waits for the next start. The helper counts HTTP requests only. A server sent events stream counts until the client disconnects, but an open WebSocket connection doesn't. If your application uses WebSockets, also count the sockets of the server's upgrade event until they close. Things to keep in mind Use Restart=on failure , not Restart=always . With always , systemd starts the application again right after it exits on idle. Health checks and uptime monitors that send requests to the application start it and keep it running. Scheduled jobs (see Task scheduling) and queue consumers don't run while the application is stopped. Run them in a process that stays up. The first request after a pause waits for the whole bootstrap, including database connections opened by async providers. The Serverless chapter shows ways to shorten it. Node.js can also reuse its compile cache between starts add Environment=NODE COMPILE CACHE=/var/cache/my app and CacheDirectory=my app to the service unit. Node.js writes the cache when the process exits, and a process killed by SIGTERM without enableShutdownHooks() doesn't write it.
recipes/express-migration: Migrating from Express An Express application can move to Nest one route at a time, with both serving requests, or all at once, in a single release. This page covers both. Choose an approach Question One route at a time All at once How does it work? Nest runs on your Express app, and routes move to it one by one A new Nest application replaces the Express app in one release What gets deployed? Each moved route, on its own Everything, once What happens to feature work? It continues, and new endpoints go into Nest It waits, or gets written twice, until the switch How do you go back? Restore one route Deploy the last Express release Which Express version? Express 5, so upgrade first Any, since the Express app isn't touched What about existing middleware? It keeps running, for Nest's routes too It moves to Nest with everything else How long are there two styles in the code? Until the last route moves Never Move one route at a time when the application is large, when several people work on it, or when it can't wait. Move it all at once when it's small enough to review as one change and you can pin what it does with tests. That also suits a coding agent, which can translate a whole application in one go, but can't tell on its own what must stay the same. One route at a time The Express app keeps its routes, middleware and error handler, new endpoints are written in Nest, and existing ones move over when you next change them. Both answer on the same port, behind the same middleware, so clients, sessions and authentication don't notice, and every step can be deployed on its own. Requirements Express 5. Nest's Express adapter drives an Express 5 application, and an Express 4 one fails as soon as Nest starts. Upgrade the app first, with Express's migration guide and its codemod, npx @expressjs/codemod upgrade . TypeScript. The Nest code on this page is TypeScript. If the Express app is written in JavaScript, its files can stay as they are TypeScript's allowJs option compiles them with the rest. A CommonJS app can stay CommonJS. Nest's packages are ESM, which a CommonJS application loads on the Node.js versions listed in the migration guide. Install Nest next to Express Run Nest on the Express app Nest normally creates its own Express app. Give it yours instead. Stop the Express app from listening, and export a function that builds it, so that tests can build their own Then pass it to the ExpressAdapter , and let Nest listen Express runs its middleware and routes in the order they were added. Everything the Express app added comes first. Nest adds its routes when the application starts, in listen() or init() , and then a handler that answers the requests no route matched with a 404 . So The Express routes answer as they did before. Nest's routes answer the requests the Express routes don't. Nest's routes see what the Express middleware put on the request, such as req.user , and the body its parsers read. A request for a route neither has gets Nest's 404 response. warning Warning Remove a catch all 404 handler, such as app.use((req, res) = res.status(404).send()) , from the Express app. It comes before Nest's routes, so it answers their requests too, and Nest's handler answers unknown routes in its place. Keep the error handler an Express error handler only receives the errors of the middleware and routes added before it, so it keeps handling the Express routes' errors, while Nest's exception filters handle the errors of Nest's. Which part of the application runs for which routes Part Express routes Nest routes Middleware added to the Express app (body parsers, sessions, authentication) Yes Yes The Express app's error handler Yes No Middleware added through Nest MiddlewareConsumer , app.use() , app.enableCors() No Yes Guards, interceptors, pipes and exception filters No Yes The middleware the Express app already runs is in front of Nest's routes as well, so a guard can check the user that the existing authentication middleware put on the request info Hint With a global prefix, Nest's 404 handler answers only the paths under the prefix. A path outside it that no Express route matches gets Express's default 404 page. Move a route Write new endpoints in Nest. To move an existing one, write it as a Nest route and delete it from the Express router. Because the Express routes come first, a Nest route with the same method and path doesn't answer until the Express one is gone, so both can be in the code until you're ready to switch GET /orders is still answered by Express, and GET /orders/ id falls through the Express router to Nest. End to end tests cover both kinds of route when the test application is built on the Express app too. Pass the adapter to createNestApplication() , and the same test checks a route before and after it moves Share code between the two The Express app already has objects that Nest code needs, such as a database pool, repositories, or a mailer. Register them as value providers, so that Nest injects the same instances the Express code uses Import LegacyModule once in AppModule , and any provider can inject OrdersRepository by its class. It works the other way too. Once NestFactory.create() returns, app.get() returns any provider, so a route that stays in Express can call logic that has already moved into a Nest service. Add the route before listen() , and it comes before Nest's routes like the rest of the Express app Finish the migration When the Express routers are empty, move what's left of the Express app into Nest middleware into Nest middleware or app.use() , and the error handler into an exception filter. Then delete the legacy folder, and create the application without an adapter argument All at once A new Nest application replaces the Express app in one release. Until then the Express app stays as it is, on whichever version of Express it runs, and it's the reference for what the new application must do. Most of the risk isn't in the translation, because a wrong translation usually fails loudly. It's in what changes without an error a status code, the shape of an error response, how a query string is parsed. So the migration starts with tests that notice those changes. Pin the API with tests Write tests that know only URLs, so that the same tests run against both applications. Go through every router and app.use() call, and cover each route's status code, body and important headers, for failures as well as successes Run them against the Express app until they all pass, before writing any Nest code Translate the application Create the Nest application with nest new next to the Express one, and move each router to a controller Express Nest express.Router() for a resource A controller in a module ( nest generate resource ) router.get('/ id', handler) @Get(' id') on a method req.params , req.query , req.body @Param() , @Query() , @Body() Validating req.body by hand A schema or a DTO, or keep the check if the tests pin its status and message Authentication middleware that sets req.user A guard that sets it, and a custom decorator that reads it requireRole('admin') Metadata on the route, read by a guard router.param('id', load) A pipe @Param('id', OrderByIdPipe) . No client should depend on those, so accept them rather than pinning old versions of Express's libraries to reproduce them. The filter and main.ts hold most of it. They must keep your error shape for every error, including the ones Nest raises itself, so check which of them your tests expect. This filter, for example, reports any BadRequestException as malformed JSON Switch over Run the same tests against the Nest application, and fix the application rather than the tests When they pass, deploy it in place of the Express app, and keep the last Express release deployable until the new one has served real traffic. Give it to a coding agent Either approach works with a coding agent, and all at once is the better fit when the application is small enough to review in one change.
